meta.description: Candidate backlog for quotle.info ingestion. Documented misattribution/famous-quote targets from Wikiquote + Quote Investigator, harvested by the harvest-candidates Workflow. Managed by tools/harvest.js — do not hand-edit counts. Lifecycle: queued → selected → ingested (or skipped).

candidates.quote: Friendship is born at that moment when one man says to another "What! You too? I thought that no one but myself . . .
candidates.trueOrigin: C. S. Lewis
candidates.whyNotable: The modern canonical line on how friendships actually begin — recognition of a shared inner world; no public-domain equal captures the moment of discovery.

candidates.quote: No great idea in its beginning can ever be within the law.
candidates.trueOrigin: A condensed paraphrase of Goldman's own 1917 Address to the Jury: 'Never can a new idea move within the law... The law is stationary, fixed, mechanical, "a chariot wheel" which grinds all alike...' Substance is hers; the popular wording is not.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as Goldman verbatim, but Wikiquote flags the popular wording as a modern gloss on her 1917 address to the jury, where she actually said 'Never can a new idea move within the law' — the real, longer sentence is documented in the speech transcript.

candidates.quote: I'd rather have roses on my table than diamonds on my neck.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown. No appearance in any Goldman text located; carried entirely by aggregator sites. Wikiquote moved it to the Talk page's 'Unsourced' list in the 2009 purge and it has never been sourced back.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-printed 'Goldman' lines in gift-shop and florist copy, yet it survives only on quote aggregators — Wikiquote lists it among the unsourced quotations removed from her page for want of any reliable and precise source.

candidates.quote: If voting changed anything, they'd make it illegal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; earliest documented use is a 1976 Robert S. Borden op-ed in The Sun (Lowell, MA). Also wrongly pinned on Mark Twain and Philip Berrigan. Variants: 'If voting changed anything, it would be made illegal' / 'If voting made any difference, they wouldn't let us do it.'
candidates.whyNotable: A protest-placard staple credited to Goldman for decades with zero evidence; Wikiquote's Disputed section traces the earliest known appearance to a 1976 opinion piece by Robert S. Borden in The Sun (Lowell, Massachusetts) — 36 years after Goldman died.

candidates.quote: Women need not always keep their mouths shut and their wombs open.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unpinned. Goldman was jailed in 1916 for birth-control lecturing, so the sentiment is genuinely hers, but the earliest documented instance of this wording is a 1976 poster in the Schlesinger Library Poster collection (Gr-15, Oversize folder 7B), Radcliffe Institute.
candidates.whyNotable: A cornerstone quote of reproductive-rights iconography whose earliest traceable appearance is not Goldman at all but a 1976 movement poster held by Harvard's Schlesinger Library; no primary Goldman text carrying the wording has been found.

candidates.quote: Famous for being famous.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Godfrey Leland used the phrase in 1896 ('an actress famous for being famous, nothing more'); Daniel J. Boorstin popularised the modern idea in The Image (1962) as 'The celebrity is a person who is known for his well-knownness.' Warhol attracted the credit because the phrase was repeatedly applied TO him — e.g. The Guardian in 1974.
candidates.whyNotable: The standard shorthand for modern celebrity, routinely handed to Warhol, but QI dates it to 1896 and shows Warhol was its subject rather than its author.

candidates.quote: Art is what you can get away with.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marshall McLuhan — the line 'Art is anything you can get away with' appears in The Medium Is the Massage (McLuhan and Quentin Fiore, 1967), with a February 1967 newspaper preview of the book already citing it. Wikiquote lists the Warhol form on its Unsourced pile with no citation.
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly pinned on Warhol as the ultimate pop-art credo; QI traces it to McLuhan in 1967, and the confusion is helped by Warhol and McLuhan being 1960s media-theory contemporaries.

candidates.quote: We go to openings of envelopes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Gossip columnist Jack O'Brian coined the gag in 1974, writing that Sylvia Miles 'attended half a dozen openings, including one envelope, two appendectomies and a cellar door.' Warhol adopted it about himself in 1977 ('We go to openings of envelopes, openings of books — which are better — and closings of doors'), which is how he became its popular author.
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive joke about celebrity over-exposure, now credited to Warhol by default; QI shows he was the populariser, not the originator.

candidates.quote: Our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure.
candidates.trueOrigin: Sogyal Rinpoche, The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying (1992) — his own formulation, loosely riffing on Rilke's dragons-into-princesses passage. No such sentence exists anywhere in Rilke.
candidates.whyNotable: The single best-documented fake Rilke line: quote researcher Gerald Krieghofer traces its first appearance to Sogyal Rinpoche's 1992 bestseller, which introduced it as something 'the Western poet Rainer Maria Rilke has said', and the German translators then dropped the footnote entirely — and it pairs perfectly with the real Rilke dragon passage as a hub.

candidates.quote: Don't pay any attention to what they write about you. Just measure it in inches.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Warhol source; Wikiquote carries it on its Unsourced list. It is a variant of an older press-agent maxim about column inches that circulated long before Warhol.
candidates.whyNotable: The go-to quote for PR and personal-branding decks, always credited to Warhol, and Wikiquote has never been able to source it.

candidates.quote: Don't think about making art, just get it done. Let everyone else decide if it's good or bad, whether they love it or hate it. While they are deciding, make even more art.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Warhol source. Wikiquote parks it on its Unsourced list. Aggregators point vaguely at Christopher Makos's Warhol Memoir (2003), a second-hand recollection published sixteen years after Warhol's death, not a Warhol text.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-shared 'Warhol' quote on art-and-creativity social media, and it is the top entry on Wikiquote's Unsourced pile for him — no citation has ever been produced.

candidates.quote: I am a deeply superficial person.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified source. Wikiquote lists it as Unsourced. The only source ever gestured at is the same 1968 Stockholm catalogue that is itself under suspicion (see the 15-minutes entry); Ava Gardner's 'Deep down, I'm pretty superficial' is an earlier line in the same shape.
candidates.whyNotable: The perfect-sounding Warhol paradox, quoted in essays and exhibition copy for decades, and Wikiquote can attach no citation to it at all.

candidates.quote: The idea is not to live forever, it is to create something that will.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Warhol source; Wikiquote lists it as Unsourced. The nearest documented published line is Chuck Palahniuk's novel Diary (2003): 'We all die. The goal isn't to live forever, the goal is to create something that will.'
candidates.whyNotable: A graduation-speech and gallery-wall staple credited to Warhol everywhere, yet Wikiquote flags it unsourced and a near-identical line is traceable to a 2003 novel.

candidates.quote: In the future everyone will be world-famous for 15 minutes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Probably curator Pontus Hultén, who told Olle Granath to insert the line into the 1968 Moderna Museet (Stockholm) exhibition catalogue's compendium of Warhol quotes even though Granath could find no trace of it in the source material — Hultén reportedly said 'if he didn't say it, he could very well have said it.' Photographer Nat Finkelstein separately claimed he coined it in 1966 ('Yeah, for about 15 minutes, Andy'), and a 1967 book preface credits a similar line to Larry Rivers. QI's earliest match is Time magazine, 13 October 1967, already crediting Warhol.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line of the 20th century about fame, and Warhol himself denied originating it in 1980 — Blake Gopnik's verdict is 'We've decided it's by Warhol, whether he likes it or not.'

candidates.quote: And now we welcome the new year, full of things that have never been.
candidates.trueOrigin: A condensation of a real Rilke sentence — his letter to Clara Rilke of 1 January 1907, written on the roof of his house on Capri: 'And now let us believe in a long year that is given to us, new, untouched, full of things that have never been, full of work that has never been done, full of tasks, claims, and demands…' (Letters of Rainer Maria Rilke 1892–1910, p. 253).
candidates.whyNotable: Reposted by the million every 31 December as a Rilke quotation, but Rilke never wrote that sentence — it is a modern trim of a much longer letter passage, and the real line is better than the popular one.

candidates.quote: Make your ego porous. Will is of little importance, complaining is nothing, fame is nothing. Openness, patience, receptivity, solitude is everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unlocated in Rilke. Wikiquote's only citation is Sy Safransky's quotation anthology Sunbeams: A Book of Quotations (1990), p. 42 — an anthology, not a Rilke text; no letter, poem or notebook source has been identified.
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily shared in creative-practice and meditation circles as Rilke's advice to artists, but even Wikiquote can only pin it to a 1990 quote anthology — a textbook 'credibly credited but unpinned' case.

candidates.quote: The purpose of life is to be defeated by greater and greater things.
candidates.trueOrigin: A modern English condensation of Rilke's 1901 German poem (published as 'Gedicht' in Deutsche Arbeit, later known as 'Der Schauende' / 'The Man Watching'); QI's earliest located use of this compact wording as a Rilke epigraph is James Marshall Galbraith's 1993 book Fear of Failure, and it also circulates via Tim O'Reilly.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted 'Rilke' line in business and self-help writing; QI shows Rilke never wrote this sentence — it is a paraphrase of a poem whose actual translations read 'his triumph is to be defeated by ever loftier powers than he' (Lewisohn 1920) and 'this is how he grows: by being defeated, decisively, by constantly greater beings' (Bly 1981).

candidates.quote: I'm so fast last night I cut the light switch and was in bed before the room was dark.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ali delivered this version (recorded by a Village Voice reporter in 1974); QI notes the underlying 'in bed before the room was dark' joke circulated earlier, so Ali adapted an existing gag.
candidates.whyNotable: A classic Ali speed boast that is genuinely his; QI traces the wording to a 1974 Village Voice report, while noting the joke form predates him.

candidates.quote: If you walk far enough you'll meet yourself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous — the earliest known instance is in The Boston Post in 1895, used by Vina Howland about Boston's confusing streets; QI searched Myths to Live By, the book Goodreads cites, and the line is absent
candidates.whyNotable: Pinned on Campbell (and on Terry Pratchett, Marion Woodman and David Mitchell) but QI traces it to an anonymous saying already in circulation in 1895, nine years before Campbell was born.

candidates.quote: Love is a friendship set to music.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — the line is also widely credited to Jackson Pollock, and Wikiquote lists it among the Campbell quotes removed for having no source at all
candidates.whyNotable: A wedding-and-Valentine's perennial credited to Campbell everywhere and to Jackson Pollock nearly as often, with Wikiquote confirming it has no source in Campbell's work.

candidates.quote: Not one shred of evidence exists that life is serious.
candidates.trueOrigin: Brendan Gill, Here at The New Yorker (1975), ch. 6, p. 49: "In fact, not a shred of evidence exists in favor of the argument that life is serious, though it is often hard and even terrible." The Campbell credit first appears on Usenet (rec.games.diplomacy) on 29 March 1993
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook documented reassignment: QI pins the line to New Yorker writer Brendan Gill's 1975 memoir and dates the Campbell misattribution to a specific 1993 Usenet post.

candidates.quote: Ask for work. If they do not give you work, ask for bread. If they do not give you bread, then take bread.
candidates.trueOrigin: Goldman's Union Square speech, 21 August 1893 (delivered partly in German, so exact wording was contested at trial). Her own recollection in Living My Life reads: 'Well then, demonstrate before the palaces of the rich; demand work. If they do not give you work, demand bread. If they deny you both, take bread.'
candidates.whyNotable: The line that put her in prison — spoken to thousands of unemployed workers at Union Square on 21 August 1893 and prosecuted as incitement to riot — though the popular wording is a smoothed version of what she recorded herself saying.

candidates.quote: The most violent element in society is ignorance.
candidates.trueOrigin: Emma Goldman, 'Anarchism: What It Really Stands For', Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) — full sentence: 'How is the ordinary man to know that the most violent element in society is ignorance; that its power of destruction is the very thing Anarchism is combating?'
candidates.whyNotable: Her most-quoted genuine aphorism and a useful real anchor beside the fakes — it appears verbatim in the primary text of 'Anarchism: What It Really Stands For' in Anarchism and Other Essays (1910), even though Wikiquote's editors once parked it on the unsourced list.

candidates.quote: I do not believe in God, because I believe in man.
candidates.trueOrigin: Emma Goldman, Living My Life (1931).
candidates.whyNotable: Her best-known statement of atheist humanism, carried in Wikiquote's sourced section from her 1931 autobiography — a clean verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — listed among the quotes Wikiquote removed from Campbell's page for lack of a reliable, precise and verifiable source; the longer viral variant ("If you can see your path laid out in front of you step by step, you know it's not your path...") has aggregator-only support
candidates.whyNotable: A career-advice and commencement favourite that Wikiquote stripped from Campbell's page as unsourced, and whose longer viral form has never been located in anything he wrote.

candidates.quote: Myth is much more important and true than history. History is just journalism and you know how reliable that is.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — Wikiquote flags it as widely attributed to Campbell with no known source anywhere in his works; the talk page traces the circulating version only to a social-media image
candidates.whyNotable: The only entry Wikiquote's Campbell page carries in its Disputed section, and a heavily shared line among writers and screenwriters despite having no source at all.

candidates.quote: Computers are like Old Testament gods; lots of rules and no mercy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph Campbell, but the on-camera wording is singular and much longer — in The Power of Myth (PBS, 1988), Episode 2, discussing his own IBM machine, he says "I'm rather an authority on gods, so I identified the god, and it seems to me an Old Testament god with a lot of rules, and no mercy."
candidates.whyNotable: Campbell's most-quoted quip and a tech-conference staple, but the punchy plural form everyone shares is a paraphrase — Wikiquote's talk page sets it against the actual broadcast transcript.

candidates.quote: Follow your bliss and the universe will open doors for you where there were only walls.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph Campbell, but embellished — his actual sentence is "I say, follow your bliss and don't be afraid, and doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be" (The Power of Myth, book edition, 1988, p. 120); neither "the universe" nor "where there were only walls" is his
candidates.whyNotable: The most-posted version of Campbell's most famous advice is a wholly rewritten sentence, with the sourced original on Wikiquote showing exactly which words were added.

candidates.quote: The cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph Campbell, but telescoped by others — his recorded wording is "Where you stumble, there lies your treasure. The very cave you are afraid to enter turns out to be the source of what you are looking for. The damned thing in the cave, that was so dreaded, has become the center." in Reflections on the Art of Living: A Joseph Campbell Companion, ed. Diane K. Osbon (HarperCollins, 1991), ch. 1
candidates.whyNotable: Almost certainly the single most-shared Campbell line on the internet, and both QI and Wikiquote's talk page find the pithy form nowhere in his published works — it is a compression of a longer passage Osbon recorded from him in 1991.

candidates.quote: We must be willing to let go of the life we have planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph Campbell as recorded by Diane K. Osbon, whose 1991 text reads "We must be willing to get rid of the life we've planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us" (A Joseph Campbell Companion, p. 18); the widespread E. M. Forster credit is unsupported
candidates.whyNotable: A graduation-speech and wedding-reading staple that circulates in a reworded form and under a rival E. M. Forster credit, which QI examined and found unfounded.

candidates.quote: Making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art.
candidates.whyNotable: Verified in The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (1975), p. 92, in the 'Business art' passage — the single most-quoted Warhol line in business writing, and this one is actually his.

candidates.quote: The reason I'm painting this way is that I want to be a machine.
candidates.whyNotable: Warhol's defining artistic statement, sourced to Gene Swenson's 'What Is Pop Art? Interviews with Eight Painters, Part 1', Art News 62, November 1963 — a primary-publication anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: They always say that time changes things, but you actually have to change them yourself.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, cleanly sourced Warhol line — The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (From A to B and Back Again), 1975, Ch. 7 'Time' — and one of his most-shared, so it anchors the hub against the fakes.

candidates.quote: Live the questions now. Perhaps you will then gradually, without noticing it, live along some distant day into the answer.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Letters to a Young Poet, fourth letter, 16 July 1903: 'Leben Sie jetzt die Fragen. Vielleicht leben Sie dann allmählich, ohne es zu merken, eines fernen Tages in die Antwort hinein.'
candidates.whyNotable: Rilke's most-quoted sentence in English, carried by Wikiquote with the German original alongside — the highest-demand verified anchor for the author hub.

candidates.quote: Love consists of this: two solitudes that meet, protect, and greet each other.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Letters to a Young Poet, seventh letter, 14 May 1904: 'dass zwei Einsamkeiten einander schützen, grenzen und grüßen.'
candidates.whyNotable: The standard wedding-reading Rilke line; verified against the German text of the seventh letter, though the popular English wording is a smoothing of 'protect, border and greet'.

candidates.quote: Perhaps all the dragons in our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us act, just once, with beauty and courage.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Letters to a Young Poet, eighth letter to Franz Xaver Kappus, 12 August 1904: 'vielleicht sind alle Drachen unseres Lebens Prinzessinnen, die nur darauf warten, uns einmal schön und mutig zu sehen.'
candidates.whyNotable: The real dragon line, verified against the German text of the eighth letter — the essential anchor for the fabricated 'dragons guarding our deepest treasure' page, since the fake is a distortion of exactly this passage.

candidates.quote: First, do no harm
candidates.trueOrigin: Not in the Hippocratic Oath. King (Hippocrates Now, ch.5, pp.101-105) notes the nearest corpus wording is Epidemics 1.11 ('to help, or at least to do no harm'), and that the Latin tag primum non nocere is a 19th-century coinage — Hippocrates wrote in Greek. Cedric M. Smith (J Clin Pharmacol, 2005) dates the Latin/English pairing to 1860, attached there to Thomas Sydenham.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-cited line in all of medicine, near-universally believed to open the Hippocratic Oath — and it appears nowhere in it, in a language Hippocrates never wrote.

candidates.quote: It is more important to know what sort of person has a disease than to know what sort of disease a person has
candidates.trueOrigin: Quote Investigator's 2019 study found the earliest close match spoken by Henry George Plimmer in 1899; Woods Hutchinson popularized it from 1902 and credited Walter Moxon, but QI found no support in Moxon's writings. Originator remains unknown. Also widely pinned on William Osler and Caleb Hillier Parry.
candidates.whyNotable: A four-way orphan quote — pinned variously on Hippocrates, Osler and Parry — that QI traced to an 1899 London pathologist nobody has heard of.

candidates.quote: All disease begins in the gut
candidates.trueOrigin: Not in the corpus. Helen King (Hippocrates Now, ch.6, pp.127-131) documents it as a modern gut-health slogan retrofitted onto Hippocrates, growing out of early-20th-century autointoxication and fibre enthusiasm (John Harvey Kellogg claimed in 1928 that 'Hippocrates was also a believer in bran').
candidates.whyNotable: The founding scripture of the modern microbiome and gut-health industry, repeated even in medical journals without a reference; King finds no Hippocratic text behind it.

candidates.quote: Death begins in the colon
candidates.trueOrigin: Etymologist Barry Popik could find no source for Hippocrates or Elie Metchnikoff ever writing it; he traces the English phrase to at least 1944, peaking in use after 1976. Also claimed by/for Bernard Jensen, the 'Father of Colonics'. King notes the sibling line 'Death sits in the bowels' is elsewhere given as an old German proverb.
candidates.whyNotable: The colon-cleanse industry's motto, variously pinned on Hippocrates, a Nobel laureate and a colonic therapist — Popik's dating puts it in 1940s America, not classical Kos.

candidates.quote: Foolish the doctor who despises knowledge acquired by the ancients
candidates.trueOrigin: King (Hippocrates Now, end of ch.6) reports finding no attempt by anyone to locate it in a Hippocratic text — and no challenge to it either. It circulates chiefly on herbal and superfood retail sites.
candidates.whyNotable: King calls it 'perhaps the most convenient of all' the fake Hippocrates quotes: a fabricated line whose entire function is to pre-authorise every other fabricated line.

candidates.quote: Leave your drugs in the chemist's pot if you can heal the patient with food
candidates.trueOrigin: Helen King states flatly that this quote is not authentic (Hippocrates Now, p.96), and records a 2011 historum.com thread in which users failed to locate any Hippocratic source. 'Chemist's pot' is an anachronism no Greek text could contain.
candidates.whyNotable: A companion slogan to 'let food be thy medicine' in alternative-medicine marketing, and its giveaway is built in — Hippocrates had no chemist's shop to leave drugs in.

candidates.quote: Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food
candidates.trueOrigin: Not in the Hippocratic Corpus. Diana Cardenas (e-SPEN Journal, Oct 2013) established it as a misquotation; Helen King traces the earliest circulating forms to 1920s American naturopathic/diet literature — Gustave Haas, Health Through Sunshine and Diet (1926) and Otto Carque, The Key to Rational Dietetics (1926), neither of which credits Hippocrates. The archaic 'thy' wording is a later antiquing.
candidates.whyNotable: By Helen King's assessment the single most-repeated Hippocrates 'quote' in existence — the load-bearing slogan of the entire food-as-medicine industry — and it is not in the corpus at all.

candidates.quote: The natural healing force within each of us is the greatest force in getting well
candidates.trueOrigin: Not in the corpus. King (Hippocrates Now, pp.1-2 and ch.7) records it as one of the standard fitness-industry 'Hippocrates said' lines, linked to the Latin tag vis medicatrix naturae — which some scholars attribute to the 18th-century physician William Cullen, and which often circulates in the garbled form 'vis mediatrix naturae'.
candidates.whyNotable: The core self-healing slogan of holistic and naturopathic medicine; its Latin anchor is 18th-century, not Hippocratic, and is frequently misspelled in the bargain.

candidates.quote: Walking is man's best medicine
candidates.trueOrigin: Does not occur in any surviving work. Helen King (Hippocrates Now, p.109) identifies the closest real text as Regimen II.LXII: 'Walking is a natural exercise, much more so than the other exercises, but there is something violent about it' — which is markedly less enthusiastic than the meme.
candidates.whyNotable: Used as the slogan for public-health walking schemes, gyms and a 2012 Occupational Medicine article title, yet Wikiquote and King both find no Hippocratic source; the real line half-disparages walking.

candidates.quote: Follow your bliss.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph Campbell — the Joseph Campbell Foundation notes the phrase appears in none of the books he completed in his lifetime and first reached print in a Psychology Today interview in July 1971, the year he retired from teaching; it was popularized by The Power of Myth (PBS, 1988), Episode 1
candidates.whyNotable: The genuine anchor for this author and one of the best-known three-word phrases in twentieth-century American thought, with a precise first-print date established by the foundation that owns his legacy.

candidates.quote: Myths are public dreams; dreams are private myths.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph Campbell — from his 1961 talk "The Impact of Science on Myth," reprinted in Myths to Live By, p. 14: "Myths, according to Freud's view, are of the psychological order of dream. Myths, so to say, are public dreams; dreams are private myths."
candidates.whyNotable: The most-cited one-line distillation of Campbell's Freud-and-Jung inheritance, and one of the few widely circulated Campbell aphorisms with an exact talk, book and page behind it.

candidates.quote: We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph Campbell — QI verified it against the HarperCollins hardcopy of Reflections on the Art of Living: A Joseph Campbell Companion (1991), pp. 8 and 17, compiled by Diane K. Osbon from journals she kept in his company
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where QI investigated a much-shared Campbell line and confirmed rather than debunked it, down to the page numbers in the hardcopy.

candidates.quote: He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how.
candidates.trueOrigin: Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols (1889), 'Maxims and Arrows'. Frankl quoted it repeatedly in Man's Search for Meaning and always credited Nietzsche; popular reuse dropped the credit and it is now widely circulated as Frankl's own.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the most-quoted line from Man's Search for Meaning, routinely captioned 'Viktor Frankl' — QI credits Nietzsche 1889, and Frankl himself never claimed it.

candidates.quote: What is to give light must endure burning.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anton Wildgans (1881–1932), final line of his 1916 poem 'Helldunkle Stunde': 'Was leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt.' The line does not appear anywhere in Man's Search for Meaning.
candidates.whyNotable: Pinned on Frankl by quote sites and even by the documentary Jodorowsky's Dune; Wikiquote's talk page traces it to Austrian poet Anton Wildgans, and it is absent from Frankl's best-known work.

candidates.quote: When a person can't find a deep sense of meaning, they distract themselves with pleasure.
candidates.trueOrigin: No known source. Wikiquote's talk page flags it as commonly attributed to Frankl with no locatable source in his major works; I searched the full English text of Man's Search for Meaning (4th ed., Lasch translation, all three parts plus the 1984 postscript) and the phrase does not occur. It is a modern paraphrase of his 'existential vacuum' idea, not a quotation.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral social-media 'Frankl' line that reads exactly like logotherapy but has no source — Wikiquote lists it under (mis)Attributed and it is absent from his best-known book.

candidates.quote: To live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering.
candidates.trueOrigin: Gordon W. Allport, in his preface to the English edition of Man's Search for Meaning (1959). Allport wrote it while summarizing Frankl's argument: 'It is here that we encounter the central theme of existentialism: to live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering.' Frankl never wrote it. Some aggregators also mis-credit it to Nietzsche.
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook 'inside the book but not by the author' misattribution — the line really is in Man's Search for Meaning, but in Harvard psychologist Gordon Allport's preface, not in Frankl's text.

candidates.quote: If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail.
candidates.trueOrigin: Nobody's exact words. Quote Investigator's chronology: philosopher Abraham Kaplan produced the earliest strong match in February 1962 — 'Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded' — with no 'nail'; Silvan Tomkins introduced the nail in 1963 ('If one has a hammer one tends to look for nails'); Maslow's 1966 sentence is the closest published ancestor of the modern form but reads 'I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail.' QI finds the common Mark Twain credit entirely unsupported.
candidates.whyNotable: Known everywhere as 'Maslow's hammer', but the crisp popular wording is nobody's — QI shows Abraham Kaplan got there four years before Maslow and that the compact modern phrasing evolved through several hands.

candidates.quote: Life is never made unbearable by circumstances, but only by lack of meaning and purpose.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified. The line is carried by aggregators only (Goodreads, AZQuotes) with no page citation; searching the complete English text of Man's Search for Meaning (4th ed., Lasch translation — camp memoir, 'Logotherapy in a Nutshell', and the 1984 postscript) returns no occurrence of the word 'unbearable' at all. Most likely a paraphrase of Frankl's existential-vacuum argument that hardened into a quotation.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the top-ten most-shared 'Frankl' lines online, and every source that carries it is a quote aggregator with no citation — it is not in the standard English text of the book it is always credited to.

candidates.quote: If you plan on being anything less than you are capable of being, you will probably be unhappy all the days of your life.
candidates.trueOrigin: A polished rewrite. Maslow's own harsher sentence runs 'If you deliberately plan to be less than you are capable of being, then I warn you that you'll be deeply unhappy for the rest of your life. You will be evading your own capacities, your own possibilities.' Wikiquote's earliest trace for the popular smoothed wording is Joan Neehall-Davidson, Perfecting Private Practice (2004), p. 95.
candidates.whyNotable: A graduation-speech and LinkedIn staple that aggregators routinely cite to Motivation and Personality (1954) — where it does not appear; Wikiquote can only get back to a 2004 clinical-practice handbook.

candidates.quote: In any given moment we have two options: to step forward into growth or to step back into safety.
candidates.trueOrigin: A smoothed paraphrase. Maslow's actual sentence in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), ch. 4 'Defense and Growth', reads: 'One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth. Growth must be chosen again and again; fear must be overcome again and again.' Wikiquote can trace the popular self-help rewording no earlier than Brian Tracy's How the Best Leaders Lead (2010).
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared 'Maslow' line on social media and in corporate slide decks, and the wording nobody can find in Maslow — Wikiquote's earliest trace for the reworded form is a 2010 business book, 40 years after his death.

candidates.quote: Laugh at what you hold sacred, and still hold it sacred.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unlocated in Maslow's writings. Wikiquote's earliest printing is Loretta LaRoche, Relax — You May Have Only a Few Minutes Left (1998), p. xvii, a humour-and-stress self-help book.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted in writing on humour, religion and resilience; the oldest documented source is a 1998 stress-management paperback, not Maslow.

candidates.quote: The story of the human race is the story of men and women selling themselves short.
candidates.trueOrigin: Almost certainly a compression of Maslow's real line in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), p. 5: 'Human nature is not nearly as bad as it has been thought to be... In fact it can be said that the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short.' Wikiquote's earliest trace for the punchy version is Jim Whitt, Road Signs for Success (1993), p. 61.
candidates.whyNotable: A motivational-poster classic where the memorable aphorism is a 1990s rewrite of a longer, blander sentence Maslow actually wrote.

candidates.quote: The way to recover the meaning of life and the worthwhileness of life is to recover the power of experience, to have impulse voices from within, and to be able to hear these impulse voices from within.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote files it under 'Attributed', citing only Richard T. Kinnier (ed.), The Meaning of Life: According to the Great and the Good (2007) — an anthology, not a Maslow text.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates heavily in meaning-of-life and mindfulness writing, but its only located printing is a 2007 quotation anthology rather than any work by Maslow.

candidates.quote: What is necessary to change a person is to change his awareness of himself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unlocated in Maslow. Wikiquote's earliest printing is William M. Stephens, Life In the Open Sea (1972), p. 21 — a marine-biology book published two years after Maslow's death.
candidates.whyNotable: A therapy-and-coaching favourite whose oldest documented appearance is a 1972 book about ocean life, not any Maslow publication.

candidates.quote: You will either step forward into growth, or you will step backward into safety.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote lists this exact wording under 'Attributed' with its earliest located printing in Brian Tracy, How the Best Leaders Lead (2010), p. 35 — i.e. a secondary self-help source, not Maslow. The nearest genuine Maslow text is Toward a Psychology of Being (1962): 'One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth.'
candidates.whyNotable: The second-most-circulated variant of the growth/safety line, and the specific wording Wikiquote flags as unsourced to Maslow himself.

candidates.quote: As to diseases, make a habit of two things — to help, or at least, to do no harm
candidates.whyNotable: The real Hippocratic line that 'First, do no harm' is a corruption of — sourced to Epidemics Book I, and the perfect counterpart page to the fake.

candidates.quote: Extreme remedies are very appropriate for extreme diseases
candidates.whyNotable: Sourced to Aphorisms 1:6 and the ancestor of the everyday proverb 'desperate times call for desperate measures', with a documented descent through Montaigne, Shakespeare's Hamlet and Guy Fawkes.

candidates.quote: Life is short, and Art long; the crisis fleeting; experience perilous, and decision difficult
candidates.whyNotable: The genuine opening of Aphorisms 1:1 and the source of 'Ars longa, vita brevis' — a real anchor whose famous Latin form actually reverses Hippocrates' word order, and whose 'Art' means craft, not fine art.

candidates.quote: Don't aim at success. The more you aim at it and make it a target, the more you are going to miss it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Frankl — from his preface to the 1992 edition of Man's Search for Meaning, quoting what he tells his students; continues 'For success, like happiness, cannot be pursued; it must ensue…'. Wikiquote cites p. 16–17 of the 60th anniversary edition.
candidates.whyNotable: Frankl's best-known line outside the camp narrative and a staple of the happiness literature, cleanly sourced to his own preface with a page citation.

candidates.quote: Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Frankl — Man's Search for Meaning (1946; English 1959), in the camp-memoir section. Verified against the full text.
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive real Frankl line and the anchor of his whole argument, worth having as a verified counterweight to the four fakes that surround it.

candidates.quote: When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Frankl — Man's Search for Meaning, part two, 'The Meaning of Suffering'. Verified in the full text; the sentence in the book runs 'When we are no longer able to change a situation — just think of an incurable disease such as inoperable cancer — we are challenged to change ourselves.'
candidates.whyNotable: Among the most-shared Frankl lines and, unlike the stimulus-and-response one it usually travels beside, genuinely his and locatable in the book.

candidates.quote: A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately at peace with himself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Maslow: 'A Theory of Human Motivation', Psychological Review vol. 50, no. 4 (1943), p. 382, and Motivation and Personality (1954), p. 93. Note the widely reproduced misquote ending 'if he is to be ultimately happy' — which the BBC World Service itself printed in its 2013 piece on Maslow's pyramid.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most quoted sentences in psychology, and a rare case where a mainstream outlet (BBC World Service, 2013) reprinted the corrupted ending 'ultimately happy' instead of Maslow's 'ultimately at peace with himself'.

candidates.quote: I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Maslow: The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (New York: Harper, 1966), ch. 2, p. 15. QI credits this as the primary published source for the modern saying while documenting Abraham Kaplan's earlier 1962 hammer analogy.
candidates.whyNotable: The real, sourced sentence behind 'Maslow's hammer' — a verified anchor that lets the page show exactly how far the popular paraphrase has drifted.

candidates.quote: What a man can be, he must be.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Maslow: 'A Theory of Human Motivation', Psychological Review vol. 50, no. 4 (1943), p. 382; repeated in Motivation and Personality (1954), p. 93. Wikiquote notes the widely circulated variant 'What one can be, one must be!' is unsourced.
candidates.whyNotable: The defining self-actualization line, traceable to the exact page of the 1943 paper that introduced the hierarchy of needs — with a popular gender-neutral rewording Wikiquote flags as unsourced.

candidates.quote: At a football club, there's a holy trinity - the players, the manager and the supporters.
candidates.trueOrigin: Shankly, cited in 'Bill Shankly: Life, death and football,' The Guardian (18 Oct 2009).
candidates.whyNotable: A defining statement of Shankly's fan-first football philosophy, sourced at Wikiquote to a Guardian retrospective.

candidates.quote: Football is not a matter of life and death. It's much more important than that.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Shankly, but the popular meme wording is a tidied paraphrase. In a 1981 Granada TV interview he actually said: 'Someone said to me To you football is a matter of life or death! and I said Listen, it's more important than that.'
candidates.whyNotable: Shankly's most-shared line, endlessly repeated in this polished form; the real 1981 TV wording documented by Wikiquote is looser and was said with regret, not bravado.

candidates.quote: The socialism I believe in is everyone working for each other, everyone having a share of the rewards. It's the way I see football, the way I see life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Shankly, documented in Powley & Gillan, 'Shankly's Village' (Pitch, 2015).
candidates.whyNotable: Shankly's much-quoted articulation of football-as-socialism; sourced at Wikiquote to a 2015 biography of his home village of Glenbuck.

candidates.quote: No man will make a great business who wants to do it all himself, or to get all the credit of doing it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Carnegie, interview published in the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 15 October 1899, discussing his thirty-two partners; also carried by The Philadelphia Times and The St. Paul Globe. QI confirms Carnegie deserves credit for the 1899 statement.
candidates.whyNotable: The verified anchor behind the mangled 'great leader' version — QI pins the exact 1899 interview wording.

candidates.quote: Put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Carnegie's: address to the students of Curry Commercial College, Pittsburgh, 23 June 1885. Mark Twain popularized a version as a Pudd'nhead Wilson epigraph (serialized April 1894) and credited Carnegie in a notebook entry of April 1893; Carnegie's 1920 Autobiography revises it to 'all good eggs'. Twain now frequently gets the credit.
candidates.whyNotable: A real Carnegie line that Mark Twain is routinely given credit for — QI confirms Carnegie said it first, in 1885, and that Twain's own notebook acknowledged him.

candidates.quote: The man who dies rich dies disgraced.
candidates.trueOrigin: Carnegie, 'Wealth', North American Review (1889), p. 664 — where the sentence actually reads 'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.' The universally circulated form drops 'thus', which in context pointed back to the specific hoarding Carnegie had just described.
candidates.whyNotable: Carnegie's defining line, verified on Wikiquote to Wealth (1889), but circulated in a subtly clipped form that drops the word 'thus' and broadens the claim.

candidates.quote: The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced
candidates.trueOrigin: Andrew Carnegie
candidates.whyNotable: The richest man of his age indicting hoarding in his own words — still the quote behind the Giving Pledge and every modern argument about what fortunes are for.

candidates.quote: Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference.
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularized via Ziglar's 'See You at the Top' (1977); also widely misattributed to Winston Churchill and Theodore Roosevelt.
candidates.whyNotable: Contested between Ziglar (who wrote a matching line in 'See You at the Top,' 1977) and Winston Churchill; QI treats the modern one-liner as a shared/evolving adage rather than clearly either man's.

candidates.quote: There is no road too long to the man who advances deliberately and without undue haste.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jean de La Bruyère
candidates.whyNotable: The best long-haul/endurance line on the list: it addresses scale and intimidation directly, making it a natural fit for a slide about a multi-year effort.

candidates.quote: Strong, deeply rooted desire is the starting point of all achievement.
candidates.trueOrigin: Napoleon Hill, The Law of Success in Sixteen Lessons (1928), p. 109.
candidates.whyNotable: A properly page-cited Hill line from his 1928 pre-1931 work, so it is both verifiable and clearly public domain — the cleanest anchor in the set.

candidates.quote: Do not wait; the time will never be just right. Start where you stand, and work with whatever tools you may have at your command, and better tools will be found as you go along.
candidates.trueOrigin: Napoleon Hill, Think and Grow Rich (1937/1938), p. 127. Wikiquote carries it with a page citation, and a near-identical sentence also appears at p. 86.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-shared genuinely sourced Hill line — a real anchor with a page number, useful as a verified counterweight to the unsourced material.

candidates.quote: Every adversity has the seed of an equivalent or greater benefit.
candidates.trueOrigin: Napoleon Hill, cited explicitly as a maxim of Hill's in Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960, with W. Clement Stone), Ch. 14, p. 222. Note the far more common paraphrase — "Every adversity, every failure, every heartache carries with it the seed of an equal or greater benefit" — is on Wikiquote's talk page as unsourced.
candidates.whyNotable: Sourced in its short form but almost always shared in a longer 'every failure, every heartache' wording that Wikiquote lists among the unsourced Hill quotations — a genuine quote with a fake popular wording.

candidates.quote: From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Napoleon's, said in December 1812 about the Russian campaign, recorded by Abbe de Pradt.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, sourced Napoleon line — his remark on the disastrous 1812 Russian retreat, recorded by Abbe de Pradt and confirmed by QI.

candidates.quote: Baseball always has been and always will be a game demanding team play. You can have the nine greatest individual ball players in the world, but if they don't play together the club won't be worth a dime.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ruth's; 'Babe Ruth's Own Book of Baseball' (1928), Chapter X (also carried in The Pittsburgh Press, January 18, 1929).
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, well-sourced Ruth line from his own 1928 book, giving the hub a real team-play anchor; cited by Wikiquote to Babe Ruth's Own Book of Baseball (1928), Chapter X.

candidates.quote: I always swing at the ball with all my might. I hit or miss big.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ruth's; Chicago Tribune, August 13, 1920 (as told to Westbrook Pegler), reprinted in 'Playing the Game: My Early Years in Baseball' (2011).
candidates.whyNotable: A verified early Ruth quote captured in his own words, sourced by Wikiquote to the Chicago Tribune (August 13, 1920) as told to Westbrook Pegler.

candidates.quote: You just can't beat the person who never gives up.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ruth's; published under his byline in 'Bat It Out!', The Rotarian, July 1940.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, sourced Ruth line and a rare confirmed one: QI verifies Ruth wrote it under his own byline in the article 'Bat It Out!' in The Rotarian, July 1940.

candidates.quote: Often we are so busy with sawing that we forget to sharpen the saw.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote lists it among First Things First (1994) attributions it cannot verify — a paraphrase of Covey's genuine Habit 7 ('Sharpen the Saw') rather than a quotable sentence he wrote.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates as a verbatim Covey quote off the back of his genuinely famous Habit 7; Wikiquote flags the exact wording as an unverified attribution.

candidates.quote: Change happens at the speed of trust.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote lists it as an unverified attribution under First Things First (1994). The 'speed of trust' formulation belongs to his son Stephen M. R. Covey, whose 2006 book is titled The Speed of Trust — a father/son mix-up.
candidates.whyNotable: A leadership-conference favorite credited to Stephen Covey that Wikiquote flags as unverified; the phrase actually belongs to his son Stephen M. R. Covey's 2006 book.

candidates.quote: Courage is not the absence of fear but the awareness that something else is more important.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote carries it in Covey's unsourced list with no citation. The canonical version — 'Courage is not the absence of fear, but rather the judgement that something else is more important than fear' — is by Ambrose Redmoon (James Neil Hollingworth), 'No Peaceful Warriors!', Gnosis magazine #21, Fall 1991. Also misattributed to FDR and Mark Twain.
candidates.whyNotable: A top-tier motivational-poster line pinned on Covey with no source; Wikiquote leaves it unsourced and the documented 1991 original is Ambrose Redmoon's.

candidates.quote: They that love beyond the World, cannot be separated by it. Death cannot kill, what never dies.
candidates.trueOrigin: William Penn
candidates.whyNotable: The standard Quaker funeral reading for three centuries, and the epigraph J. K. Rowling chose for Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows — instantly familiar without being worn out.

candidates.quote: I owe the public nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Reported in the New York World, May 11, 1901.
candidates.whyNotable: Morgan's most notorious verified line, printed in the New York World in 1901 and endlessly recycled as shorthand for Gilded Age arrogance.

candidates.quote: Money is gold, and nothing else.
candidates.trueOrigin: Morgan's own words, House Banking and Currency (Pujo) Committee testimony, December 1912: '[Credit] is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else.' The viral wording 'Gold is money. Everything else is credit.' is a later compression, not the transcript.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced line from Morgan's 1912 Pujo Committee testimony that circulates online almost exclusively in the punchier fabricated paraphrase 'Gold is money. Everything else is credit.'

candidates.quote: The first thing is character, before money or anything else. Money cannot buy it. A man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom.
candidates.trueOrigin: Morgan's own testimony before the Pujo Committee, December 1912, under questioning by counsel Samuel Untermyer.
candidates.whyNotable: Morgan's best-documented statement — sworn 1912 Pujo Committee testimony on credit and character — and a real anchor for a hub full of fabrications.

candidates.quote: Fashion fades, only style remains the same.
candidates.trueOrigin: Coco Chanel articulated it in a 1965 McCall's interview; the underlying idea predates her (an anonymous beauty expert wrote 'Fashion comes and goes, style goes on forever' in 1929).
candidates.whyNotable: Chanel's single most-quoted line; QI credits her 1965 McCall's articulation ('Fashion passes, style remains') while noting the fashion-vs-style idea circulated as early as 1929, so it is a real Chanel line built on a pre-existing concept.

candidates.quote: Fashion is always a reflection of the times, but it is forgotten if it is foolish.
candidates.trueOrigin: Coco Chanel, 'Maximes et Sentences,' Paris Vogue, September 1938.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Chanel maxim from her September 1938 Paris Vogue 'Maximes et Sentences,' which QI presents as authentically hers rather than disputed.

candidates.quote: Fashion is architecture. It is a matter of proportions.
candidates.trueOrigin: Coco Chanel, via Marcel Haedrich's 1971 biography 'Coco Chanel Secrète.'
candidates.whyNotable: A signature Chanel design maxim on Wikiquote; QI concludes Chanel deserves credit based on her biographer Marcel Haedrich's testimony.

candidates.quote: Nothing is ugly as long as it is alive.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Coco Chanel through Marcel Haedrich's 1971 biography 'Coco Chanel Secrète.'
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently shared Chanel aphorism that QI credits to her, though only via her authorized 1971 biography, so it rests on a single posthumous source.

candidates.quote: Where should one use perfume? Wherever one wants to be kissed.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI credits Coco Chanel; earliest citation a 1962 Boston Globe column, corroborated by Marcel Haedrich's 1971 biography 'Coco Chanel Secrète.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of Chanel's most-quoted witticisms; QI believes she deserves credit, citing a 1962 Boston Globe column and her 1971 authorized biography, though the earliest source is decades after she supposedly said it.

candidates.quote: Gentlemen, we are going to relentlessly chase perfection, knowing full well we will not catch it, because nothing is perfect. But we are going to relentlessly chase it, because in the process we will catch excellence. I am not remotely interested in just being good.
candidates.trueOrigin: Vince Lombardi, attributed to his first team meeting as Packers coach (1959); reported in Chuck Carlson, Game of My Life: 25 Stories of Packers Football (2004).
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'chase perfection, catch excellence' passage — a genuine, well-known Lombardi anchor that circulates constantly in leadership contexts.

candidates.quote: If you aren't fired with enthusiasm, you will be fired with enthusiasm
candidates.trueOrigin: Vince Lombardi, as reported in Lee Green, Sportswit (1984), p. 169 (secondary compilation).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Lombardi's most-shared clever wordplay lines; sourced on Wikiquote though only to a 1984 quotation compilation.

candidates.quote: Winning isn't a sometime thing; it's an all the time thing
candidates.trueOrigin: Vince Lombardi — this is the line Lombardi actually said, which Wikiquote contrasts against the misattributed 'it's the only thing' version.
candidates.whyNotable: The real Lombardi line, and the perfect anchor/foil to the far-more-famous misquote it gets confused with.

candidates.quote: Failure is an event, not a person.
candidates.trueOrigin: Zig Ziglar, 'See You at the Top' (full form: 'Failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night').
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Ziglar line sourced by Wikiquote to 'See You at the Top' — verified anchor content for the hub.

candidates.quote: You can have everything in life you want, if you will just help enough other people get what they want.
candidates.trueOrigin: Zig Ziglar, 'Secrets of Closing the Sale' (1984), a staple of his talks since 'See You at the Top.'
candidates.whyNotable: Ziglar's signature line, sourced by Wikiquote to 'Secrets of Closing the Sale' (1984) — a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: I don't give advice; I give opinions.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wooden did say a version in Feb 1994 ('I don't like to give advice... I can give an opinion. That's a big difference'), but QI finds the tidy epigram's origin murky, also linked to Bill Walton and Joyce Fittro.
candidates.whyNotable: A pithy line widely quoted as vintage Wooden; QI confirms he expressed the idea but the polished one-liner form has an unclear origin.

candidates.quote: We abuse land because we regard it as a commodity belonging to us. When we see land as a community to which we belong, we may begin to use it with love and respect.
candidates.trueOrigin: Aldo Leopold
candidates.whyNotable: The land ethic in two sentences — the defining modern conservation quote, and the one place where no pre-1931 line does the same work as precisely.

candidates.quote: I believe in a benevolent dictatorship - as long as I am the benevolent dictator.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source located; Wikiquote editors moved it to the talk page as unsourced. The 'benevolent dictator, as long as I'm the dictator' joke is a stock management-humour formula predating Branson.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly reproduced in leadership listicles as vintage Branson, yet Wikiquote demoted it to the unsourced holding area for want of any reliable citation.

candidates.quote: I never get the accountants in before I start up a business. It's done on gut feeling, especially if I can see that they are taking the mickey out of the consumer.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — flagged on Wikiquote's talk page as unsourced and slated for removal absent a precise citation.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of 'trust your gut' entrepreneurship advice attributed to Branson, but Wikiquote found no reliable source for it.

candidates.quote: If you want to be a Millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote's only citation is a secondhand MSNBC piece (October 2001), not a primary source; the underlying gag is older aviation folklore ("How do you make a small fortune in aviation? Start with a large one"), and the line circulates in several incompatible wordings including "The quickest way to become a millionaire in the airline business is to start out as a billionaire."
candidates.whyNotable: Branson's most-shared business one-liner, but it survives only as a journalist's paraphrase and is a restatement of a much older aviation joke that circulated long before Virgin Atlantic.

candidates.quote: What's the quickest way to become a millionaire? Borrow fivers off everyone you meet.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — Wikiquote lists it among quotes removed from the article for lacking any reliable and precise source.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely reshared Branson quip about bootstrapping that Wikiquote could not source to any interview, book, or article.

candidates.quote: With the casino and the beds, our passengers will have at least two ways to get lucky on one of our flights.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — held on Wikiquote's talk page as an unsourced attribution pending a reliable citation.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-repeated Branson PR-stunt lines, quoted in airline-marketing writeups for years with no traceable original source.

candidates.quote: Crazy-busy is a great armor, it's a great way for numbing. What a lot of us do is that we stay so busy, and so out in front of our life, that the truth of how we're feeling and what we really need can't catch up with us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Brené Brown, Washington Post interview, October 2012 (as cited on Wikiquote).
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently excerpted 'crazy-busy as armor' line; sourced on Wikiquote to an October 2012 Washington Post interview, giving the Brown hub a verifiable anchor.

candidates.quote: Shame hates to have words wrapped around it. If we talk about it, it loses its grip on us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Brené Brown, University of Houston 'Pride Stories' (as cited on Wikiquote).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as the core of Brown's shame-resilience message ('shame derives its power from being unspeakable'); sourced on Wikiquote to a University of Houston Pride Stories piece.

candidates.quote: Vulnerability is not weakness; it's our greatest measure of courage.
candidates.trueOrigin: Brené Brown, Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience (2021).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Brown's signature lines and the thesis of her whole body of work on vulnerability; sourced on Wikiquote to her 2021 book Atlas of the Heart.

candidates.quote: Find the good. It's all around you. Find it, showcase it and you'll start believing in it.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently doubted as too pat to be real, but Quote Investigator CONFIRMS it — traced to Owens's 1970 Blackthink, ch. 8 'Showcase the Good,' via scans of the original.

candidates.quote: Hitler didn't snub me; it was our president who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram.
candidates.whyNotable: Owens's own words debunking the ubiquitous 'Hitler snubbed Owens at the 1936 Olympics' myth; documented in Jeremy Schaap's Triumph (2007) and on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals.
candidates.whyNotable: Iconic Owens line about racing horses for money after 1936; verified from a 1971 interview cited by ESPN SportsCentury and Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: The battles that count aren't the ones for gold medals. The struggles within yourself — the invisible, inevitable battles inside all of us — that's where it's at.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared inspirational Owens lines online; genuinely his, from his 1970 book Blackthink, and a strong real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: The road to the Olympics, leads to no city, no country. It goes far beyond New York or Moscow, ancient Greece or Nazi Germany. The road to the Olympics leads — in the end — to the best within us.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely circulated Owens Olympic quote; verified via Voice of America's People In America (2002) and reproduced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success; leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Covey: The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), p. 101 — his own sourced formulation, distinct from the older anonymous 'wrong wall' proverb QI traces to 1915.
candidates.whyNotable: The verified Covey sentence that sits directly alongside the misattributed 'wrong wall' proverb, letting the hub show the real line and the folk version side by side.

candidates.quote: Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Covey: The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), p. 239.
candidates.whyNotable: His single most-quoted line and a real anchor for the hub — Wikiquote gives it a page-level citation in 7 Habits.

candidates.quote: The key is not to prioritize what's on your schedule, but to schedule your priorities.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Covey: The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), p. 161.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-repeated productivity line in the Covey canon, with a sourced Wikiquote entry and a specific page number.

candidates.quote: Most of the important things in the world have been accomplished by people who have kept on trying when there seemed to be no hope at all.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Carnegie. QI's earliest match is his newspaper column "Being Discouraged Never Pays," The Marshall News Messenger, 29 January 1942, written about inventor Lee de Forest's perseverance; it was later collected in Dale Carnegie's Scrapbook (1959, ed. Dorothy Carnegie) and is often misdated to How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948).
candidates.whyNotable: His single most-shared line and a rare one QI positively CONFIRMS as his — traced to a dated 1942 column, though nearly every quote site misfiles it under his 1948 book.

candidates.quote: You can make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Carnegie — How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936), Part 2, cited on Wikiquote at p. 52 of the 1998 edition. Wikiquote's condensed rendering reads "You can make more friends in two months by being interested in them, than in two years by making them interested in you."
candidates.whyNotable: The thesis sentence of the best-selling self-help book of all time, and a real sourced anchor to sit beside the debunks — worth a page if only to pin down which of its two circulating wordings is the book's.

candidates.quote: Every kid around the world who plays soccer wants to be Pelé. I have a great responsibility to show them not just how to be like a soccer player, but how to be like a man.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pelé — as quoted in Sports Illustrated (1 June 1999).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, sourced Pelé quote and a strong real anchor for a hub — cited on Wikiquote to Sports Illustrated's 1999 'SI Flashback: Soccer's greatest genius.'

candidates.quote: I was born for soccer, just as Beethoven was born for music.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pelé — quoted in Parton Keese, The Measure of Greatness (1980).
candidates.whyNotable: A famous, sourced Pelé line — Wikiquote cites it to Parton Keese, 'The Measure of Greatness' (1980); a clean verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Strive manfully; custom is overcome by custom.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas à Kempis
candidates.whyNotable: Six words containing the whole modern habit-replacement insight — you do not delete a habit, you displace it with another. Unexpected, and nobody else will have it.

candidates.quote: A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (as told to Alfred Duckett), 1972
candidates.whyNotable: Robinson's single most-shared line and the epitaph on his gravestone; a genuine, well-sourced anchor worth a page as a verified hub for this magnet author.

candidates.quote: I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag. I know that I am a black man in a white world.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (as told to Alfred Duckett), 1972
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently doubted or challenged online as too pointed to be real, yet it is genuinely sourced to his 1972 autobiography - high fact-check value for a 'did he really say this?' page.

candidates.quote: I'm not concerned with your liking or disliking me. All I ask is that you respect me as a human being.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jackie Robinson, response to an umpire c.1954; quoted in Baseball Has Done It (1964), pp. 9-10
candidates.whyNotable: One of Robinson's most-quoted lines on dignity and respect; Wikiquote sources it firmly to Baseball Has Done It (1964), making it a strong verified anchor.

candidates.quote: True heroism is remarkably sober, very undramatic. It is not the urge to surpass all others at whatever cost, but the urge to serve others at whatever cost.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ashe; from his commencement address to Ohio Wesleyan University's class of 1991 (May 12, 1991), confirmed by Quote Investigator.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Ashe's most-quoted genuine lines and a QI-confirmed real anchor, useful as a verified counterpoint to the fakes on the hub.

candidates.quote: We must reach out our hand in friendship both to those who would befriend us and those who would be our enemy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ashe; from his memoir 'Days of Grace' (1994), p. 186, per Wikiquote's sourced entry.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, sourced Ashe line from his memoir that provides a real anchor alongside the debunked material.

candidates.quote: People use statistics as a drunk uses a lamppost — for support rather than illumination.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI traces the simile to A. E. Housman's 1903 edition of Manilius, where scholars 'use MSS as drunkards use lamp-posts,—not to light them on their way but to dissimulate their instability.' The common Andrew Lang credit first appears in print 25 years after Lang's death and looks like a memory error. Ogilvy used the simile in Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963) with no attribution, which is why marketing writers now pin it on him.
candidates.whyNotable: A quip Ogilvy printed unattributed in 1963 and thereby popularized in business circles; QI shows the image is Housman's from 1903 and the popular Andrew Lang credit is unsupported.

candidates.quote: Strategy is about making choices, trade-offs; it's about deliberately choosing to be different.
candidates.trueOrigin: Michael E. Porter, "What Is Strategy?", Harvard Business Review, November–December 1996 (page not pinned by Wikiquote; competing paraphrases circulate)
candidates.whyNotable: The most-shared Porter line on business social media and the one aggregators reproduce in the most variant wordings ("Competitive strategy is about being different" is a common paraphrase circulated as an exact quote); Wikiquote sources it to the 1996 HBR piece but gives no page number.

candidates.quote: The essence of formulating strategy is relating a company to its environment.
candidates.trueOrigin: Michael E. Porter, Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors (1980), p. 3
candidates.whyNotable: The opening thesis of Competitive Strategy (1980), the book that introduced the Five Forces framework; Wikiquote cites it to p. 3, making it one of the few Porter lines with a hard primary-source pin.

candidates.quote: The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do.
candidates.trueOrigin: Michael E. Porter, "What Is Strategy?", Harvard Business Review, November–December 1996, p. 70
candidates.whyNotable: Porter's single most-quoted line and the load-bearing sentence of modern strategy discourse; Wikiquote pins it to a specific page of his 1996 HBR article "What Is Strategy?" (p. 70), and it is frequently confused with Steve Jobs' "focus is about saying no" framing.

candidates.quote: Make each day your masterpiece.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely a Wooden signature line; he credited the lesson to his father and repeated it throughout his life (e.g. Charlie Rose interview, 2000).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Wooden's best-known and genuinely-his maxims, closely tied to his teaching identity.

candidates.quote: Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wooden — his own definition of success, foundational to his Pyramid of Success; stated in his Charlie Rose interview (2000) and his writings.
candidates.whyNotable: Wooden's single most important and genuinely-authored idea, the definition of success he built his whole philosophy on — a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Talent is God-given; be humble. Fame is man-given; be thankful. Conceit is self-given; be careful.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wooden, sourced to his 1972 memoir 'They Call Me Coach'.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared and genuinely-sourced Wooden line, useful as a verified anchor in the hub.

candidates.quote: The main ingredient of stardom is the rest of the team.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wooden, sourced to his 1972 memoir 'They Call Me Coach'.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, sourced Wooden line on teamwork that anchors the hub against the misattributed material.

candidates.quote: Don't pray when it rains if you don't pray when the sun shines.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Paige via a 1959 AP column, but QI notes it is also credited to evangelist Billy Sunday and columnist Hal Boyle — a shared/contested credit rather than a clean Paige original.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as pure Paige, but QI documents competing credits to Billy Sunday and Hal Boyle, making the origin genuinely disputed.

candidates.quote: There's a lot of blood, sweat and guts between dreams and success.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely attributed to Bryant on Wikiquote's sourced 'Quotes' section (cited via Saturday Down South, 2012).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Bryant's most-shared real motivational lines and a solid verified anchor to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: There is a land of the living and a land of the dead, and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thornton Wilder
candidates.whyNotable: The closing sentence of the Pulitzer-winning novel, and the passage Tony Blair read at the Manhattan memorial for the British victims of 9/11 — a secular consolation line with real ceremonial weight.

candidates.quote: We can only be said to be alive in the moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thornton Wilder
candidates.whyNotable: A closing-slide line: the Our Town idea eight years early. The version that circulates online ('in those moments … our treasures') is drifted — the Thornton Wilder Society's sourced text reads 'in the moments' and 'treasure' singular, which is what I have given. US rights: 1930 publications entered the public domain on 1 January 2026.

candidates.quote: A good PR story is infinitely more effective than a front page ad.
candidates.whyNotable: Branson's best-known marketing maxim, carried on Wikiquote with a Virgin website blog citation and quoted constantly in PR and growth writing.

candidates.quote: I became an entrepreneur by mistake. Ever since then I've gone into business, not to make money, but because I think I can do it better than it's been done elsewhere.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, Wikiquote-sourced Branson line from a 1997 Martyn Lewis interview — a solid verified anchor for a hub page otherwise full of unsourced attributions.

candidates.quote: My general attitude to life is to enjoy every minute of every day.
candidates.whyNotable: Sourced by Wikiquote to a Guardian interview of 20 September 2008; note that the longer circulating version ("I never do anything with a feeling of, 'Oh God, I've got to do this today'") is an expansion beyond the sourced sentence.

candidates.quote: Lead, follow, or get out of the way
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote's Thomas Paine page lists this in Misattributed and points to George S. Patton's actual wording, 'Lead me, follow me, or get out of my way' (quoted in Pocket Patriot: Quotes from American Heroes, 2005, ed. Kelly Nickell, p. 157). Iacocca did not originate it — he popularised the corporate form via Chrysler's 1992 ad campaign ('In the automobile industry, you either lead, follow, or get out of the way'), which is how his name got attached.
candidates.whyNotable: The one genuinely strong misattribution hub available for Iacocca — the line is a business-poster staple credited variously to Iacocca, Thomas Paine, and Patton, and Wikiquote debunks the Paine credit while reassigning it to Patton.

candidates.quote: Can't anybody here play this game?
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, on the hapless 1962 New York Mets; used as the title of Jimmy Breslin's 1963 book
candidates.whyNotable: Stengel's signature lament over the expansion Mets and one of baseball's most-quoted lines, verified via Breslin's 1963 book title.

candidates.quote: I'll never make the mistake of being 70 years old again
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, on being fired by the Yankees after the 1960 World Series (quoted in Joseph Durso's 1967 biography)
candidates.whyNotable: Stengel's famous quip on his forced retirement from the Yankees, sourced in his 1967 biography.

candidates.quote: The secret of managing is to keep the guys who hate you away from the ones who are undecided
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, popular condensation of a longer remark at the December 1964 Winter Meetings (recalled by Bob Sudyk, Hartford Courant, 1993)
candidates.whyNotable: One of Stengel's most-repeated management aphorisms; the pithy popular wording is a condensation of a longer sourced 1964 remark on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: There comes a time in every man's life, and I've had plenty of them
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, quoted in Parade magazine, August 23, 1953
candidates.whyNotable: A quintessential piece of self-aware 'Stengelese', sourced to a 1953 Parade profile.

candidates.quote: Without losers, where would the winners be?
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, quoted in The Gospel According to Casey (1992), ed. Berkow & Kaplan, p. 19
candidates.whyNotable: A characteristic Stengel one-liner on competition, sourced to the 1992 anthology of his sayings.

candidates.quote: Patience is the art of hoping.
candidates.magnetAuthor: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues
candidates.creditedTo: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues
candidates.trueOrigin: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues
candidates.whyNotable: Five words and the most elegant definition in the set — it links patience to hope rather than to endurance, which lifts a slide out of the grim-perseverance register.

candidates.quote: In all my years of football I've never known a man who talked more and won less than Steve Gutman.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Belichick, 2000 resignation remarks (reprinted in From Darkness to Dynasty)
candidates.whyNotable: Belichick's famously blunt parting shot at the Jets president when he resigned as 'HC of the NYJ' after one day; a verified, widely reprinted line.

candidates.quote: We're on to Cincinnati.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Belichick, New England Patriots press conference, September 29, 2014
candidates.whyNotable: Belichick's most iconic press-conference line, repeated to deflect every question after a 41-14 loss to Kansas City; now shorthand for tuning out noise and moving to the next game.

candidates.quote: Every king springs from a race of slaves, and every slave has had kings among his ancestors.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely from Seneca, Epistle XLIV ('On Philosophy and Pedigrees'), but Seneca himself is quoting Plato ('Plato says...'), whose idea traces to Socrates in the Theaetetus (c. 369 BCE). So it is a real Seneca line relaying Plato.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, sourced Seneca line on equality of ancestry that doubles as a teachable attribution-chain (Seneca quoting Plato quoting Socrates); QI confirms it.

candidates.quote: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Seneca, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, Letter II ('On Discursiveness in Reading').
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-quoted, properly sourced Seneca line on wealth and desire; a solid genuine anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: The wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Seneca, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, Letter LXX ('On the Proper Time to Slip the Cable').
candidates.whyNotable: A famous, sourced Seneca line on death and Stoic autonomy; a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: An organization's ability to learn, and translate that learning into action rapidly, is the ultimate competitive business advantage.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Welch, cited in Robert Slater, Jack Welch & The G.E. Way: Management Insights and Leadership (1998), p. 12.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-reproduced Welch line in management writing and business content, and one of the few with a hard citation on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: Getting the right people in the right jobs is a lot more important than developing a strategy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Welch, Jack: Straight from the Gut (2001), Ch. 24.
candidates.whyNotable: Welch's best-known people-over-strategy maxim, widely quoted in hiring and leadership contexts, and directly sourced to a chapter of his own autobiography.

candidates.quote: Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Welch, originally said to the Wall Street Journal; the primary WSJ article is unpinned on Wikiquote, which quotes it via Mark Ames, Going Postal (2005), p. 98.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-contested Welch line, routinely cited in critiques of at-will corporate culture, but Wikiquote's citation chain is second-hand: a Wall Street Journal remark quoted only via Mark Ames's 2005 book rather than the original WSJ piece.

candidates.quote: Baseball is the only field of endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer.
