candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared inspirational baseball lines pinned on Williams, yet Wikiquote lists it as Unsourced with no primary citation and it circulates attributed to multiple figures.

candidates.quote: By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it.
candidates.whyNotable: A clever aphorism heavily attributed to Williams but unsourced on Wikiquote; the general form floats among several athletes and comedians, a classic reassignment risk.

candidates.quote: God gets you to the plate, but once you're there you're on your own.
candidates.whyNotable: A feel-good line widely circulated as Williams wisdom on quote sites, but it appears only in Wikiquote's Unsourced list with no located origin.

candidates.quote: Golf is the only sport where the ball doesn't move until you hit it.
candidates.whyNotable: A quippy line commonly credited to Williams yet unsourced; the same observation is attributed to many golfers and comics, so the Williams credit is doubtful.

candidates.quote: Hitting a baseball — I've said it a thousand times — is the single most difficult thing to do in sport.
candidates.whyNotable: Williams genuinely championed this idea, but the exact wording varies wildly across sources and this version sits in Wikiquote's Unsourced list rather than any primary text.

candidates.quote: I'd have been a .290 hitter without a Louisville Slugger.
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently repeated Williams line crediting his bat, but Wikiquote carries it only as Unsourced with no primary citation.

candidates.quote: I've found that you don't need to wear a necktie if you can hit.
candidates.whyNotable: A characterful Williams one-liner about his disdain for formality, popular on quote sites but unsourced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: The only thing dumber than a pitcher is two pitchers.
candidates.whyNotable: A punchy insult-joke repeated as a Williams zinger but with no source on Wikiquote; the format is a common recycled baseball gag.

candidates.quote: They invented the All-Star game for Willie Mays.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous tribute line credited to Williams and widely quoted, yet it appears only in Wikiquote's Unsourced section without a located origin.

candidates.quote: There has always been a saying in baseball that you can't make a hitter, but I think you can improve a hitter. More than you can improve a fielder.
candidates.whyNotable: Reflects Williams' teaching from The Science of Hitting and is often quoted as his, but Wikiquote lists this wording as Unsourced rather than tying it to the book.

candidates.quote: Do not wait to strike till the iron is hot; but make it hot by striking.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Yeats. QI's earliest instance is Benjamin Franklin's 1782 letter to Rev. Richard Price ("it is not only right to strike while the iron is hot, but that it may be very practicable to heat it by continually striking"), with Richard Sharp's 1806 letter second; the polished form circulated anonymously through the 1800s. Also pinned on Oliver Cromwell and Hemingway. Neil Mann likewise assigns it to Franklin.
candidates.whyNotable: A motivational-poster perennial credited to Yeats, Cromwell and Hemingway alike; QI shows the earliest version is Franklin's, 82 years before Yeats was born.

candidates.quote: Happiness is neither virtue nor pleasure nor this thing nor that but simply growth. We are happy when we are growing.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Butler Yeats, the poet's father, in a 1909 letter to a Miss Grierson — documented by Yeats scholar Neil Mann (author of A Reader's Guide to Yeats's A Vision) on his YeatsVision site.
candidates.whyNotable: A heavily shared self-help line credited to the poet; the Yeats scholarship attributes it to his father's correspondence, making it the second father-son mix-up in the Yeats corpus.

candidates.quote: People who lean on logic and philosophy and rational exposition end by starving the best part of the mind.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Butler Yeats, in a 1906 letter to his son W. B. Yeats — identified by Neil Mann (YeatsVision) among the lines routinely reassigned from father to son.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely circulated on aggregators under the poet's name; the Yeats scholarship pins it to a 1906 letter from his father, the same drift that produced "What can be explained is not poetry."

candidates.quote: What can be explained is not poetry.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Butler Yeats — the poet's father, a painter — in a letter to his son dated 6 September 1915, printed in Passages from the Letters of John Butler Yeats (1917), edited by Ezra Pound. Full original: "What can be explained is not poetry. It is when the powers of explanation desert him that the poet writes verse." Carl Sandburg quoted it correctly in Early Moon (1930) and was later miscredited himself.
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook name-collision misattribution: the line drifts from the obscure father to the Nobel-winning son, and QI documents both the drift and the exact 1915 letter.

candidates.quote: Being Irish, he had an abiding sense of tragedy which sustained him through temporary periods of joy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown/anonymous. QI's earliest citation is a 1991 San Francisco Chronicle piece in which Oliver Stone used a variant about Jim Morrison and credited Yeats; nothing in Yeats's published work supports it, though QI expects a pre-1991 citation exists.
candidates.whyNotable: The go-to "Irish" epigraph in obituaries and St Patrick's Day columns; QI finds zero basis in Yeats and calls it a false consensus built on repetition.

candidates.quote: Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions, but in getting rid of them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Probably genuine Yeats, but resting entirely on one second-hand recollection: Leonard A. G. Strong's 1955 London Magazine article "Yeats at His Ease," recalling Yeats saying it to two English dons at Oxford — published 16 years after Yeats's death. QI notes the long delay detracts from the solidity of the testimony.
candidates.whyNotable: A quotable Yeats line that is real-ish but unpinned to any text — QI shows the whole attribution hangs on one man's memory of an overheard remark, recorded 16 years posthumously.

candidates.quote: I want to take the calculated risk; to dream and to build, to fail and to succeed. I refuse to barter incentive for a dole. I prefer the challenges of life to the guaranteed existence; the thrill of fulfillment to the stale calm of utopia
candidates.trueOrigin: Dean Alfange. It is an excerpt from his creed beginning "I do not choose to be a common man", known as "My Creed" or "An American's Creed", originally published in This Week Magazine and reprinted in The Reader's Digest, October 1952, p. 10 and January 1954, p. 122. The text was later carried at the end of Alfange's own entry in successive editions of Who's Who in America. Also frequently misattributed to Thomas Paine and Abraham Lincoln.
candidates.whyNotable: The strongest candidate by far: a documented misattribution visible inside Wikiquote itself, where the Barter page credits the passage to Sam Walton via a 2010 Bergdahl book while the Opportunity page credits Dean Alfange with full 1952 sourcing.

candidates.quote: The more numerous the laws, the more corrupt the government.
candidates.trueOrigin: Tacitus, Annals, Book III, 27. Also circulates in the loose paraphrase "The closer the collapse of the Empire, the crazier its laws are."
candidates.whyNotable: A libertarian-meme staple credited to Cicero; the Latin (Corruptissima re publica plurimae leges) is Tacitus, not Cicero.

candidates.quote: Time heals all wounds.
candidates.trueOrigin: Terence, Heauton Timorumenos, Act III, scene i — the Latin line circulated as Cicero's is Terence's.
candidates.whyNotable: An everyday English proverb frequently credited to Cicero with a fake Latin tag (Diem adimere aegritudinem hominibus); Wikiquote assigns the Latin to Terence.

candidates.quote: Times are bad. Children no longer obey their parents, and everyone is writing a book.
candidates.trueOrigin: No ancient source. QI traces the "world is coming to an end / everyone wants to write a book" family of sayings through 20th-century humor columns from 1908 onward; the Cicero credit is a late graft (Wikiquote cites InfoWorld, 16 April 2001).
candidates.whyNotable: The classic "kids these days" fake — QI traces the joke's family back to 1908 and shows it has been pinned in turn on an Assyrian tablet, an Egyptian priest, and Cicero, with no ancient source for any version.

candidates.quote: A bureaucrat is the most despicable of men, though he is needed as vultures are needed, but one hardly admires vultures whom bureaucrats so strangely resemble.
candidates.trueOrigin: Taylor Caldwell, A Pillar of Iron (1965), p. 451 — one of three passages from the novel routinely passed off as Cicero.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial anti-government-quote-card line; Wikiquote pins it to Taylor Caldwell's 1965 novel, p. 451, with nothing corresponding in Cicero.

candidates.quote: A nation can survive its fools, and even the ambitious. But it cannot survive treason from within.
candidates.trueOrigin: Taylor Caldwell, A Pillar of Iron (1965), a novel about Cicero — the passage is her fictional Cicero's speech, not Cicero's. Wikiquote notes it may loosely paraphrase the Second Catiline Oration but drastically changes the rhetoric; it was also spread by a 1965 essay by Florida Justice Millard Caldwell.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the single most-shared fake Cicero line in political memes; Wikiquote pins it to Taylor Caldwell's 1965 novel A Pillar of Iron (p. 661), not to any Cicero text.

candidates.quote: The budget should be balanced, the treasury should be refilled, public debt should be reduced, the arrogance of officialdom should be tempered and controlled, and the assistance to foreign lands should be curtailed lest Rome become bankrupt. People must again learn to work, instead of living on public assistance.
candidates.trueOrigin: Taylor Caldwell, A Pillar of Iron (1965), p. 483 — narration describing what Antonius agreed with, not a Cicero quotation. Spread as fact via US congressional hearings from 1966.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly recirculated as "Cicero, 55 B.C." in budget debates; QI shows it is a rewrite of Taylor Caldwell's 1965 novel that Congressman Otto Passman entered into the record as genuine Cicero from 1966 on.

candidates.quote: The evil was not in bread and circuses, per se, but in the willingness of the people to sell their rights as free men for full bellies and the excitement of the games which would serve to distract them from the other human hungers which bread and circuses can never appease.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ben Moreell, "Of Bread and Circuses," The Freeman, January 1956, p. 31. Moreell's piece correctly attributes the phrase "bread and circuses" to Juvenal and says nothing about Cicero.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted "Cicero on bread and circuses" line, but Wikiquote traces it to a 1956 Freeman essay by Admiral Ben Moreell that never mentions Cicero at all.

candidates.quote: Cool Papa was so fast that he could turn off the light switch and get into bed before the room got dark.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paige's tribute to teammate Cool Papa Bell; QI dates his use of the expression to 1969 (also recorded in The Washington Post, April 29, 1969).
candidates.whyNotable: A famous, verified Negro Leagues one-liner genuinely from Paige, giving the hub a real anchor with a clean 1969 citation.

candidates.quote: Don't look back. Something might be gaining on you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paige's — published in the sidebar 'How to Stay Young' of Richard Donovan's June 13, 1953 Collier's profile 'Time Ain't Gonna Mess with Me.' QI concludes Paige deserves credit.
candidates.whyNotable: Paige's single most iconic line and a verified anchor; QI credits it to Paige via the 1953 Collier's 'How to Stay Young' feature.

candidates.quote: I have never thrown an illegal pitch. The trouble is some of my pitches were never seen by this generation until I came along.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paige's — QI's earliest citation is the March 5, 1958 Miami Herald ('Psychiatrist Satch Set for Season'); Paige delivered it repeatedly with varying wording.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, widely-quoted Paige wisecrack with a solid 1958 source, useful as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ogilvy wrote the 1958 Rolls-Royce print advertisement in which the line is the headline; Wikiquote sources it there and calls it the most famous headline in advertising history. Worth noting on the page: the ad itself presents the sentence as a quotation, attributing it to the Technical Editor of The Motor magazine, so Ogilvy's authorship is of the headline rather than of the observation.
candidates.whyNotable: The best-known advertising headline ever written and reliably credited to Ogilvy, with a built-in provenance wrinkle — the ad body credits the observation to a motoring journalist.

candidates.quote: If each of us hires people who are smaller than we are, we shall become a company of dwarfs. But if each of us hires people who are bigger than we are, we shall become a company of giants.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising, p. 47, where he explains he mailed each new office head a Matrioshka doll from Gorky containing this message inside the smallest doll.
candidates.whyNotable: A management-advice staple reshared constantly in truncated form ('hire people bigger than you are'); Wikiquote preserves the full nesting-doll wording that the popular versions strip out.

candidates.quote: Never write an advertisement which you wouldn't want your own family to read.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ogilvy's. QI verified it against hardcopy: Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963), Chapter 5, page 99, where it appears as a chapter maxim followed by 'You wouldn't tell lies to your own wife. Don't tell them to mine.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of the rare heavily-shared Ogilvy lines QI actually confirms as his, verified page-and-chapter against the 1963 hardcopy — a clean anchor beside the debunks.

candidates.quote: The consumer isn't a moron; she is your wife.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ogilvy, Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963), p. 96 (Ballantine Books): 'The consumer isn't a moron; she is your wife. You insult her intelligence if you assume that a mere slogan and a few vapid adjectives will persuade her to buy anything.' A later variant appears in Ogilvy on Advertising, p. 170, as 'The consumer is not a moron, she is your wife.'
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the most-quoted sentence in advertising history and genuinely Ogilvy's, though it circulates in two competing wordings from two different books — a useful wording-drift page.

candidates.quote: I pay low wages. I can take advantage of that. We're going to be successful, but the basis is a very low-wage, low-benefit model of employment.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source identified. Wikiquote's own Sam Walton page hedges it as "Attributed in" Adam L. Penenberg, "Why Google Is Like Wal-Mart", Wired, 21 April 2005 — thirteen years after Walton's death.
candidates.whyNotable: The only quote on Walton's own Wikiquote page and a fixture of Walmart labour-practice commentary, yet Wikiquote sources it merely as "attributed in" a 2005 Wired column rather than to Walton directly.

candidates.quote: Outstanding leaders go out of their way to boost the self-esteem of their personnel. If people believe in themselves, it's amazing what they can accomplish.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source identified. Wikiquote flags the entry with an explicit "attributed" marker and cites only the secondary anthology The 101 Greatest Business Principles of All Time.
candidates.whyNotable: A leadership-poster and corporate-training staple that Wikiquote itself marks with an explicit "attributed" caveat, with no primary Walton record behind it.

candidates.quote: There is only one boss. The customer. And he can fire everybody in the company from the chairman on down, simply by spending his money somewhere else.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source identified. Wikiquote's only citation is Layna Fischer, 2010 BPM and Workflow Handbook, Future Strategies Inc., 2010, p. 178 — published 18 years after Walton's death. Quote Investigator has never examined it.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared line on the internet credited to Sam Walton, yet its earliest documented source is a 2010 business handbook rather than anything Walton is recorded as saying.

candidates.quote: A room without books is like a body without a soul.
candidates.trueOrigin: Sir John Lubbock, "On the Pleasure of Reading," The Contemporary Review vol. 49 (1886), p. 241: Lubbock wrote that "Cicero described a room without books as a body without a soul." Lubbock was probably thinking of Cicero, Ad Atticum 4.8, where the house acquires a mens (mind) once Tyrannio arranges the books.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-printed "Cicero" lines on bookshop merchandise; the exact wording is Sir John Lubbock's 1886 description OF Cicero, not Cicero's own sentence.

candidates.quote: Freedom is participation in power.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown. Wikiquote's Talk:Cicero page states flatly that there is no reference or source to a Latin original anywhere; the aphorism appears to be a modern English coinage loosely evoking De Re Publica's account of libertas, later hardened into a Cicero credit by aggregators.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as Cicero in civic and political writing (Ralph Nader among others), but Wikiquote's editors record it as a misquotation with no Latin original traceable anywhere in Cicero.

candidates.quote: So I close in saying that I might have been given a bad break, but I've got an awful lot to live for
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Gehrig, closing line of his July 4, 1939 farewell speech at Yankee Stadium
candidates.whyNotable: The genuine closing line of Gehrig's 1939 farewell address, sourced on Wikiquote; frequently truncated, paraphrased, or blended with the movie script in circulation, so a verified-wording page has real value.

candidates.quote: Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Gehrig, Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day, Yankee Stadium, July 4, 1939 (his farewell speech)
candidates.whyNotable: The most famous line in American sports oratory and a real anchor for the hub; genuinely Gehrig's, but the popular memory of it is disputed — Wikiquote's exact wording is 'Yet today, I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth,' the line actually OPENED the speech rather than closing it, the Pride of the Yankees (1942) film moved it to the climax, and no complete recording survives, so most people 'remember' the Hollywood version.

candidates.quote: It pains me to see my old company, which has meant so much to America, on the ropes.
candidates.whyNotable: His widely-quoted reaction to Chrysler's 2009 collapse, sourced by Wikiquote to a dated Newsweek interview by Julie Halpert — a clean verified anchor tied to a moment people still search.

candidates.quote: Safety doesn't sell.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-searched line tied to Iacocca, because it is the moral centre of the Ford Pinto scandal — Wikiquote dates it to 1972 and cites both Mark Dowie's 1977 Mother Jones 'Pinto Madness' and a 1990 New York Times piece.

candidates.quote: We've got a gang of clueless bozos steering our ship of state right over a cliff
candidates.whyNotable: The most-shared soundbite from his 2007 bestseller Where Have All the Leaders Gone?, and the rare Iacocca line with a clean primary-source citation on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: A man has to have goals — for a day, for a lifetime — and that was mine, to have people say, 'There goes Ted Williams, the greatest hitter who ever lived.'
candidates.whyNotable: Williams' signature life ambition, primary-sourced to his autobiography My Turn at Bat (1970) — a real anchor amid the fakes and his single most-quoted line.

candidates.quote: If you don't think too good, don't think too much.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous Williams witticism carried on the main Wikiquote page, though sourced only to a 2007 quotations compendium rather than a primary record, so its exact provenance is soft.

candidates.quote: Care about what other people think and you will always be their prisoner.
candidates.trueOrigin: Stephen Mitchell's interpretive translation of the Tao Te Ching (1988), Ch.9; not a faithful rendering of Laozi's words
candidates.whyNotable: Shared endlessly as a direct Lao Tzu quote, but it is Stephen Mitchell's loose 1988 rendering of Tao Te Ching Ch.9, not a literal translation of the original text.

candidates.quote: Friendship is born at that moment when one person says to another, 'What! You too? I thought I was the only one.'
candidates.trueOrigin: C.S. Lewis, The Four Loves (1960).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced and beloved Lewis line on friendship, a strong verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: There are two kinds of people in the end: those who say to God, 'Thy will be done,' and those to whom God says, 'Thy will be done.'
candidates.trueOrigin: C.S. Lewis, The Great Divorce (1945).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted Lewis line with a documented source, useful as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: In dreams begins responsibility.
candidates.trueOrigin: Yeats used it as the epigraph to Responsibilities (1914), crediting it to an unnamed "Old Play" — a source no scholar has located, so the line is generally taken as Yeats's own invention. Delmore Schwartz took it for his 1937 story title, which spread it further.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely Yeatsian anchor with a twist worth a page: Yeats attributed his own famous line to an "Old Play" that appears never to have existed.

candidates.quote: We make out of the quarrel with others, rhetoric, but of the quarrel with ourselves, poetry.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Yeats: Per Amica Silentia Lunae (1918), his prose meditation — Wikiquote carries it as a sourced entry.
candidates.whyNotable: Yeats's most-quoted line of prose and a staple of writing-craft essays; a properly sourced anchor for the hub alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Man can embody truth but he cannot know it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Yeats, letter to Lady Elizabeth Pelham, 4 January 1939 — written weeks before his death and often called his last testament. Sourced on Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: Yeats's most-quoted late aphorism and effectively his final word; a sourced letter makes it a clean verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Let's win one for the Gipper
candidates.trueOrigin: Knute Rockne, halftime speech vs. Army, November 10, 1928
candidates.whyNotable: Rockne's genuinely-delivered 1928 halftime exhortation invoking the late George Gipp, immortalized in the 1940 film Knute Rockne, All American and later adopted as a Reagan-era political catchphrase.

candidates.quote: Football is a game played with arms, legs and shoulders but mostly from the neck up
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Knute Rockne; earliest print citation is Great Quotes from Great Sports Heroes (1997)
candidates.whyNotable: One of Rockne's most-repeated coaching maxims, though its only Wikiquote sourcing is a 1997 quote anthology decades after his 1931 death, so the exact wording is credibly credited rather than contemporaneously documented.

candidates.quote: The secret is to work less as individuals and more as a team. As a coach, I play not my eleven best, but my best eleven
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Knute Rockne; earliest cited in Coaching Champions (1994)
candidates.whyNotable: The iconic 'not my eleven best, but my best eleven' teamwork line is one of Rockne's signature sayings, though its Wikiquote sourcing traces only to a 1994 book, well after his death.

candidates.quote: He had shoulder surgery on his elbow.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Holtz (credibly credited; Wikiquote lists it as Attributed via Bleacher Report without a firm primary source).
candidates.whyNotable: A well-known Holtz malapropism showcasing his folksy verbal style; listed in the Attributed section of his Wikiquote page.

candidates.quote: If what you did yesterday seems big, you haven't done anything today.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Holtz (credibly credited; Wikiquote lists it as Attributed without a firm primary source).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely circulated Holtz motivational line and a real anchor quote for a provenance hub; listed in the Attributed section of his Wikiquote page.

candidates.quote: On this team, we're all united in a common goal: to keep my job.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Holtz (widely attributed to him; no primary date/venue firmly sourced on Wikiquote).
candidates.whyNotable: A signature self-deprecating Holtz one-liner, one of his most-quoted coaching quips; listed in the Attributed section of his Wikiquote page.

candidates.quote: The next flag they plant will be all white, and it'll be surrender.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Holtz (Sports Illustrated, 2005, on Michigan State's flag-planting).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, sourced Holtz zinger about Michigan State's midfield flag-planting; documented via Sports Illustrated (2005) on his Wikiquote page.

candidates.quote: They say a tie is like kissing your sister. I guess that is better than kissing your brother.
candidates.trueOrigin: The base phrase 'a tie is like kissing your sister' predates Holtz (attributed to coach Eddie Erdelatz, 1953); the added 'better than kissing your brother' twist is credited to Lou Holtz.
candidates.whyNotable: Holtz's twist on the classic 'a tie is like kissing your sister' sports saying (which itself predates him, coined by coach Eddie Erdelatz in 1953); his added line is credited to him on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Tullius Cicero
candidates.whyNotable: The origin of the single most-quoted claim about gratitude — that it is the parent of every other virtue; Cicero says it of gratitude specifically (Latin: mater virtutum omnium reliquarum). NOTE: the slide-famous compression 'Gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all others' is a modern paraphrase, not any published translation — use the Yonge wording above if you want a line you can defend.

candidates.quote: Let the welfare of the people be the ultimate law.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine: Cicero, De Legibus, Book III, section 3.
candidates.whyNotable: Salus populi suprema lex esto — a real, precisely sourced Cicero line that is the state motto of Missouri and a standing citation in constitutional argument.

candidates.quote: Not to know what happened before you were born is to be a child forever.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine: Cicero, Orator ad M. Brutum, ch. XXXIV, sec. 120 — Nescire autem quid ante quam natus sis acciderit, id est semper esse puerum.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Cicero line (Orator 120) that is heavily quoted in history and education contexts, usually in the shorter variant "To be ignorant of the past is to be forever a child."

candidates.quote: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
candidates.trueOrigin: Tao Te Ching, Chapter 64 (genuine, though English wording varies by translation)
candidates.whyNotable: The single most famous genuinely-sourced Lao Tzu line, from Tao Te Ching Ch.64 (千里之行始於足下) — a real anchor for the hub, though it is itself often re-misattributed to Confucius.

candidates.quote: He who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know.
candidates.trueOrigin: Tao Te Ching, Chapter 56 (genuine)
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely-sourced Tao Te Ching line (Ch.56) that anchors the hub with real, verifiable Laozi material alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Don't just do something, sit there.
candidates.trueOrigin: A rearranged cliche in print well before him: Quote Investigator's earliest close match is journalist Ollie Crawford in The Philadelphia Inquirer, August 1954 ('Don't just do something. Sit there.'), with producer Martin Gabel's 'Don't just do something; stand there' from 1945. Thich Nhat Hanh used it in a 1983 Vajradhatu Sun interview and Sylvia Boorstein titled a 1996 book with it — both after it was already circulating.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared 'Thich Nhat Hanh' one-liner on mindfulness social media, and the only QI investigation that touches him — QI shows he popularized it but did not coin it, ~30 years after it appeared in a newspaper column about radar platforms.

candidates.quote: If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, quoted in 'Meditations for Living In Balance' (2000).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, heavily shared compassion line with a sourced Wikiquote entry (Meditations for Living In Balance, 2000) — a real anchor to sit beside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Love and compassion are necessities, not luxuries. Without them humanity cannot survive.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, 'The Art of Happiness' / compassion writings (cited via A Small Drop of Ink, 2003).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, frequently cited line with a sourced Wikiquote entry, useful as a verified hub anchor alongside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: My true religion is Kindness.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, 'Kindness, Clarity, and Insight' (1984).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted anchor line with a sourced Wikiquote entry from his book Kindness, Clarity, and Insight (1984).

candidates.quote: We must all suffer from one of two pains: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret. The difference is discipline weighs ounces while regret weighs tons.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Jim Rohn (American motivational speaker, 1930-2009); listed in the main Quotes section of his Wikiquote page, though without a precise book/seminar citation.
candidates.whyNotable: The lone quote featured on Jim Rohn's Wikiquote page and one of his signature motivational lines, widely circulated as a real Rohn aphorism.

candidates.quote: Change the way you look at things, and the things you look at change.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wayne Dyer, who included the line in his 2004 book The Power of Intention. QI found no substantive evidence for the popular Max Planck attribution — that error likely arose because Dyer tied the idea to quantum physics, and Planck was the famous quantum theorist.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous 'quantum' inspirational quote falsely pinned on physicist Max Planck; QI credits it to Wayne Dyer's 2004 The Power of Intention.

candidates.quote: We are not human beings having a spiritual experience. We are spiritual beings having a human experience.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wayne W. Dyer is QI's most-likely originator (a version appeared in a 1988 Time magazine ad of his writing; the exact statement is in his 1989 book You'll See It When You Believe It). No instance has been found in Teilhard de Chardin's actual works; Stephen Covey's Teilhard attribution appears to have spread the error.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared spiritual quotes on the internet, near-universally credited to Teilhard de Chardin — but QI traces it back to Wayne Dyer himself, making Dyer the real author of a line pinned on a French philosopher-priest.

candidates.quote: The most rewarding things you do in life are often the ones that look like they cannot be done
candidates.trueOrigin: Likely Arnold Palmer — QI found no competing ascription — but the earliest evidence is indirect: an August 1966 speech by U.S. Steel president Leslie B. Worthington who credited Palmer, not Palmer's own words.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely reshared motivational line often doubted as a 'fake Palmer' quote; QI actually leans toward it being genuine but flags that only indirect second-hand sourcing exists.

candidates.quote: It's hard not to play golf that's up to Jack Nicklaus standards when you are Jack Nicklaus.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Nicklaus
candidates.whyNotable: A rare sourced Nicklaus line on Wikiquote, said on WINS Radio after winning his 70th PGA tournament, useful as a verified anchor alongside debunks.

candidates.quote: The older you get the stronger the wind gets - and it's always in your face.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Nicklaus
candidates.whyNotable: One of the two quotes Wikiquote actually sources to Nicklaus (International Herald Tribune, 28 Feb 1990); a widely-shared, verifiable anchor line.

candidates.quote: Those who play with the devil's toys will be brought by degrees to wield his sword.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Fuller, The Profane State (1642): 'they which play with the devils rattles, will be brought by degrees to wield his sword.' Reprinted with correct attribution in Chambers's Cyclopaedia of English Literature (1902); an ambiguous 'Fuller' credit in The Evening World (1921) likely seeded the confusion, and citations to Buckminster Fuller appear from about 2005 onward.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as a Buckminster Fuller warning about technology — a textbook name-collision misattribution: QI found no evidence Buckminster ever said it, and traced it to the 17th-century English clergyman Thomas Fuller.

candidates.quote: The miracle is not to walk on water. The miracle is to walk on the green earth in the present moment.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Wikiquote sources it to Touching Peace (1992). A close variant appears in The Miracle of Mindfulness ('People usually consider walking on water or in thin air a miracle. But I think the real miracle is to walk on earth').
candidates.whyNotable: His single best-known line and a real anchor for the hub, with the added hook that two different published wordings circulate as if they were one quote.

candidates.quote: The most precious gift we can offer others is our presence.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine teaching, published by Plum Village — the monastic community Thich Nhat Hanh founded and the institutional keeper of his legacy — as the ground of the first of the Six Mantras of True Love ('Darling, I am here for you'). Exact published wording varies across his books and talks.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably his most-shared line about relationships; verified against his own community's teaching library rather than an aggregator, though no single page-level citation pins the exact wording.

candidates.quote: Your true home is in the here and the now.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Wikiquote sources it to his essay 'Returning Home', Shambhala Sun, March 2006.
candidates.whyNotable: The compressed statement of his central teaching and one of the most-reproduced lines from his obituaries in 2022; carries a precise periodical citation, which is rare for his viral quotes.

candidates.quote: Everyone is born a genius, but the process of living de-geniuses them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote's sourced version, a statement made in 1974 and quoted in People magazine (via Thomas T. K. Zung, Buckminster Fuller: Anthology for the New Millennium, 2002, p. 174): 'I am convinced all of humanity is born with more gifts than we know. Most are born geniuses and just get de-geniused rapidly.' The Buckminster Fuller Institute notes that Fuller 'said the same thing many times in various ways' and that many circulating 'rogue' quotes cannot be sourced.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of education-reform talks and TED-style keynotes; Wikiquote's sourced entry carries a materially different 1974 wording, so the aphorism in circulation is a tightened paraphrase rather than anything Fuller is documented saying.

candidates.quote: There's nothing in a caterpillar that tells you it's going to be a butterfly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fuller's documented original, from 'Planetary Planning' (1970, based on a November 1969 lecture): 'The single-frame picture of a caterpillar does not foretell its transformation into a butterfly.' The streamlined modern wording was published by Helen Hayes in Our Best Years (1984); QI states it cannot confirm Fuller used it.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial motivational-poster and commencement-speech line credited to Fuller; QI traced the underlying idea to Fuller's 1970 article but could not confirm he ever used the simplified popular wording, which surfaced in Helen Hayes's 1984 book.

candidates.quote: You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete.
candidates.trueOrigin: Popular wording first documented in Daniel Quinn, Beyond Civilization: Humanity's Next Great Adventure (1999), p. 137, uncited. The best-documented Fuller original is from Mike Vance's pre-1983 interview, published in Think Out of the Box (1995): 'You never change anything by fighting it; you change things by making them obsolete through superior technology.' QI: 'Other versions of this quotation do not have solid supporting evidence.'
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared 'Fuller' line on the internet — the staple of innovation decks and startup manifestos — yet QI found the popular wording has no support from Fuller himself and traces it to Daniel Quinn's 1999 book Beyond Civilization, which printed it without citation.

candidates.quote: When you stop talking, you've lost your customer. When you turn your back, you've lost her.
candidates.trueOrigin: Credited to Estée Lauder herself; Wikiquote's citation is secondary — 'Run your own business: Make your company a success with help from classic thinkers', Infinite Ideas, 4 May 2012, p. 69 — not a primary Lauder source. Her 1985 memoir 'Estée: A Success Story' is the likely primary origin but is unconfirmed.
candidates.whyNotable: The only Estée Lauder quote documented anywhere on Wikiquote — her signature customer-service maxim, widely reproduced in business writing and the closest thing to a verifiable anchor line for this author.

candidates.quote: You handle animals. You deal with people.
candidates.trueOrigin: Red Auerbach; sourced in Billy Packer & Roland Lazenby, Why We Win (Masters Press, 1999), p. 15.
candidates.whyNotable: Auerbach's genuinely-sourced signature line on his people-first coaching philosophy — the one quote Wikiquote documents with a citation, useful as a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: In a world of individuals, comparison is a senseless activity.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wayne Dyer — sourced by Wikiquote to his 1978 book Pulling Your Own Strings.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, book-sourced Dyer line (Pulling Your Own Strings, 1978) that serves as a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: You will never win if you have to prove that you are the winner.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wayne Dyer — sourced by Wikiquote to his 1978 book Pulling Your Own Strings.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, Wikiquote-sourced Dyer line from Pulling Your Own Strings (1978), a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: I've always believed the British Open is one of the greatest championships in the world
candidates.trueOrigin: Arnold Palmer, Arnold Palmer: Memories, Stories, and Memorabilia from a Life on and Off the Course (2004), p. 52.
candidates.whyNotable: A cleanly book-sourced Palmer quote credited with reviving American interest in the Open Championship; a documented, verifiable anchor.

candidates.quote: Maybe you'll fail most of the time, but until you've dared to try and have brought off an impossible shot from the rough or from the water, you haven't really tasted the game
candidates.trueOrigin: Arnold Palmer, My Game and Yours (1965), p. 83.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, book-sourced Palmer line on daring the impossible shot — a real anchor to sit alongside the debunked feel-good quotes.

candidates.quote: For the love of money is the root of all evil
candidates.trueOrigin: Paul the Apostle
candidates.whyNotable: The correct wording of the most-misquoted money line in English — putting the real verse on a slide quietly corrects the audience's "money is the root of all evil" and makes the sharper point that the fault is in the craving, not the coin.

candidates.quote: In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paul the Apostle
candidates.whyNotable: The scriptural anchor of the whole theme and the source of the phrase 'in everything give thanks'; the KJV wording is the one audiences recognise and is free of translation-copyright risk (unlike NIV/ESV/NRSV).

candidates.quote: Death is nothing at all. I have only slipped away into the next room.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry Scott Holland
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the most-read funeral text in the English-speaking world. Worth knowing it is prose from a sermon delivered while Edward VII lay in state, not a poem — and that Holland offered it as one attitude to death among several.

candidates.quote: Don't fight forces, use them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Shelter magazine, Vol. 2 No. 4 (May 1932), p. 36, and No. 5 (November 1932), p. 108; cited in Krausse and Lichtenstein (eds.), Your Private Sky: Discourse (2001), p. 17. Sometimes paraphrased as 'Don't oppose forces, use them.' Fuller repeated it in the 1981 Norie Huddle interview.
candidates.whyNotable: Fuller's earliest famous maxim and the seed of the much-mangled 'never change things by fighting' family of quotes; unlike those, this one has a hard 1932 periodical citation, which makes it useful for contrast on the same hub.

candidates.quote: God, to me, it seems is a verb, not a noun, proper or improper.
candidates.trueOrigin: R. Buckminster Fuller, No More Secondhand God (1963), where it appears as verse. The popular short form 'God is a verb' is a compression of this passage.
candidates.whyNotable: Fuller's most-quoted theological line, endlessly recirculated in shortened form as 'God is a verb'; Wikiquote carries it with a firm book source, so it anchors the hub as a verified counterweight.

candidates.quote: Now there is one outstandingly important fact regarding Spaceship Earth, and that is that no instruction book came with it.
candidates.trueOrigin: R. Buckminster Fuller, Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth (1969), Chapter 4, pp. 52-53. QI verified with scans of the original text and credits Fuller with the formulation.
candidates.whyNotable: Fuller's signature idea and the line that made 'Spaceship Earth' a permanent phrase in environmental language; QI verified it against scans of the original 1969 book, making it a clean anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Last year over one million quarter-inch drills were sold, not because people wanted quarter-inch drills but because they wanted quarter-inch holes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Leo McGivena — Levitt credited him by name in 'The Marketing Mode' (1969), and Percy H. Whiting's 1947 book had already attributed the line to McGivena; QI finds an earlier anonymous 1942 advertisement using the same argument.
candidates.whyNotable: The long-form original of the drill/hole adage, still printed under Levitt's byline in marketing textbooks even though Levitt was quoting someone else and Wikiquote's own Levitt entry sources it only to a Christensen anthology.

candidates.quote: A real decision is measured by the fact that you've taken a new action
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Awaken the Giant Within (1992), p. 49.
candidates.whyNotable: Signature Robbins line on decision-making, sourced by Wikiquote to Awaken the Giant Within (1992).

candidates.quote: All personal breakthroughs begin with a change in beliefs
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Awaken the Giant Within (1992), p. 85.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently reshared genuine Robbins line, sourced by Wikiquote to Awaken the Giant Within (1992).

candidates.quote: Beliefs have the power to create and the power to destroy
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Awaken the Giant Within (1992), p. 75.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared genuine Robbins line, sourced by Wikiquote to Awaken the Giant Within (1992).

candidates.quote: The quality of your life is the quality of your communication
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Unlimited Power (1986), p. 198.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Robbins' most-quoted genuine lines, sourced by Wikiquote to his 1986 book Unlimited Power; a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: It's easier to hold to your principles 100% of the time than it is to hold to them 98% of the time.
candidates.trueOrigin: Clayton Christensen — the line comes from 'How Will You Measure Your Life?' (HBR, July 2010; book edition 2012), not from The Innovator's Dilemma (1997) where Wikiquote currently files it. The source, not the speaker, is what's in question.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Christensen line whose source is routinely misdated to The Innovator's Dilemma — including by Wikiquote itself — making it a clean 'right author, wrong book' correction page.

candidates.quote: Management is the most noble of professions if it's practiced well. No other occupation offers as many ways to help others learn and grow.
candidates.trueOrigin: Clayton Christensen, 'How Will You Measure Your Life?', Harvard Business Review (2010), collected in HBR's 10 Must Reads on Managing Yourself (2011).
candidates.whyNotable: The most-shared inspirational Christensen line on LinkedIn and in leadership decks, and one of the few with a clean, citable Wikiquote source behind it.

candidates.quote: The prediction of my disruption theory would be that Apple won't succeed with the iPhone. History speaks pretty loudly on that.
candidates.trueOrigin: Clayton Christensen, quoted in a June 2006 interview (Jeremy's Blog / Business Week era commentary); genuine and sourced at Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: Christensen's most-circulated line on the internet is a real one he came to regret, and it is almost always paraphrased down to 'the iPhone will fail' — a documented-wording page has obvious search value.

candidates.quote: The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Archilochus, Greek lyric poet, 7th century BC (Fragment 201). The line entered modern currency through Isaiah Berlin's 1953 essay 'The Hedgehog and the Fox'; Collins borrowed it in Good to Great (2001) as the basis of his 'Hedgehog Concept,' and business readers have credited him for the aphorism ever since.
candidates.whyNotable: The only documented reassignment in Collins's orbit — business writers routinely present this ~2,700-year-old Greek fragment as 'Jim Collins's hedgehog,' when Wikiquote sources it to Archilochus Fragment 201 by way of Isaiah Berlin.

candidates.quote: Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Gospel of Matthew (King James Version)
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted consolation line in the English language and the backbone of Western funeral liturgy; the KJV wording is the one audiences recognise.
candidates.notes: King James Version · King James Version

candidates.quote: A culture of discipline is not a principle of business, it is a principle of greatness.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Collins — Good To Great And The Social Sectors (2005), p. 1.
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily reproduced on leadership slide decks and nonprofit-management sites, usually with no source at all; Wikiquote pins it to a specific monograph and page.

candidates.quote: For no matter what we achieve, if we don't spend the vast majority of our time with people we love and respect, we cannot possibly have a great life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Collins — Good to Great (2001), as cited in Lisa Marshall, Speak the Truth and Point to Hope (2004), p. 32.
candidates.whyNotable: His most-shared line on social media and the one most often stripped of attribution entirely, since it reads as generic inspirational copy rather than business research.

candidates.quote: Good is the enemy of great.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Collins — the opening line of Good to Great (2001). Note the much older antecedent in Voltaire's 'le mieux est l'ennemi du bien' (the best is the enemy of the good), which Collins inverted rather than coined.
candidates.whyNotable: His single most-quoted line and the first sentence of the book that sold over 4 million copies; Wikiquote sources it, and the page can add value by tracing the Voltaire antecedent that Collins reworked.

candidates.quote: It is better to first get the right people on the bus, the wrong people off the bus, and the right people in the right seats, and then figure out where to drive.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Collins — Good to Great (2001), p. 41.
candidates.whyNotable: The 'right people on the bus' metaphor is the most-paraphrased idea in modern management writing; the short form circulates so widely that most searchers have never seen the full sourced sentence.

candidates.quote: There is a direct relationship between the absence of celebrity and the presence of good-to-great results.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Collins — interview in Fast Company, October 2001.
candidates.whyNotable: The clearest one-sentence statement of his Level 5 leadership finding, and the rare Collins quote with a datable primary interview source rather than a book page.

candidates.quote: Those who built the visionary companies wisely understood that it is better to understand who you are than where you are going, for where you are going will almost certainly change.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Collins, with Jerry I. Porras — Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies (1994), p. xx.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared in truncated form as 'It is better to understand who you are than where you are going,' which strips both the co-author Jerry Porras and the qualifying clause.

candidates.quote: Oh, the comfort—the inexpressible comfort of feeling safe with a person—having neither to weigh thoughts, nor measure words, but pouring them all right out, just as they are, chaff and grain together; certain that a faithful hand will take and sift them, keep what is worth keeping, and then with the breath of kindness blow the rest away
candidates.trueOrigin: Dinah Maria Mulock Craik
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive passage on trust and ease between friends — and a rare chance to attribute correctly: it is near-universally credited to George Eliot, who did not write it. Can be trimmed at "chaff and grain together" for a slide.

candidates.quote: He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase
candidates.trueOrigin: The Preacher (Qoheleth), Book of Ecclesiastes
candidates.whyNotable: The oldest and cleanest statement of the "enough" problem: appetite scales with supply, so accumulation can never terminate itself. Three thousand years ahead of the hedonic-treadmill literature.
candidates.notes: Qoheleth), Book of Ecclesiastes · Qoheleth), Book of Ecclesiastes

candidates.quote: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Book of Isaiah (King James Version)
candidates.whyNotable: The most widely quoted waiting passage in English, and the one that most explicitly promises that waiting restores rather than depletes — the core "waiting well" claim.
candidates.notes: King James Version · King James Version

candidates.quote: The strength of the team is each individual member. The strength of each member is the team.
candidates.trueOrigin: Phil Jackson's own phrasing, closely echoing Rudyard Kipling's 'For the strength of the pack is the wolf, and the strength of the wolf is the pack'
candidates.whyNotable: Jackson's most-circulated leadership line is genuinely his wording, but a near-direct adaptation of Kipling's wolf-pack couplet.

candidates.quote: You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wayne Gretzky, January 1983 interview with Bob McKenzie of The Hockey News
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely Gretzky's, first said in a January 1983 Hockey News interview; the rarely-quoted follow-up added 'even though there's only a 1-5% chance of scoring.'

candidates.quote: Less is more.
candidates.magnetAuthor: R. Buckminster Fuller; Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
candidates.creditedTo: R. Buckminster Fuller; Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
candidates.trueOrigin: Robert Browning, 'Andrea del Sarto' (1855); earlier German analogue 'minder ist oft mehr' in Christoph Martin Wieland, Der Teutsche Merkur (1774). Fuller's actual contribution was 'doing more with less,' part of his definition of ephemeralization — a distinct idea.
candidates.whyNotable: The founding motto of minimalism, pinned on Fuller (and on Mies van der Rohe) constantly; Wikiquote's Misattributed section flags it for both men and points to a Victorian poem and an 18th-century German original long predating either.

candidates.quote: Sometimes I think we're alone in the universe, and sometimes I think we're not. In either case the idea is quite staggering.
candidates.magnetAuthor: Arthur C. Clarke; R. Buckminster Fuller
candidates.creditedTo: Arthur C. Clarke; R. Buckminster Fuller
candidates.trueOrigin: Origin genuinely unresolved. Earliest close match: a November 1966 New Yorker profile in which Stanley Kubrick credited it to an unnamed English science-fiction writer; by September 1968 in Playboy he ascribed it instead to an unnamed 'prominent astronomer.' A thematically related but less dramatic passage appears in Clarke's The Exploration of Space (1951), and a similar idea in Walt Kelly's Pogo (1959). No documented Fuller usage.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared lines in science-popularization culture, credited to Clarke and to Fuller alike; QI found neither man can be documented saying it and that Stanley Kubrick popularized it in 1966 while explicitly declining to claim it.

candidates.quote: Revenge is a dish best served cold
candidates.trueOrigin: Not spoken in The Godfather (1972) or its sequels, and not a Sicilian proverb. Quote Investigator records the wording in Mario Puzo's 1969 novel The Godfather as "Revenge is a dish that tastes best when it is cold" — and traces the saying itself back at least to Eugène Sue's 1841 French novel Mathilde: Mémoires D'une Jeune Femme ("Et puis la vengeance se mange très-bien froide, comme on dit vulgairement" — "And revenge is best eaten cold, as they say vulgarly"), where Sue presents it as already in common circulation, so its coiner is unknown. Sue suggested in 1847 it was a Roman proverb; QI found no support. Metternich, Talleyrand and Bismarck have all been wrongly credited, all long after the saying was in circulation.
candidates.whyNotable: Very widely believed to be an 'old Sicilian proverb' delivered in The Godfather. It is in neither film; the novel's wording differs from the popular form; and the saying predates Puzo by at least 128 years. This is exactly the borrowed-line error class — a work being credited with a saying it inherited.

candidates.quote: Alone bad. Friend good.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wrong punctuation/emphasis and wrong film. Actual line: "Alone: bad. Friend: good!" — The Monster (Boris Karloff) in BRIDE OF FRANKENSTEIN (1935), not Frankenstein (1931). Written by William Hurlbut (screenplay and adaptation) with John L. Balderston (adaptation), directed by James Whale, Universal Pictures. As above, the 1931 Monster is mute; the creature only gains speech in the 1935 sequel after the hermit teaches him words.
candidates.whyNotable: Routinely quoted as 'the Frankenstein monster's line' and used as the stock template for broken-monster speech. The clipped popular form drops the colons that structure Karloff's actual delivery, and the attribution silently moves it back four years to a film where the character cannot talk.

candidates.quote: Fire bad!
candidates.trueOrigin: Wrong words AND wrong film. Actual line: "Fire: no good." — spoken by The Monster (Boris Karloff) in BRIDE OF FRANKENSTEIN (1935), not in Frankenstein (1931). Screenplay and adaptation by William Hurlbut, adaptation by John L. Balderston; directed by James Whale; Universal Pictures (work for hire — Universal is the rights holder). Decisive point: the Monster in the 1931 film is MUTE and has no dialogue whatsoever, so no talking-monster line can originate there. Wikiquote's 1931 page lists zero lines for the Monster; every Monster line is on the 1935 Bride page.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted 'Frankenstein monster' line in circulation, used constantly as shorthand for lumbering primitive speech (and riffed on directly in Buffy's "Fire bad, tree pretty"). It is a paraphrase of a line from the sequel, pinned on a film in which the creature never speaks. Both halves — the real wording and the real film — are transcribed at Wikiquote, which is exactly the popular-vs-transcript pair this site exists to publish.

candidates.quote: It's not personal, it's strictly business
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "It's not personal, Sonny. It's strictly business." — Michael Corleone (Al Pacino), arguing the case for killing Sollozzo and McCluskey, as transcribed at Wikiquote. Screenplay by Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo; The Godfather (1972), Paramount Pictures. The freestanding aphorism drops the vocative "Sonny" that anchors it to that specific argument, and it commonly drifts further into "it's just business" / "it's nothing personal, it's business" — none of those are the spoken line.
candidates.whyNotable: A stock phrase of corporate and negotiating speech that almost nobody quotes in the form it was said. Wikiquote's transcription gives the exact wording, which lets the drift be shown rather than asserted.

candidates.quote: Never take sides against the family
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "Fredo, you're my older brother and I love you, but don't ever take sides with anyone against the family again, ever." — Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) to Fredo, as transcribed at Wikiquote. Screenplay by Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo, from Puzo's 1969 novel; The Godfather (1972), Paramount Pictures. The short imperative "Never take sides against the family" is a popular compression that is not spoken in the film.
candidates.whyNotable: The compressed form circulates as a standalone maxim on posters, in listicles and in business writing, and is far shorter and more absolute than the line actually delivered. Wikiquote's transcription pins the real wording exactly.

candidates.quote: We belong dead.
candidates.trueOrigin: Right words, wrong film. Actual line in full: "Yes, go! You live! Go! [to Dr. Pretorius] You stay! We BELONG dead!" — The Monster (Boris Karloff) in BRIDE OF FRANKENSTEIN (1935), not Frankenstein (1931). Written by William Hurlbut (screenplay and adaptation) and John L. Balderston (adaptation); directed by James Whale; Universal Pictures. Not in Mary Shelley's 1818 novel and not in Peggy Webling's 1927 play — it is an invention of the 1935 screenplay.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as the emotional climax of 'Frankenstein' and frequently credited to the 1931 original or loosely to Mary Shelley. The wording survives intact in popular use; the error is purely one of source, and both the correct film and the surrounding sentence are transcribed at Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: What we have here is a failure to communicate.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line (the famous one): "What we've got here is... failure to communicate." — spoken by the Captain (Strother Martin), and the form honoured by AFI at #11 on 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes, with no article before "failure". Luke (Paul Newman) echoes it near the end in a second, distinct form: "What we've got here is a failure to communicate." Neither in-film line uses "we have" — the popular wording swaps "we've got" for "we have", and the Captain's AFI-listed line has no "a". Written by Frank R. Pierson; screenplay credit is shared, Donn Pearce and Frank R. Pierson, from Pearce's own 1965 novel Cool Hand Luke. The line did NOT originate in the novel — TCM reports "Pearce never wrote the line in his novel; it was added by screenwriter Frank Pierson" (https://www.tcm.com/articles/369667/pop-culture-101-cool-hand-luke), and Pearce objected to it as too intellectual for the Captain. Film released 1967 by Warner Bros.-Seven Arts (Jalem Productions); screen writing is work-for-hire, so the studio holds the rights, not Pierson.
candidates.whyNotable: The signature wrong-words case for this title and one of the most-quoted lines in American film. The public form is a double drift: "we have" for "we've got", plus an "a" the AFI-honoured line does not contain. It is also a wrong-writer case underneath — the line is routinely credited to novelist Donn Pearce, whose novel does not contain it. Wikiquote transcribes both in-film variants, so the wording claim rests on a transcription rather than recall.

candidates.quote: You want the truth? You can't handle the truth!
candidates.trueOrigin: Never spoken as one line. Actual exchange, per the Wikiquote transcription — Col. Jessup: "You want answers?" / Lt. Kaffee: "I want the truth!" / Jessup: "You can't handle the truth!" The popular version collapses three speech acts into one and hands Kaffee's demand for the truth to Jessup as a taunt. Written by Aaron Sorkin, adapted from his own 1989 Broadway play of the same name (Music Box Theatre, opened 15 November 1989); A Few Good Men (1992), directed by Rob Reiner, produced by Castle Rock Entertainment and released by Columbia Pictures. Rights holder is the studio, not Sorkin — screen writing is work-for-hire.
candidates.whyNotable: This is the classic wrong-words-from-the-right-source error and the highest-value record for this title. The line is AFI's #29 movie quotation, so the misremembering is extremely widespread: the setup question in the film is "You want answers?", not "You want the truth?", and the words "I want the truth" belong to Kaffee, not Jessup. Wikiquote transcribes the actual exchange verbatim, so the wording claim rests on a transcription rather than recall. Corroborated as a documented misquote by NBC/TODAY's "movie quotes you always get wrong" roundup and by published iconic-misquote lists, which give the same wrong version and the same actual dialogue.

candidates.quote: Charity begins at home
candidates.whyNotable: A proverb, not scripture; earliest forms trace to Terence and Wycliffe, not the Bible.

candidates.quote: Neither a borrower nor a lender be
candidates.whyNotable: Shakespeare (Polonius, Hamlet), not the Bible.

candidates.quote: Pride goeth before a fall
candidates.whyNotable: A compression of Proverbs 16:18 ('Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall').

candidates.quote: Spare the rod, spoil the child
candidates.whyNotable: The exact wording is from Samuel Butler's Hudibras (1663), echoing but not quoting Proverbs.

candidates.quote: The lion shall lie down with the lamb
candidates.whyNotable: A popular conflation; Isaiah 11:6 actually reads 'the wolf shall dwell with the lamb.'

candidates.quote: This too shall pass
candidates.whyNotable: Widely believed to be scripture; it is not in the Bible — a Persian-adage / Sufi origin retold by Edward FitzGerald and Lincoln.

candidates.quote: To thine own self be true
candidates.whyNotable: It's Shakespeare (Polonius in Hamlet), routinely mistaken for scripture.

candidates.quote: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
candidates.magnetAuthor: Jesus, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke
candidates.creditedTo: Jesus, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke
candidates.trueOrigin: Jesus, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke
candidates.whyNotable: The most famous act of forgiveness in Western culture, in the most quotable English rendering; the KJV text is free of copyright everywhere outside the UK.

candidates.quote: He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
candidates.trueOrigin: Proverbs 25:28
candidates.whyNotable: The strongest image available for the absence of self-restraint: not weakness but defencelessness. Carries weight on a slide without needing a religious frame.

candidates.quote: A census taker once tried to test me. I ate his liver with some fava beans and a nice Chianti.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Ted Tally, adapting Thomas Harris's 1988 novel; spoken by Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins); The Silence of the Lambs (1991), dir. Jonathan Demme, Orion Pictures (rights holder). Wikiquote transcribes this wording exactly and AFI lists it identically at #21. Origination nuance: the line is Harris's from the novel, but the novel reads "a big Amarone" — "a nice Chianti" is Ted Tally's substitution for the film (Tally has said he had never heard of Amarone). So the famous WORDING is the film's even though the line is not.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. AFI #21 on 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes, and the wording is confirmed identically by two independent authorities (Wikiquote transcription and AFI). Doubles as a quiet origination lesson: the single word everyone remembers, "Chianti", is the one word the novelist did not write.

candidates.quote: All we've got is cotton, and slaves and...arrogance.
candidates.trueOrigin: Transcribed verbatim at Wikiquote, spoken by Rhett Butler (Clark Gable) at Twelve Oaks. ORIGINATION: adapted from Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel, chapter 6, which Wikiquote transcribes as: "Why, all we have is cotton and slaves and arrogance. They'd lick us in a month." The film tightened the novel's sentence; it did not originate the line. Gone with the Wind (1939), Selznick International Pictures, dist. MGM. Screen credit Sidney Howard; writing shared/disputed (Hecht, Selznick, Swerling, Garrett, Keon, Van Druten uncredited).
candidates.whyNotable: The single best-evidenced origination case on this title: both the film wording AND the earlier novel wording are transcribed at Wikiquote, so the film-borrowed-this claim can be cited on both sides from the authority itself rather than inferred. Lower search demand than the others, but the strongest provenance.

candidates.quote: Elementary, my dear Holmes, elementary.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Edwin Blum and William A. Drake for The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1939), 20th Century Fox. Spoken by Nigel Bruce as Dr. Watson, answering Rathbone's Holmes ('Very effective, my dear Watson!') in the film's closing exchange, after Watson swats a fly Holmes was trying to shoo with his violin. Rights holder is the studio (work-for-hire).
candidates.whyNotable: The film's actual closing beat, and the exact counterweight to the misquote above: what this film demonstrably ends on is Watson INVERTING the catchphrase back onto Holmes, not Holmes delivering it. Wikiquote transcribes it verbatim with both speakers. Load-bearing context for any page asserting what the 1939 film did or did not say.

candidates.quote: Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn.
candidates.trueOrigin: Transcribed verbatim at Wikiquote as the closing line of the film, spoken by Rhett Butler (Clark Gable). Gone with the Wind (1939), Selznick International Pictures, distributed by MGM. ORIGINATION: the film is widely credited with coining this, but the line is adapted from Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel, where Rhett's line reads "My dear, I don't give a damn" — the film's contribution is the word "Frankly." AUTHORSHIP: sole screen credit to Sidney Howard, but disputed/shared in practice (Hecht, Selznick, Swerling, Garrett, Keon, Van Druten all uncredited; Selznick claimed most of the dialogue).
candidates.whyNotable: AFI #1 of the top 100 movie quotations. Serves as the verified anchor for this title, and carries the origination correction: the film sharpened a novel line rather than inventing one.

candidates.quote: Gentlemen, it's been a privilege flying with you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apollo 13 (1995), spoken by the Jim Lovell character (Tom Hanks). Screenplay by William Broyles Jr. & Al Reinert (uncredited rewrite by John Sayles); Imagine Entertainment, distributed by Universal Pictures; based on Lost Moon (1994) by Jim Lovell & Jeffrey Kluger. A written screen line, not a transcribed 1970 transmission — the writers are the authors; Lovell is the character, Hanks the actor.
candidates.whyNotable: Transcribed exactly on Wikiquote under Jim Lovell, with no dispute note. Serves as a clean anchor for the title: widely quoted and correctly sourced to the film, so the page asserts no correction. Worth stating plainly that it is a scripted line rather than something the real crew radioed, since this title's whole problem is readers assuming film dialogue is transcript.

candidates.quote: Here's looking at you, kid.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein and Howard Koch — Casablanca (1942), dir. Michael Curtiz, Warner Bros. (work-for-hire; rights holder Warner Bros., not the writers). Spoken by Rick Blaine, played by Humphrey Bogart — the actor is the speaker, not the author. Adapted from the unproduced 1940 play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison; Wikiquote does not establish whether the line originated in the play.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor for the title: sourced exactly on Wikiquote and ranked #5 in AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes. Transcribed in full context ("All right, I will. Here's looking at you, kid.") and repeated in the airport farewell. Useful as a control against the misquotes — this one the public actually gets right, while still misattributing its authorship to Bogart rather than the Epsteins and Koch. (A persistent legend holds Bogart ad-libbed it while teaching Bergman poker between takes; that is NOT documented at Wikiquote or QI and must not be asserted on the page.)

candidates.quote: He's dead, Jim.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine recurring line of Dr. Leonard McCoy (DeForest Kelley) across many Star Trek: The Original Series episodes (Desilu/Paramount for NBC, 1966-69) — e.g. "The Changeling" — with variants "She's dead, Jim" and "It's dead, Jim". As a catchphrase repeated across episodes by different writers it has no single writing credit. Wikiquote records that Kelley had already delivered a near-identical line, "He's dead, Captain", as a military physician in the 1956 film The Man in the Grey Flannel Suit — a decade before Star Trek.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor, and the control case for the "You're dead, Jim" misquote above — pairing them shows readers the exact axis of the error. Wikiquote transcribes it and adds a genuine pre-history: the same actor said essentially the same line in a 1956 film, so even the real catchphrase has an origin story that predates the show.

candidates.quote: I do wish we could chat longer, but I'm having an old friend for dinner.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Ted Tally, adapting Thomas Harris's 1988 novel; spoken by Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins) in the film's closing scene; The Silence of the Lambs (1991), dir. Jonathan Demme, Orion Pictures (rights holder). Wikiquote transcribes the line with an ellipsis and a closing beat: "I do wish we could chat longer, but … I'm having an old friend for dinner. Bye." — the popular form simply drops the pause and the "Bye", which is compression rather than a misquote. Whether the line originates in Harris's novel or is Tally's for the film is not established here.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. The film's closing line and one of its two most-quoted; Wikiquote sources it directly. Useful as a contrast case for the two misquote pages — here the public's version is a harmless trim of the transcript, not a rewrite of it, which is precisely the line between compression and misquotation.

candidates.quote: I love you." / "I know.
candidates.trueOrigin: Star Wars: Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back (1980), directed by Irvin Kershner; screenplay credited to Leigh Brackett & Lawrence Kasdan, story by George Lucas. Lucasfilm Ltd. / Twentieth Century-Fox. Leia Organa (Carrie Fisher) / Han Solo (Harrison Ford), in the carbon-freezing chamber. Wikiquote transcribes the exchange exactly as above. AUTHORSHIP EXCEPTION: "I know" was not in the shooting script and did not come from the credited screenwriters. Kershner had settled on a pared-down "I'll be back"; at Harrison Ford's suggestion on set, Han's reply became "I know." This is a rare documented case where the house convention (author = the writer, never the actor) does not resolve cleanly — the line is an on-set contribution by the actor, adopted by the director, and should be recorded as such rather than credited to Brackett or Kasdan.
candidates.whyNotable: Consistently ranked among the best-loved exchanges in film, and heavily searched. Its value to the corpus is the authorship record: the credited screenwriters did not write the famous half of it, which is a real-world stress test of the writer-not-actor rule and worth documenting before someone credits it to Kasdan.

candidates.quote: If you build it, he will come.
candidates.trueOrigin: Originated in W. P. Kinsella's novel Shoeless Joe (Houghton Mifflin, 1982) — spoken by the voice of a ballpark announcer heard by narrator Ray Kinsella. Screenplay by Phil Alden Robinson for Field of Dreams (1989, Universal Pictures), based on Kinsella's novel; Robinson also directed. Spoken on screen by The Voice (credited as "Himself"); heard by Ray Kinsella, played by Kevin Costner. Per house convention the author of the screen line is the writer — but here the line predates the screenplay, so the originating author is Kinsella, and Robinson is the adapter who brought it to screen. Ranked #39 on AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes.
candidates.whyNotable: The anchor for the misquote above: this is the line as actually written and spoken, transcribed exactly at Wikiquote and independently ranked by AFI. Carrying it as its own verified record gives the corpus the correct string alongside the popular wrong one, and lets the page make the "he, not they" contrast concrete. Also carries the borrowed-from-the-novel correction on its own.

candidates.quote: I'll get you, my pretty, and your little dog too!
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line as transcribed, spoken by the Wicked Witch of the West (Margaret Hamilton) to Dorothy. Screenplay by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, The Wizard of Oz (1939), Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (rights holder). ORIGINATION: film-original — the Witch has no such line in L. Frank Baum's 1900 novel. AFI ranks it #99 on "100 Years...100 Movie Quotes", rendered identically.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor record, and the necessary counterpart to the "Fly, my pretties" misquote: this is the real line whose singular "my pretty", addressed to Dorothy, gets pluralised and redirected at the flying monkeys in the phantom version. Carrying both lets the two pages cite each other and show exactly where the error comes from. Wording is confirmed by two independent sources (Wikiquote transcription and AFI #99), so 'verified' is safe.

candidates.quote: I'm gonna make him an offer he can't refuse
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine. Transcribed at Wikiquote verbatim as "I'm gonna make him an offer he can't refuse." — Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) to Johnny Fontane. Screenplay by Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo, adapted from Puzo's 1969 novel; The Godfather (1972), Paramount Pictures. Ranked #2 on AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes. Note the common written drift to "I'm going to..." and "I'll make him an offer he can't refuse"; the spoken contraction is "gonna".
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor record. The film's signature line, AFI #2, and the one Godfather quote people reproduce roughly correctly — useful as a control against the misquote pages.

candidates.quote: It's alive! It's alive!
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine, but the popular form is a heavy compression. Full transcribed line, Dr. Henry Frankenstein (Colin Clive): "Look! It's moving. It's sha — it's... it's alive. It's alive... It's alive, it's moving, it's alive! It's alive, it's alive, it's alive! It's ALIVE!" Screenplay by Garrett Fort and Francis Edward Faragoh, adaptation by John L. Balderston, from Peggy Webling's 1927 play 'Frankenstein: An Adventure in the Macabre' and Mary Shelley's 1818 novel; directed by James Whale; Universal Pictures (work for hire — Universal holds the rights, not the writers). ORIGINATION: the exclamation is the film's own. Shelley's novel narrates the animation rather than shouting it, and the two-beat form the public quotes is the wording the American Film Institute canonised at #49 of its 100 Movie Quotes.
candidates.whyNotable: The anchor line of the film and of the whole mad-scientist genre. Worth carrying because the transcript shows Clive's line starts quietly — Wikiquote punctuates the opening with periods and an ellipsis, not exclamation marks — and builds across six repetitions, while the popular version is a flat two-beat shout. Also useful for correcting the common assumption that the line comes from Mary Shelley.

candidates.quote: Leave the gun, take the cannoli
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine. Wikiquote transcribes it as two sentences — "Leave the gun. Take the Cannoli." — spoken by Peter Clemenza (Richard S. Castellano) to Rocco Lampone after Rocco kills Paulie Gatto. Screenplay by Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo; The Godfather (1972), Paramount Pictures. The frequent plural "take the cannolis" is not what is said.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor record. AFI-listed and endlessly repeated; the only routine drift is the comma splice and the plural 'cannolis', so it serves as a second control alongside the 'offer he can't refuse' page.

candidates.quote: Let's work the problem, people. Let's not make things any worse by guessing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apollo 13 (1995), spoken by the Gene Kranz character (Ed Harris). Screenplay by William Broyles Jr. & Al Reinert (uncredited rewrite by John Sayles); Imagine Entertainment, distributed by Universal Pictures. Wikiquote transcribes it with emphasis on "work" and "guessing" (italicised in the source). A written screen line; the writers are the authors, Kranz the character, Harris the actor.
candidates.whyNotable: Transcribed exactly on Wikiquote with no dispute note. Pairs instructively with "Failure is not an option" — both are lines given to the Kranz character by the same writers, but only one of them has escaped the film and been pinned on the real man. Useful anchor showing the corpus is not claiming every Kranz-character line is misattributed.

candidates.quote: Lips red as the rose, hair black as ebony, skin white as snow.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken by the Slave in the Magic Mirror (voiced by Moroni Olsen), naming Snow White for Queen Grimhilde, in Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937). Shared story credit: Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith; Walt Disney Productions (rights holder). ORIGINATION: the imagery is the Brothers Grimm's, not Disney's — the 1812 tale describes the child as white as snow, red as blood, and black as ebony.
