candidates.quote: I see little commercial potential for the internet for the next 10 years
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to remarks at COMDEX in November 1994, but Wikiquote's only citation is a 2009 Danish book (Kommunikation erstatter transport) — no contemporaneous record
candidates.whyNotable: The "respectable" version of the passing-fad myth; Wikiquote parks it in Attributed with a single second-hand 2009 citation and no 1994 primary record.

candidates.quote: People often overestimate what will happen in the next two years and underestimate what will happen in ten
candidates.trueOrigin: An anonymous "modern maxim" recorded in J. C. R. Licklider's 1965 Libraries of the Future; passed through Alfred Mayo (1969), George Heilmeier (1976) and Roy Amara (1983) before Gates published this wording in The Road Ahead
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted line about technology forecasting; Gates really did write this phrasing in The Road Ahead, but QI shows the idea was already an unattributed maxim by 1965 — a rare case where the popularizer is not the originator.

candidates.quote: A woman is like a tea bag; you never know how strong it is until it's in hot water.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Roosevelt source; a similar remark was attributed to Nancy Reagan in 1981.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'empowerment' line constantly credited to Roosevelt, but Wikiquote finds no original source and notes a closely related quip attributed to Nancy Reagan in 1981.

candidates.quote: Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery, and today is a gift, that's why they call it the present.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified originator; QI documents anonymous earlier variants of the 'present/gift' wordplay with no link to Roosevelt.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous inspirational line attributed to Roosevelt (and others, e.g. Kung Fu Panda); QI finds no genuine Roosevelt source and traces the saying to anonymous earlier wordplay.

candidates.quote: You must learn from the mistakes of others. You can't possibly live long enough to make them all yourself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous folk saying circulating by the 1940s; the attribution to Roosevelt appeared much later.
candidates.whyNotable: Folk-wisdom aphorism attributed to Roosevelt, but QI traces it to 1940s sources circulating without her name and finds the Roosevelt ascription is a later addition.

candidates.quote: Age before beauty. Pearls before swine.
candidates.trueOrigin: The famous doorway exchange with Clare Boothe Luce is not documented. Luce herself denied the story. The earliest citation QI finds is The Spectator, 16 September 1938, where Parker's foil is an unnamed 'snooty debutante', not Luce; other retellings swap in different participants.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-retold celebrity put-downs in American letters, and the named victim, Clare Boothe Luce, publicly denied it ever happened — the earliest printed version doesn't name her at all.

candidates.quote: If all the girls who attended the Yale prom were laid end to end, I wouldn't be at all surprised.
candidates.trueOrigin: Credibly Parker's but unverified: the earliest substantive evidence is Alexander Woollcott crediting her in 1934. The 'laid end to end' joke family itself dates to at least 1843, and the target institution shifts between retellings (Yale prom, Vassar, 'all those present'), which is a classic marker of a floating gag.
candidates.whyNotable: The Parker line most often repeated as a Round Table set piece; QI shows the joke structure predates her by ninety years and that even the school named in it drifts from telling to telling.

candidates.quote: Money cannot buy health, but I'd settle for a diamond-studded wheelchair.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source. It surfaces in English newspapers in January 1959 already credited to Parker while she was alive, but appears nowhere in her published writing or interviews. It spread widely after Evan Esar's 1968 quotation collection. QI credits her only tentatively, for want of any alternative candidate.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of 'best Dorothy Parker quotes' listicles that has never been located in anything she actually wrote or said — QI credits it to her only by default.

candidates.quote: You can lead a horticulture, but you can't make her think.
candidates.trueOrigin: Probably genuinely Parker's, but unpinned. QI finds the pun in cryptic form in Walter Winchell's March 1935 column and in full only in John Mason Brown's 1962 Horizon article; the well-known 'word game at the Algonquin' framing comes later, and Marc Connelly's 1976 recollection gives a different origin story. An earlier variant runs 'You may lead a whore to culture, but you can't make her think.'
candidates.whyNotable: Parker's most-quoted pun, always told with a tidy Algonquin Round Table anecdote that QI shows was attached decades after the fact — and the punchline circulated in a cruder earlier form.

candidates.quote: The thing about smart people is that they seem like crazy people to dumb people.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown. A Wikiquote Talk-page thread opened specifically on this line reports that no source can be found; the one page that claimed a source pointed to Robert Carroll's 'Unnatural Acts: Critical Thinking, Skepticism, and Science Exposed', but a book search shows no mention of Hawking there — the book attributes the remark to 'one commenter' (p. 138).
candidates.whyNotable: Described by Wikiquote editors as 'one of the most common quotes I hear attributed to Hawking', yet the single claimed source turns out to credit an anonymous internet commenter, not Hawking.

candidates.quote: It matters if you don't just give up.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest located appearance is Shirley MacLaine's 'Going Within' (1990), p. 303, where it is presented as Hawking's reply to MacLaine — no primary Hawking source. Wikiquote files it under a Disputed wrapper.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-reproduced 'inspirational Hawking' lines, but Wikiquote can only trace it to a second-hand anecdote in a 1990 Shirley MacLaine self-help book, and flags it as disputed rather than sourced.

candidates.quote: There are hopes the bloom of whose beauty would be spoiled by the trammels of description.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ellen Pickering, The Merchant's Daughter (1836). Henry Southgate credited Dickens in an 1862 compilation; by 1884 Edward Parsons Day had merged Pickering's passage with similar language from Dombey and Son and filed the whole thing under Dickens.
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook anthology-error misattribution QI traced end to end — a forgotten woman novelist's line absorbed into the Dickens canon by two Victorian quote books.

candidates.quote: Well, every one for himself, and Providence for us all — as the elephant said when he danced among the chickens.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Reade, A Simpleton (1873) — a Wellerism mistaken for Dickens because the Wellerism form itself was popularised by Sam Weller in The Pickwick Papers.
candidates.whyNotable: The only entry in Wikiquote's Misattributed section for Dickens; misfiled to him because the joke format is literally named after a Dickens character.

candidates.quote: A day wasted on others is not wasted on one's self.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unsourced. Carried by every major aggregator with no work or chapter cited; the phrase "wasted on one's self" returns zero hits across Wikisource's full-text corpus, including its Dickens novels.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of volunteering and charity messaging always credited to Dickens, yet no aggregator has ever named a source and it is absent from his texts.

candidates.quote: Family not only need to consist of merely those whom we share blood, but also for those whom we'd give blood.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown, and almost certainly a modern internet fabrication — the sentence is ungrammatical in a way Dickens never was, and the distinctive phrase "those whom we'd give blood" returns zero hits across Wikisource's full-text corpus.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared "found family" meme quote pinned on Dickens; its broken syntax is the tell, and it has no source anywhere.

candidates.quote: The most important thing in life is to stop saying 'I wish' and start saying 'I will'.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — modern motivational-poster origin. The longer circulating version ("Consider nothing impossible, then treat possibilities as probabilities") is frequently pinned on David Copperfield, but neither clause appears anywhere in Wikisource's Dickens corpus (which hosts the 1850 David Copperfield in full).
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the highest-volume fake Dickens quote online — endemic on LinkedIn, school walls and quote sites, with a fabricated David Copperfield citation attached.

candidates.quote: Everyone is necessarily the hero of his own life story.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Barth, short story "The Remobilization of Jacob Horner" (1958). Dickens's David Copperfield (1850) opens with the interrogative precursor "Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life...", which is why the declarative version gets reassigned to him.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as Dickens because of the David Copperfield opening, but QI pins the actual declarative formulation on John Barth in 1958.

candidates.quote: All compounded things are subject to decay. Strive with diligence.
candidates.trueOrigin: Traditionally the Buddha's last words, recorded in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16, 6:8).
candidates.whyNotable: Traditionally the Buddha's final words (Digha Nikaya 16); a well-sourced genuine anchor quote.

candidates.quote: No one saves us but ourselves. No one can and no one may. We ourselves must walk the path.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rendering of the Dhammapada (verse 165); a genuinely sourced Buddhist teaching.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Buddha line from the Dhammapada, useful as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Hell, there are no rules here. We're trying to accomplish something.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed via Martin André Rosanoff, Harper's Magazine (1932); original dialect version 'Hell! there ain't no rules around here! We are tryin' to accomplish somep'n!'
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved innovation-culture quote; QI rates it only 'probable,' resting on a single second-hand account (Rosanoff, Harper's Magazine 1932) of a remark from around 1903.

candidates.quote: I'd put my money on the sun and solar energy. What a source of power! I hope we don't have to wait until oil and coal run out before we tackle that.
candidates.trueOrigin: Reported second-hand in James D. Newton, Uncommon Friends (1987); reliability unverified.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous in renewable-energy messaging; QI notes it comes only from James Newton's 1987 book Uncommon Friends, recalling a 1931 conversation over 50 years later with no archived diary to verify it.

candidates.quote: Non-violence leads to the highest ethics, which is the goal of all evolution.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; first documented in The A-V Magazine (1981).
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared in vegetarian/animal-rights circles as an Edison line, but Wikiquote finds no source earlier than The A-V Magazine (1981) despite claims of an 1890 origin.

candidates.quote: A decline of public morals in the United States will probably be marked by the abuse of the power of impeachment as a means of crushing political adversaries or ejecting them from office.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Innes Clark Hare, American Constitutional Law, Vol. 1 — Hare offered this as something 'long since remarked by De Tocqueville' without a citation. Tocqueville's actual line (Democracy in America, Ch. VII) is: 'When the American republics begin to degenerate it will be easy to verify the truth of this observation, by remarking whether the number of political impeachments augments.'
candidates.whyNotable: Resurfaces in every impeachment news cycle as a Tocqueville prophecy; Wikiquote shows it is a 19th-century legal writer's loose paraphrase, not Tocqueville's words.

candidates.quote: In a democracy, the people get the government they deserve.
candidates.trueOrigin: Joseph de Maistre, letter of 1811: 'Toute nation a le gouvernement qu'elle mérite' — 'Every nation gets the government it deserves.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-repeated political aphorisms on the internet, credited to Tocqueville constantly; Wikiquote reassigns it to Joseph de Maistre, who wrote it in an 1811 letter.

candidates.quote: America is great because America is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown American sermon/periodical tradition; earliest located printing is Herald and Presbyter (6 Sept 1922, p. 8), popularized by Sherwood Eddy's 1941 The Kingdom of God and the American Dream. Documented as bogus in Michael A. Ledeen, Tocqueville on American Character (2001), p. 25, and in 'The Tocqueville Fraud', The Weekly Standard, 13 Nov 1995.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most famous fake Tocqueville line — quoted as his by Eisenhower, Reagan, Clinton, Colin Powell, Ross Perot and Pat Buchanan, yet it appears nowhere in his writings; Wikiquote traces the full form to the Herald and Presbyter, 6 September 1922.

candidates.quote: I sought for the greatness and genius of America in her commodious harbors and her ample rivers, and it was not there. In the fertile fields and boundless prairies, and it was not there. In her rich mines and her vast world commerce, and it was not there. Not until I went into the churches of America and heard her pulpits, aflame with righteousness, did I understand the secret of her genius and power. America is great because she is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great.
candidates.trueOrigin: An anonymous American pulpit composition; no text resembling it exists in Tocqueville. Earliest located printing of the closing line is 1922; the full passage is documented as a fabrication in 'The Tocqueville Fraud', The Weekly Standard (13 November 1995).
candidates.whyNotable: The long 'commodious harbors' sermon version routinely cited as coming straight from Democracy in America; Wikiquote and the Weekly Standard's 'The Tocqueville Fraud' show Tocqueville never wrote a word of it.

candidates.quote: The American Republic will endure until the day Congress discovers that it can bribe the public with the public's money.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous 20th-century coinage. Earliest known occurrence is an unsourced attribution to Alexander Fraser Tytler in Elmer T. Peterson, 'This Is the Hard Core of Freedom', The Daily Oklahoman, 9 December 1951.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of political email forwards and op-eds pinned on Tocqueville (and on Alexander Fraser Tytler); Wikiquote traces the earliest occurrence only to a 1951 Oklahoma newspaper column, roughly a century after Tocqueville died.

candidates.quote: It's not an endlessly expanding list of rights — the 'right' to education, the 'right' to health care, the 'right' to food and housing. That's not freedom, that's dependency. Those aren't rights, those are the rations of slavery — hay and a barn for human cattle.
candidates.trueOrigin: P. J. O'Rourke, Age and Guile Beat Youth, Innocence, and a Bad Haircut (1996), p. 227.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates widely on social media as Tocqueville's 19th-century warning about the welfare state; Wikiquote pins it to P. J. O'Rourke, writing in 1996.

candidates.quote: It is well enough that people of the nation do not understand our banking and monetary system, for if they did, I believe there would be a revolution before tomorrow morning.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase introduced by Rep. Charles Binderup (1937); no direct Ford source, though Ford wrote against finance dominance in My Life and Work.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial conspiracy/finance meme attributed to Ford; Wikiquote notes it originates as a 1937 paraphrase by Congressman Charles Binderup, not a documented Ford quote.

candidates.quote: An idea, like a ghost, must be spoken to a little before it will explain itself.
candidates.trueOrigin: A singularised corruption of Dickens's actual plural line in Dombey and Son (1848), Ch. 12: "Ideas, like ghosts (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before they will explain themselves." Henry Southgate's 1862 compilation introduced the altered form.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Dickens line that has circulated for 160+ years in wording Dickens never wrote — QI traces the corruption to an 1862 quotation anthology.

candidates.quote: Electric communication will never be a substitute for the face of someone who with their soul encourages another person to be brave and true.
candidates.trueOrigin: A heavily doctored one-sentence extract from Dickens's 1856 Household Words story "The Wreck of the Golden Mary" — "electric telegraph" was swapped for "electric communication", pronouns degendered, and the life-or-death shipwreck context stripped.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared "Dickens on technology" line on social media and in keynote slides; QI shows the viral wording is a modern rewrite, not Dickens's sentence.

candidates.quote: Have a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts.
candidates.trueOrigin: A rewritten imperative. Dickens's actual text is Jenny Wren's line in Our Mutual Friend (1865), Book 3, Ch. 2: "And if it's proud to have a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts..." — a description of a character, not advice to the reader.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-printed Dickens lines on cards and plaques; the familiar imperative wording is a paraphrase, and the aggregators that carry it cite no chapter.

candidates.quote: What we have once enjoyed we can never lose. All that we love deeply becomes a part of us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Keller's own We Bereaved (1929), but the popular form is a condensation — the original ran as two separate sentences with additional imagery about sunsets, mountains and oceans. The merged one-liner spread through reprints from the 1990s onward.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted grief and condolence line attributed to Keller; QI confirms she wrote it in We Bereaved (1929) while showing the familiar version is an edited compression of her original passage.

candidates.quote: Life is either a daring adventure or nothing at all.
candidates.trueOrigin: Keller wrote 'Life is either a daring adventure or nothing' — no 'at all' — in the chapter 'Faith Fears Not' of Let Us Have Faith (1940); the same sentence appears in The Open Door (1957) after 'Security is mostly a superstition.' The trailing 'at all' is a later corruption.
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely Keller's, but the wording almost everyone shares is wrong — QI shows the popular 'or nothing at all' appendage was added after the fact to her 1940 sentence.

candidates.quote: Many persons have a wrong idea of what constitutes true happiness. It is not attained through self-gratification but through fidelity to a worthy purpose.
candidates.trueOrigin: Keller's own journal entry of 10 December 1936, published in Helen Keller's Journal 1936–1937 (1938).
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where a heavily circulated Keller quote survives investigation intact — QI pins it to a dated 1936 journal entry, making it a clean verified anchor beside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Americans are so enamored of equality that they would rather be equal in slavery than unequal in freedom.
candidates.trueOrigin: A garbled popular condensation of Democracy in America, Vol. I, Ch. III, Pt. I: 'There is in fact a manly and legitimate passion for equality that spurs all men to wish to be strong and esteemed... But one also finds in the human heart a depraved taste for equality, which impels the weak to want to bring the strong down to their level.'
candidates.whyNotable: Among the most-shared 'Tocqueville' lines on quote sites, but Wikiquote flags it explicitly as a misquotation of a genuine but very differently worded passage on the 'depraved taste for equality'.

candidates.quote: The greatness of America lies not in being more enlightened than any other nation, but rather in her ability to repair her faults.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase of Henry Reeve's translation of Democracy in America, Vol. I, Ch. XIII: 'The great privilege of the Americans does not simply consist in their being more enlightened than other nations, but in their being able to repair the faults they may commit.'
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial presidential-speech and commencement quote; the idea is genuinely Tocqueville's (Democracy in America, Vol. I, Ch. XIII) but this modernized wording is a paraphrase, not any published translation.

candidates.quote: The saddest aspect of life right now is that science gathers knowledge faster than society gathers wisdom
candidates.whyNotable: Real Asimov line, frequently mis-worded and mis-sourced online.

candidates.quote: Don't join the book burners. Don't think you are going to conceal faults by concealing evidence that they ever existed.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eisenhower, commencement address at Dartmouth College, 14 June 1953; reported in The New York Times the next day.
candidates.whyNotable: QI confirms this McCarthy-era line as genuine and pinpoints the 1953 Dartmouth commencement, while noting the widely circulated "book banners" variant is a corruption.

candidates.quote: Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eisenhower, "The Chance for Peace" address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, 16 April 1953.
candidates.whyNotable: The "Cross of Iron" line is Eisenhower's most-quoted sentence and is fully sourced at Wikiquote to his 1953 address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors.

candidates.quote: In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eisenhower, Farewell Address to the Nation, 17 January 1961.
candidates.whyNotable: The line that put "military-industrial complex" into the language; genuine and precisely sourced, and a natural verified anchor beside the Eisenhower debunks.

candidates.quote: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything
candidates.trueOrigin: Eisenhower said it in remarks to the National Defense Executive Reserve Conference (14 November 1957), explicitly noting he had heard it in the Army; a 1950 letter of his credits an anonymous soldier, and precursors run back to Helmuth von Moltke (1871).
candidates.whyNotable: Eisenhower really did say it — but QI shows he was passing along Army lore he had already credited to an anonymous soldier in 1950, with a lineage running back to Moltke, which makes it a rare "true quote, false authorship" page.

candidates.quote: I do not feel obliged to believe that the same God who has endowed us with senses, reason, and intellect has intended us to forgo their use.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, sourced Galileo line from the 1615 Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina — his central argument that God-given reason is not meant to be set aside — and a useful genuine anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: In questions of science, the authority of a thousand is not worth the humble reasoning of a single individual.
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely Galileo's, from his third letter on sunspots to Mark Welser (December 1612); this popular English wording is the pre-1931 Arago translation, and the Italian original is on Wikiquote alongside it.

candidates.quote: A pessimist is one who sees a disaster in every opportunity. An optimist sees opportunity in every disaster.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Rockefeller, per a 1925 Detroit Free Press report of a remark he made on a golf course at age 85 — but the wording is DISASTER, not difficulty. Quote Investigator treats this as a distinct variant, not as the famous 'difficulty in every opportunity' line, which QI tentatively ascribes to Bertram Carr, Mayor of Carlisle, in a 1919 address to the Co-operative Congress. The Churchill credit for that other wording appears in the Red Herrings: False Attributions appendix of a Churchill quotations book with no citation.
candidates.whyNotable: The Rockefeller half of a family of optimist/pessimist sayings that the public collapses into one Churchill-credited line — he really did say a version, but not the one everybody quotes, which makes the pair the clearest illustration of how a real remark and a misattributed one get fused.

candidates.quote: God gave me my money.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rockefeller himself; Women's Home Companion (1915), quoted in 'God's Gold' (1932) by John T. Flynn.
candidates.whyNotable: His single most-quoted and most-attacked line, and a properly sourced one — the anchor for any page about Rockefeller's wealth-as-divine-stewardship theology.

candidates.quote: I do not think that there is any other quality so essential to success of any kind as the quality of perseverance.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rockefeller himself, as quoted in 'How They Succeeded' (1901) by Orison Swett Marden; the full line continues 'It overcomes almost everything, even nature.'
candidates.whyNotable: The most-circulated Rockefeller success quote that is actually sourced — a 1901 interview — making it a real anchor next to the fakes.

candidates.quote: The day of combination is here to stay. Individualism has gone, never to return.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rockefeller in 1880, at age 41; Allan Nevins, 'John D. Rockefeller' (Scribner, 1959), I:622.
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive statement of the trust-building era, quoted in nearly every history of American monopoly, and sourced to Nevins's authorized biography.

candidates.quote: I cannot tell a lie... I did cut it with my hatchet
candidates.whyNotable: The cherry-tree story was invented by biographer Parson Weems (1806); Washington never said it.

candidates.quote: Be courteous to all, but intimate with few, and let those few be well tried before you give them your confidence; true friendship is a plant of slow growth.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Washington, letter to his nephew Bushrod Washington, 15 January 1783.
candidates.whyNotable: An authentic, well-sourced Washington maxim on friendship from his letter to Bushrod Washington (15 January 1783), frequently and correctly quoted.

candidates.quote: To be prepared for war is one of the most effectual means of preserving peace.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Washington, First Annual Address to both Houses of Congress, 8 January 1790.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced and heavily quoted Washington line, drawn verbatim from his First Annual Address to Congress on 8 January 1790 — a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine: The Prince (1513), Chapter 18.
candidates.whyNotable: A heavily shared line that is actually authentic — useful as a verified counterweight on a hub otherwise dominated by debunks.

candidates.quote: It ought to be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine: The Prince (1513), Chapter 6.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted Machiavelli passage in business and change-management writing, and unlike most of what gets pinned on him it is genuinely his and precisely locatable.

candidates.quote: It's déjà vu all over again.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; Berra claimed it (about back-to-back Mantle/Maris homers) but no early sourcing supports him
candidates.whyNotable: Perhaps the single most-shared Yogi-ism, yet Wikiquote lists it as disputed: the earliest published attribution to Berra is 1984 and a similar line appears in a 1962 Jim Prior poem, so QI treats it as unverified.

candidates.quote: If people don't want to come to the ballpark, how are you going to stop them?
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to impresario Sol Hurok in 1952; linked to Berra in 1962
candidates.whyNotable: Often quoted as pure Berra, but Wikiquote records it was originally attributed to impresario Sol Hurok in 1952 and only linked to Berra in 1962.

candidates.quote: Ninety percent of this game is half-mental.
candidates.trueOrigin: First attributed to outfielder Jim Wohlford, April 1974
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved 'Yogi math' line, but Wikiquote notes the phrasing was first attributed in April 1974 to reserve outfielder Jim Wohlford, not Berra.

candidates.quote: The real price of every thing, what every thing really costs to the man who wants to acquire it, is the toil and trouble of acquiring it
candidates.trueOrigin: Adam Smith
candidates.whyNotable: The founding statement of price versus worth from the founder of economics: money is only a token for the life and labour it stands in for.

candidates.quote: Iron rusts from disuse; stagnant water loses its purity and in cold weather becomes frozen; even so does inaction sap the vigor of the mind.
candidates.trueOrigin: Leonardo da Vinci, 'The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci' (trans. Jean Paul Richter, 1883).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely quoted and genuinely sourced Leonardo reflection from 'The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci' (Richter, 1883), a solid verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: Painting is poetry which is seen and not heard, and poetry is a painting which is heard but not seen.
candidates.trueOrigin: Leonardo da Vinci, 'A Treatise on Painting' (Trattato della pittura), compiled by Francesco Melzi; printed 1651.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Leonardo aphorism on the sister arts, drawn from his 'A Treatise on Painting' (compiled by Francesco Melzi), serving as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Wisdom is the daughter of experience.
candidates.trueOrigin: Leonardo da Vinci, 'The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci' (trans. Jean Paul Richter, 1883).
candidates.whyNotable: A compact, genuinely sourced Leonardo aphorism from his Notebooks, useful as a short verified anchor amid the misattributions.

candidates.quote: Education is the passport to the future, for tomorrow belongs to those who prepare for it today.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely his, but the popular wording is a smoothed variant. The sourced text is 'Education is our passport to the future, for tomorrow belongs only to the people who prepare for it today' - Speech at the Founding Rally of the Organization of Afro-American Unity, 28 June 1964, collected in By Any Means Necessary (1970).
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the most-printed Malcolm X line in the world (graduation programmes, school walls), and the version everyone shares silently drops 'our', 'only' and 'the people' from what he actually said.

candidates.quote: If you aren't careful, the newspapers will have you hating the people who are being oppressed and loving the people who are doing the oppressing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine - Audubon Ballroom speech, 13 December 1964; carried in Wikiquote's sourced 1964 section.
candidates.whyNotable: His best-documented line on media manipulation, and the likely real ancestor of the far more viral but entirely unsourced 'the media is the most powerful entity on earth' paraphrase.

candidates.quote: The most disrespected person in America is the black woman. The most unprotected person in America is the black woman. The most neglected person in America is the black woman.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine - delivered 22 May 1962 in Los Angeles, at events surrounding the killing of Nation of Islam member Ronald Stokes by the LAPD. Surviving audio was sampled by Beyonce on Lemonade (2016).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, recorded anchor line that went massively viral after Beyonce sampled the original audio in 2016 - high search demand and a rare case where the primary recording still exists.

candidates.quote: Risk comes from not knowing what you're doing
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Buffett — said during his 1993 talk to Columbia University Business School students and reported by Jim Rasmussen in the Omaha World-Herald, January 2, 1994, Business section, page 17S.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, primary-sourced Buffett line that QI confirms outright — a solid verified anchor next to the debunks.

candidates.quote: How did you go bankrupt? Two ways. Gradually, then suddenly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine: spoken by the character Mike Campbell in Hemingway's novel 'The Sun Also Rises' (1926).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, sourced Hemingway line QI confirms — a solid anchor for the hub and often quoted in finance and crisis writing.

candidates.quote: The world breaks everyone, and afterward many are strong at the broken places.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine: 'A Farewell to Arms' (1929), Chapter 34.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Hemingway's most-quoted genuine lines, sourced on Wikiquote — a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Mandela; from his 1994 autobiography Long Walk to Freedom.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, widely-shared Mandela passage with a clear book source; strong genuine anchor alongside the misattribution debunks.

candidates.quote: I died as a mineral and became a plant, I died as plant and rose to animal, I died as animal and I was man.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rumi, Divan-i Shams-i Tabrizi (13th c.), translated by R. A. Nicholson (1914) — translation is public domain.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Rumi's most famous genuinely-authored passages (the 'evolution of the soul' verse from the Divan-i Shams / Masnavi), verified in R. A. Nicholson's public-domain 1914 translation.

candidates.quote: The lion who breaks the enemy's ranks is a minor hero compared to the lion who overcomes himself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, line 1389 (13th c.); public-domain translations available (e.g. Whinfield).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Rumi aphorism from the Masnavi (I, 1389), useful as a verified anchor alongside the debunks on a Rumi hub.

candidates.quote: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running. If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write.
candidates.trueOrigin: Epictetus
candidates.whyNotable: The clearest ancient statement of deliberate practice — the skill is the reps, and the closing imperative lands hard on any slide about daily work.

candidates.quote: Never say of anything, I have lost it; but, I have restored it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Epictetus
candidates.whyNotable: The sharpest Stoic reframe of bereavement — the passage continues 'Has your child died? It is restored' — and the most slide-ready line on holding what we love as lent, not owned.

candidates.quote: No great thing is created suddenly, any more than a bunch of grapes or a fig. If you tell me that you desire a fig, I answer you that there must be time. Let it first blossom, then bear fruit, then ripen.
candidates.trueOrigin: Epictetus
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive ancient statement of the ripening idea — concrete, agricultural, and impossible to argue with, which is why it survives every anti-hustle talk.

candidates.quote: Count your age by friends, not years. Count your life by smiles, not tears.
candidates.trueOrigin: A greeting-card verse documented in a 1927 newspaper, beginning 'Count your garden by the flowers, never by the leaves that fall...'. QI's leading candidate for authorship is Dixie Willson, who per a 1933 newspaper account sold the verse to the P. F. Volland Company for $5.
candidates.whyNotable: A birthday-card staple recirculated as Lennon wisdom; QI dates it to 1927 — thirteen years before Lennon was born — with the Lennon credit first traceable to social media in February 2010.

candidates.quote: Time you enjoy wasting is not wasted time.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marthe Troly-Curtin, in her 1912 novel Phrynette Married: 'He liked it—time you enjoy wasting is not wasted time.' The parallel Bertrand Russell credit came from a misread parenthetical in a Laurence J. Peter quotation book.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-reproduced 'Lennon' aphorisms, but the Lennon credit only appears by the year 2000, twenty years after his death — QI credits a 1912 novelist.

candidates.quote: When I was 5 years old, my mother always told me that happiness was the key to life. When I went to school, they asked me what I wanted to be when I grew up. I wrote down 'happy'. They told me I didn't understand the assignment, and I told them they didn't understand life.
candidates.trueOrigin: No documented Lennon source; the full anecdote first appears as an anonymous Tumblr post in November 2008. QI traces precursors to a January 1960 Peanuts strip by Charles M. Schulz (Linus answering 'Outrageously happy!') and to Goldie Hawn's own retelling in a 1992 Vanity Fair profile and her 2005 memoir A Lotus Grows in the Mud.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared fake Lennon quote on the internet — QI and Full Fact both found zero evidence he ever told the story, and the phrase 'didn't understand the assignment' points to a modern American, not a Liverpudlian, source.

candidates.quote: A dream you dream alone is only a dream. A dream you dream together is reality.
candidates.trueOrigin: Yoko Ono, who wrote the line years earlier; Lennon quoted it in his December 1980 interview with David Sheff, published as All We Are Saying: The Last Major Interview with John Lennon and Yoko Ono (2000), p. 16.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly reproduced under Lennon's name, but Wikiquote places it on Yoko Ono's page with the note that Lennon was quoting her — a clean case of a quote reassigned to the person actually beside him.

candidates.quote: Everything is OK in the end. If it's not OK, it's not the end.
candidates.trueOrigin: Traced by QI to Domingos Sabino, the father of Brazilian writer Fernando Sabino, who recorded it in his 1988 book O tabuleiro de damas: 'everything works out in the end. If it didn't, it's because it hasn't come to an end yet.' Also widely and spuriously credited to Oscar Wilde and Paulo Coelho.
candidates.whyNotable: A meme-ubiquitous consolation line pinned on Lennon; Wikiquote's Disputed section notes it first surfaced anonymously on Usenet in 2000 and only acquired a Lennon credit around 2011 — three decades after his death.

candidates.quote: It matters not who you love, where you love, why you love, when you love, or how you love, it matters only that you love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Poet and singer-songwriter Rod McKuen, who closed his performances with the simpler 'it doesn't matter who you love or how you love, but that you love' — documented in The New York Times in April 1971. The expanded Lennon-credited version emerged in online forums in 1997.
candidates.whyNotable: A Pride-season social-media perennial credited to Lennon; QI found no evidence for him and traces the line to Rod McKuen's stage sign-off in 1971.

candidates.quote: Ringo isn't even the best drummer in the Beatles.
candidates.trueOrigin: An early-1980s stand-up gag by British comedian Jasper Carrott, dated to 1983 and confirmed by Carrott to Beatles historian Mark Lewisohn in April 2012. Lennon was never asked the question the joke presupposes.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-repeated fake Beatles quip there is — printed as fact by national newspapers — yet Wikiquote lists it as apocryphal and the line originates with a comedian, not Lennon.

candidates.quote: You don't have to be crazy to work here, but it helps.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous comedic template ('You don't have to be X to Y but it helps') documented from June 1920, over a decade before it was attributed to Disney.
candidates.whyNotable: Credited to Disney via his secretary in a 1933 newspaper, but QI shows it is a 'snowclone' joke template with anonymous instances dating to 1920, so Disney did not originate it.

candidates.quote: You may not realize it when it happens, but a kick in the teeth may be the best thing in the world for you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rooted in authentic Disney interview statements (he used 'kick in the pants' in a 1956 Saturday Evening Post interview); the 'kick in the teeth' phrasing appeared in the 1957 biography The Story of Walt Disney.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular Disney resilience quote; QI finds Disney genuinely expressed the idea in 1950s interviews but as a 'kick in the pants' — the 'teeth' wording comes from his 1957 biography.

candidates.quote: Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth
candidates.trueOrigin: Tyson said the earlier form 'Everybody has plans until they get hit for the first time' (AP, Aug 1987); the underlying idea predates him in Helmuth von Moltke the Elder (1871). Sometimes reassigned to Joe Louis, which QI calls late and poorly supported.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted lines on the internet; QI credits Tyson but shows the viral 'punched in the mouth/face' wording is a paraphrase of what he actually said, and the concept has military antecedents.

candidates.quote: From the moment I picked up your book until I put it down, I was convulsed with laughter. Some day I intend reading it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Groucho — written as a dust-jacket blurb for S. J. Perelman's Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge (1929); earliest print citation October 1929, Greeley Daily Tribune.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified 1929 Groucho original whose popular wording has drifted ('laid it down' for 'put it down') — a good demonstration of quote-drift alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: I don't want to belong to any club that will accept me as a member.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Groucho — earliest citation is Erskine Johnson's column, 20 October 1949; Groucho gave a fictionalized telling in his memoir Groucho and Me (1959). No original letter or telegram survives, and the club named varies (Friars, Delaney, Hillcrest, Lambs).
candidates.whyNotable: Groucho's most famous real line and a genuine anchor for the hub, though QI shows the resignation-letter backstory is embellished and an 1891 precursor joke exists.

candidates.quote: I find television very educating. Every time somebody turns on the set, I go into the other room and read a book.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Groucho — printed in Reader's Digest, August 1950; QI prefers this wording over the later 'very educational... I go into the library and read a good book' variant.
candidates.whyNotable: Groucho's most-quoted line about television, verified to a 1950 printing, with QI adjudicating between two competing popular wordings.

candidates.quote: Great things are not done by impulse, but by a series of small things brought together.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rooted in a genuine October 1882 letter to Theo expressing this sentiment; the polished popular wording is a later condensation
candidates.whyNotable: An enormously-shared motivational line; QI ties it to a real October 1882 Van Gogh letter, though the crisp popular phrasing is a tidied-up paraphrase.

candidates.quote: If you hear a voice within you say you cannot paint, then by all means paint, and that voice will be silenced.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Van Gogh — written in Dutch in an October 1883 letter to his brother Theo
candidates.whyNotable: One of Van Gogh's most-quoted lines; QI confirms it is authentic to an October 1883 letter to Theo, a solid real anchor amid the fakes.

candidates.quote: There may be a great fire in our soul, yet no one ever comes to warm themselves at it, and the passers-by see only a wisp of smoke coming from the chimney.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Van Gogh — penned in French in a letter to Theo in 1880
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-circulated (and often shortened) Van Gogh line QI verifies to an 1880 letter, though it also gets misattributed to Joni Mitchell.

candidates.quote: Being entirely honest with oneself is a good exercise.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Freud, letter to Wilhelm Fliess (1897).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Freud line sourced on Wikiquote to his correspondence (letter to Wilhelm Fliess, 1897), often circulated online without its real source.

candidates.quote: The interpretation of dreams is the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams (1900).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Freud's genuine signature lines, sourced to The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: One day, in retrospect, the years of struggle will strike you as the most beautiful.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Freud, 1907 letter to C. G. Jung; popular English wording from the 1960 Letters of Sigmund Freud translation.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare inspirational line correctly credited to Freud; QI verified it via scans of his September 19, 1907 letter to C. G. Jung.

candidates.quote: The great question that has never been answered, and which I have not yet been able to answer, despite my thirty years of research into the feminine soul, is 'What does a woman want?'
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Freud, reported by Marie Bonaparte and quoted in Ernest Jones's biography (1953).
candidates.whyNotable: Freud's famous 'What does a woman want?' remark, documented via Marie Bonaparte's record (as cited by Ernest Jones) rather than a published Freud work.

candidates.quote: A man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: Inverts the definition of wealth from what you hold to what you can decline — the anchor quote for any talk on simplicity, minimalism or opportunity cost.

candidates.quote: I am grateful for what I am and have. My thanksgiving is perpetual.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: Two short sentences that carry the whole theme, and the surrounding letter ('my wealth is not possession but enjoyment') gives a speaker a natural follow-on. Genuinely from a dated, locatable letter, not a Walden paraphrase.

candidates.quote: In wildness is the preservation of the world.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau, Walking (1862)
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Thoreau line from Walking (1862) that is itself constantly misquoted as 'In wilderness...', making it a strong verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Men have become the tools of their tools.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854)
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Walden line that Quote Investigator confirms is authentically Thoreau's, often reshared in tech-critique contexts.

candidates.quote: That man is the richest whose pleasures are the cheapest.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau, Journal entry, March 11, 1856
candidates.whyNotable: Quote Investigator verifies this as a genuine Thoreau line from his journal (March 11, 1856), a solid verified anchor amid the fakes.

candidates.quote: I do not seek. I find.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spanish 'Yo no busco, yo encuentro'; quoted in Graham Sutherland's 1936 essay 'A Trend in English Draughtsmanship' but the direct attribution to Picasso is disputed.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous aphoristic Picasso line whose earliest sighting is a 1936 essay by Graham Sutherland, with Wikiquote flagging the direct attribution as disputed.

candidates.quote: Inspiration exists, but it has to find you working.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Picasso only in a 1994 publication (Spanish: 'La inspiración existe, pero tiene que encontrarte trabajando'); no contemporaneous source in Picasso's own words is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A studio-motivation staple credited to Picasso, but the earliest documented attribution is a 1994 posthumous source with no primary record.

candidates.quote: It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child.
candidates.trueOrigin: Only appears in print from 1998, posthumously; multiple variant wordings exist ('At eight I was Raphael...') and no contemporaneous primary source is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular Picasso maxim that surfaces only in posthumous 1998 sources with shifting wording, so Wikiquote treats it as unverified.

candidates.quote: God is really only another artist. He invented the giraffe, the elephant and the cat. He has no real style. He just goes on trying other things.
candidates.trueOrigin: Reported secondhand by Francoise Gilot in her 1964 memoir 'Life with Picasso', where she recounts hearing it from Picasso in the 1940s; no direct primary record exists.
candidates.whyNotable: Credibly credited but only through Gilot's 1964 memoir recollection, so it sits between genuine and unverified rather than fully sourced.

candidates.quote: When painters get together they talk about where you can buy the best turpentine.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest evidence located by QI is a 1966 book by screenwriter/director Garson Kanin, who ascribed the words to Picasso; no earlier primary source is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-quoted Picasso quip about artists talking shop, but QI can only trace it to a secondhand 1966 anecdote by Garson Kanin.

candidates.quote: A society gets all the criminals it deserves.
candidates.trueOrigin: Alexandre Lacassagne, quoted by Havelock Ellis in The Criminal (1890); Goldman cites both in 'Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure' (Anarchism and Other Essays), where the line reads 'EVERY SOCIETY HAS THE CRIMINALS IT DESERVES.'
candidates.whyNotable: A criminology chestnut credited to Goldman because it appears in her own essay — but she was quoting it, in capitals, as someone else's line: Wikiquote and the primary text both show she took it from Havelock Ellis quoting the French criminologist Alexandre Lacassagne.

candidates.quote: If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Frager, 1973 T-shirt slogan (paraphrasing Living My Life, 1931); popularized after Shulman supplied the source passages. Variants: 'If I can't dance, I don't want to be in your revolution' (1973 shirt) and 'If I can't dance to it, it's not my revolution' (1983 Passover Haggadah). What Goldman actually wrote: 'I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody's right to beautiful, radiant things.'
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared Goldman line on earth — buttons, T-shirts, posters, banners — and she never wrote a word of it; Goldman's own biographer/editor Alix Kates Shulman documented that anarchist printer Jack Frager coined the slogan in 1973 as a 'succinct abridgement' for a batch of fundraising T-shirts sold in Central Park.

candidates.quote: If you invent a breakthrough in artificial intelligence so machines can learn, that is worth 10 Microsofts
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Gates, answering a student during his 2004 university tour; first reported by Steve Lohr in The New York Times, March 2004
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly recirculated in the AI boom and often assumed to be apocryphal; QI verifies it, tracing it to a March 2004 New York Times report of Gates's campus Q&A.

candidates.quote: Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Gates, The Road Ahead (1995)
candidates.whyNotable: Probably Gates's best-known real aphorism, with a clean Wikiquote-sourced citation to his own 1995 book — a solid verified anchor among the debunks.

candidates.quote: Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Gates, Business @ the Speed of Thought (1999)
candidates.whyNotable: A customer-service-deck perennial that is, unusually, real — Wikiquote sources it to Gates's own 1999 book.

candidates.quote: A woman is like a tea bag; you never know how strong she is until she gets in hot water
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Eleanor Roosevelt; QI finds no evidence she wrote it in this form.

candidates.quote: Do what you feel in your heart to be right, for you'll be criticized anyway.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Eleanor Roosevelt in Dale Carnegie's How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1944); credibly hers but not traced to a first-person source document.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared Roosevelt line with a real documentary trail, credited to her in Dale Carnegie's How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1944).

candidates.quote: It takes courage to love, but pain through love is the purifying fire which those who love generously know.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eleanor Roosevelt, My Day column, April 1, 1939.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Roosevelt line, cited by Wikiquote to her My Day newspaper column of April 1, 1939.

candidates.quote: You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eleanor Roosevelt, You Learn by Living (1960), pp. 29-30.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely Roosevelt line, sourced by Wikiquote to her 1960 book You Learn by Living, serving as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Excuse my dust.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Parker's — submitted as her own epitaph to Vanity Fair, June 1925, and later inscribed on her 1988 memorial plaque. The twist QI adds: she did not invent the phrase. It was an automotive boast; a June 1913 San Francisco Chronicle piece describes a Hudson Six owner with an 'Excuse my dust' sign on his car, and Judge ran a 'Please Excuse My Dust' cartoon in December 1913. Parker's contribution was repurposing a speed brag as a mortality joke.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, precisely dated Parker line that still carries a provenance story — she borrowed a 1913 motoring slogan and turned it into the most famous epitaph in American wit.

candidates.quote: There's a hell of a distance between wise-cracking and wit.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Parker's, from her interview in The Paris Review, Summer 1956 — a sourced Wikiquote entry with a named publication and date.
candidates.whyNotable: A cleanly sourced, on-the-record Parker line about her own reputation for one-liners — the ideal verified anchor for a hub otherwise full of quips she never said.

candidates.quote: But the best evidence we have that time travel is not possible, and never will be, is that we have not been invaded by hordes of tourists from the future.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Hawking. Quote Investigator confirms he made the statement in a January 1991 Cambridge lecture, published a related version in his 1992 Physical Review D paper 'Chronology Protection Conjecture', and printed this wording in 'Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays' (1993), Ch. 13 'The Future of the Universe'. QI notes Robert Silverberg's 1968 novel 'The Masks of Time' used the phrase 'tourists from the future' as narrative colour, but not as an argument against time travel — the argument is Hawking's.
candidates.whyNotable: Hawking's most-quoted one-liner and the rare case where a full Quote Investigator article CONFIRMS rather than debunks — a strong verified anchor for the hub alongside the fakes.

candidates.quote: I don't think the human race will survive the next thousand years, unless we spread into space.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Hawking, from Roger Highfield's interview 'Colonies in space may be only hope, says Hawking', Daily Telegraph, 16 October 2001. Both Wikiquote and Quote Investigator source it there. The full Wikiquote entry continues: 'There are too many accidents that can befall life on a single planet. But I'm an optimist. We will reach out to the stars.'
candidates.whyNotable: The line that launched a thousand 'Hawking says humanity must leave Earth' headlines — QI ran a dedicated investigation and pinned it precisely to the 2001 Telegraph interview, giving the hub a heavily-searched verified anchor.

candidates.quote: We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of a very average star. But we can understand the Universe. That makes us something very special.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Hawking, from his interview in Der Spiegel, 17 October 1988 — sourced on Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably Hawking's most-quoted statement of the human condition, and unlike most of the inspirational lines pinned on him it has a hard, dated primary source on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: Before Elvis there was nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: No contemporaneous Lennon source. Wikiquote lists it under Disputed, citing only a posthumous appearance in 'Elvis Is Everywhere,' The New York Times (16 August 2007).
candidates.whyNotable: The line every Elvis tribute reaches for, always credited to Lennon — yet the only citation Wikiquote can offer is a newspaper piece published 27 years after he died.

candidates.quote: Reality leaves a lot to the imagination.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unpinned. Wikiquote's only citation is the Sunday Herald Sun (Melbourne), 13 January 2003 — a posthumous secondary source with no original interview, book or broadcast behind it.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the highest-volume Lennon one-liners on aggregator sites, and the best documentation anyone has is a 2003 Australian newspaper quoting a man who died in 1980.

candidates.quote: Books will soon be obsolete in the schools.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Edison, New York Dramatic Mirror (July 1913): 'Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools. Scholars will be instructed through the eye.'
candidates.whyNotable: An authentic but famously wrong Edison prediction, often quoted ironically; QI verifies the fuller original in a 1913 New York Dramatic Mirror interview, though the popular version drops the word 'public'.

candidates.quote: Everything comes to him who hustles while he waits.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Edison, quoted in Francis Arthur Jones, Thomas Alva Edison (1908).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, sourced Edison aphorism (his twist on the proverb 'everything comes to him who waits'), documented in the 1908 biography Thomas Alva Edison: Sixty Years of an Inventor's Life.

candidates.quote: Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Edison; 1-to-99 ratio documented from 1901, related formulations from 1898.
candidates.whyNotable: Edison's signature saying; QI confirms it is reasonable to credit him with the 1-to-99 ratio, first in print in an 1901 newspaper (earlier 1898 versions used 2-to-98).

candidates.quote: Any customer can have a car painted any color that he wants so long as it is black.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry Ford, My Life and Work (1922), p. 72.
candidates.whyNotable: Ford's genuine, sourced quip about the Model T — a real anchor line to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Failure is only the opportunity more intelligently to begin again.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry Ford (with Samuel Crowther), My Life and Work (1922); modern reordered wording emerged from a 1922 review.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where the popular attribution is correct; QI confirms Ford wrote it in his 1922 book, though the modern web wording ('Failure is the opportunity to begin again, more intelligently') is a reordering.

candidates.quote: History is more or less bunk.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry Ford, Chicago Tribune interview (May 25, 1916).
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely Ford's, from a sourced 1916 interview — a famous real line often quoted (and misquoted as 'History is bunk').

candidates.quote: Politicians are like diapers. They need to be changed regularly, and for the same reason.
candidates.trueOrigin: No support for Mark Twain; earliest documented version is a 1966 newspaper column by Dick Nolan (San Francisco Examiner), evolved from older 'change your socks/politicians' jokes. Robin Williams merely voiced a version in Man of the Year (2006), screenplay by Barry Levinson.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'politician' one-liner popularly pinned on Mark Twain and often re-credited to Robin Williams because he delivered it in the 2006 film Man of the Year; QI finds no Twain evidence and traces the earliest match to a 1966 Dick Nolan column in the San Francisco Examiner.

candidates.quote: Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Dickens
candidates.whyNotable: The most famous budgeting line ever written, and still the best: happiness and ruin separated by one shilling. A staple of personal-finance talks precisely because the margin is absurdly thin.

candidates.quote: God bless us, every one!
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Tiny Tim in A Christmas Carol (1843), Stave 3 "The Second of the Three Spirits", echoed in the closing line of Stave 5.
candidates.whyNotable: The best-known line of the best-known Christmas story in English, with seasonal search demand and constant confusion over the exact wording and comma.

candidates.quote: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — A Tale of Two Cities (1859), Book I "Recalled to Life", Ch. 1 "The Period".
candidates.whyNotable: Arguably the most recognised opening line in English fiction and a high-volume "who said it" search; a real anchor for the Dickens hub.

candidates.quote: Please, sir, I want some more.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — spoken by Oliver in Oliver Twist (serialised from 1837), Ch. 2.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted lines of dialogue in English literature and constantly searched for its exact wording and chapter.

candidates.quote: A teacher, a really good sensei, is never a giver of 'truth'; he is a guide, a pointer to the truth that the student must discover for himself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bruce Lee, 'Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate,' Black Belt magazine, September 1971
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where the popular attribution holds up: QI confirms Bruce Lee wrote it in his essay 'Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate' in the September 1971 Black Belt magazine, making it a strong verified anchor amid his many fakes.

candidates.quote: Be water, my friend.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bruce Lee, 1971 Pierre Berton interview; documented in Bruce Lee: A Warrior's Journey (2000)
candidates.whyNotable: Bruce Lee's signature line, from his 1971 Pierre Berton television interview and preserved in Bruce Lee: A Warrior's Journey (2000) — the real, sourced anchor the internet's fakes cluster around.

candidates.quote: Don't think. Feel. It is like a finger pointing away to the moon. Don't concentrate on the finger or you will miss all that heavenly glory.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bruce Lee's character in the film Enter the Dragon (1973)
candidates.whyNotable: One of Bruce Lee's most-quoted movie lines, spoken by his character in Enter the Dragon (1973) and sourced on Wikiquote — genuinely from the film even though it is often shortened and reworded online.

candidates.quote: In taking revenge, a man is but even with his enemy; but in passing it over, he is superior; for it is a prince's part to pardon.
candidates.trueOrigin: Francis Bacon
candidates.whyNotable: The cleanest cost-benefit case ever made for letting go: revenge only draws you level, forgiveness puts you above. From the same essay as 'a man that studieth revenge keeps his own wounds green.'

candidates.quote: Money is like muck, not good except it be spread
candidates.trueOrigin: Francis Bacon
candidates.whyNotable: A four-centuries-old case for circulation over hoarding, in one earthy image — the go-to epigraph for anything on inequality, velocity of money, or philanthropy.

candidates.quote: Nature to be commanded must be obeyed.
candidates.trueOrigin: Francis Bacon
candidates.whyNotable: Four centuries old and still the sharpest one-line statement of the limits of human mastery over nature — reads as a sustainability epigraph without being written as one.

candidates.quote: Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications and to watch over their fate.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Democracy in America, Volume II (1840), Book Two (Fourth Book in some editions), Chapter VI, 'What Sort of Despotism Democratic Nations Have to Fear'.
candidates.whyNotable: The opening of the famous 'soft despotism' passage — the single most quoted paragraph of Volume II and the source of a term still used in political commentary.

candidates.quote: Democracy and socialism have nothing in common but one word: equality. But notice the difference: while democracy seeks equality in liberty, socialism seeks equality in restraint and servitude.
candidates.trueOrigin: Alexis de Tocqueville, 'Discours prononcé à l'assemblée constituante le 12 septembre 1848 sur la question du droit au travail', Oeuvres complètes vol. IX, p. 546; popular English rendering via F. A. Hayek, The Road to Serfdom (1944).
candidates.whyNotable: The most-cited Tocqueville line in modern political argument and genuinely his — from his 12 September 1848 speech to the Constituent Assembly — though the familiar English wording is Hayek's condensed translation in The Road to Serfdom, which is why sceptics often assume it is fake.

candidates.quote: I know of no country in which there is so little independence of mind and real freedom of discussion as in America.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Democracy in America, Volume I (1835), Chapter XV.
candidates.whyNotable: The anchor line of Tocqueville's 'tyranny of the majority' chapter and one of his most-quoted verified observations — cited constantly in free-speech and conformity debates.

candidates.quote: Premature optimization is the root of all evil
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely Knuth (1974) but nearly always quoted without his crucial qualifier — a good 'real but mangled' entry.

candidates.quote: I never said most of the things I said.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Berra; subtitle of his 1998 book The Yogi Book: I Really Didn't Say Everything I Said!
candidates.whyNotable: A rare meta-Yogiism that is authentically his and is literally about how many quotes are wrongly attributed to him.

candidates.quote: I really didn't say everything I said.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Yogi Berra; title/text of The Yogi Book (1997)
candidates.whyNotable: The perfect anchor for a misattribution hub: a verified Berra line (title of The Yogi Book, 1997) in which he himself acknowledges the pile of quotes wrongly credited to him.

candidates.quote: It ain't over till it's over.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Yogi Berra; sourced in The Yogi Book (1997)
candidates.whyNotable: One of Berra's genuinely-sourced lines (said about the 1973 pennant race and printed in The Yogi Book), giving the hub a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: All they want to do is protest and riot. Maybe they should try doing their jobs instead.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fabricated by America's Last Line of Defense (ALLOD) in a 24 Jan 2026 Facebook post carrying a satire watermark reading 'Nothing on this page is real'; Jordan never said it.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated widely on Facebook, Threads and X in January 2026 as a real Jordan statement on Democrats — Snopes notes readers were reading it as a factual recounting, and that ALLOD has recycled Jordan political fakes repeatedly.

candidates.quote: He's got such potential. I used to really look up to him.
candidates.trueOrigin: Invented for an 11 Nov 2023 article on Dunning-Kruger-Times.com, an ALLOD-network satire site whose disclaimer reads 'Everything on this website is fiction'; the fictional interviewer 'Tara Newhole' is a recurring ALLOD tell.
candidates.whyNotable: Spread under the headline that Jordan wanted to 'slap some sense' into Colin Kaepernick — a fake that works because Jordan's real-world political reticence makes any political statement from him feel like news.

candidates.quote: If these kids can afford $8 cups of coffee, they can afford to pay their own student loans.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fabricated by America's Last Line of Defense (ALLOD), a self-labeled satire/parody Facebook network; originally posted 16 Aug 2024 as a quote meme over a photo of Jordan.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Jordan quotes of the last two years — the ALLOD post alone drew 47,000+ shares and 185,000+ likes in four days, and Snopes rates it Labeled Satire with the originating post archived.

candidates.quote: LeBron James is the GOAT in my eyes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous December 2018 social-media copypasta praising LeBron James, falsely framed as a Jordan statement; Snopes rates it False.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-searched fake Jordan quote in the GOAT debate — Snopes points out that had Jordan actually crowned LeBron, it would have led every sports site that week, and it did not.

candidates.quote: You will stand in line for my shoes but won't stand up for yourself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Invented by TMZ Hip Hop, a fake-news site unaffiliated with TMZ, in a 25 July 2016 article; it grafted the invented line onto the opening of Jordan's genuine, same-week 'I can no longer stay silent' statement in The Undefeated.
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook hybrid fake — a fabricated headline quote welded to a real Jordan statement published days earlier, which is exactly why it reads as authentic and still circulates as a meme.

candidates.quote: It's gotta be the shoes
candidates.trueOrigin: Mars Blackmon, the character played by Spike Lee in Nike's Air Jordan commercials of the late 1980s and early 1990s; Wikipedia renders the catchphrase as 'It's gotta be da shoes.' Jordan appears in the ads but does not deliver the line.
candidates.whyNotable: The most quoted line from the most famous sneaker campaign ever made, routinely pinned on Jordan because he is the man on screen — the actual speaker is Spike Lee's character, and the campaign's creative director could not recall who wrote it.

candidates.quote: He who is not courageous enough to take risks will accomplish nothing in life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ali; earliest documented instance is an April 1977 Fort Lauderdale News report, and he reused it through 1980. QI credits Ali.
candidates.whyNotable: Often shared as generic inspiration but genuinely Ali's; QI confirms he coined it, using it repeatedly from April 1977 and even asking a reporter to write it down.

candidates.quote: I am the greatest! I'm the greatest thing that ever lived.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ali; spoken after defeating Sonny Liston, February 25, 1964, as documented on Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: Ali's defining self-declaration, shouted after upsetting Sonny Liston on February 25, 1964; a genuine sourced anchor line.

candidates.quote: My conscience won't let me go shoot my brother, or some darker people, or some poor hungry people in the mud, for big powerful America
candidates.trueOrigin: Muhammad Ali, 1967, on refusing induction into the U.S. military
candidates.whyNotable: Ali's genuine, Wikiquote-sourced 1967 explanation for refusing Vietnam draft induction - a historically documented real quote to anchor the hub.

candidates.quote: The man who views the world at 50 the same as he did at 20 has wasted 30 years of his life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ali; delivered at a November 1974 London news conference (reported by UPI) and repeated in a November 1975 Playboy interview.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely quoted Ali reflection that is actually genuine; QI confirms Ali said it at a 1974 London news conference, with a concise version in a 1975 Playboy interview.

candidates.quote: To err is human, to forgive, divine.
candidates.trueOrigin: Alexander Pope
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line in English on forgiveness — a complete argument in six words, and the reason 'to err is human' entered the language at all.

candidates.quote: Republicans buy sneakers, too
candidates.trueOrigin: Jordan, off the record. First published by sportswriter Sam Smith in Second Coming (1995) as a private remark from 1990; Jordan neither confirmed nor denied it for roughly 30 years, then confirmed it in The Last Dance (2020).
candidates.whyNotable: The defining Jordan quote controversy: he told The Last Dance 'I said it in jest on a bus with Horace Grant and Scottie Pippen,' after three decades in which the line — also circulated as 'Republicans buy shoes, too' — was used to characterise his refusal to back Harvey Gantt in the 1990 North Carolina Senate race.

candidates.quote: If your house was burning and you could only take one thing with you, what would it be? I would take the fire.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jean Cocteau, in 1951 radio interviews with Andre Fraigneau (published in Entretiens, 1965/1988); Coelho retold it in 2007
candidates.whyNotable: A poetic line that circulates as a Coelho quote; QI shows Coelho was only a transmitter who shared the anecdote on his website in 2007, while the actual remark is Jean Cocteau's from 1951 radio interviews.

candidates.quote: I only hope that we never lose sight of one thing — that it was all started by a mouse.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walt Disney, from The Disneyland Story television program (27 October 1954).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Disney's most iconic genuine lines, documented from his 1954 Disneyland Story television program.

candidates.quote: We keep moving forward, opening new doors, and doing new things, because we're curious and curiosity keeps leading us down new paths.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walt Disney, as quoted in the ending credits of Meet the Robinsons (2007).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared Disney quote with a real documented source in the closing credits of Meet the Robinsons.

candidates.quote: Everybody has plans until they get hit for the first time.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mike Tyson, on opponent Tyrell Biggs, quoted by Rick Warner (Associated Press), Aug 1987 — the earliest documented form of the famous line.
candidates.whyNotable: The verified original wording behind the viral 'punched in the mouth' misquote; QI identifies this AP quote as the genuine source.

candidates.quote: I probably have a 20,000-word vocabulary. I'll match my wits with anyone on literature, science and the arts.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mike Tyson, USA Today, 2005.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared self-description that plays against his public image; sourced on Wikiquote to USA Today.

candidates.quote: I'm the best ever. I'm the most brutal and vicious, and most ruthless champion there's ever been. There's no one that can stop me. Lennox is a conqueror? No, I'm Alexander! He's no Alexander. I'm the best ever. There's never been anybody as ruthless. I'm Sonny Liston. I'm Jack Dempsey. There's no one like me. I'm from their cloth. There is no one that can match me. My style is impetuous. My defense is impregnable, and I'm just ferocious. I want your heart. I want to eat his children. Praise be to Allah!
candidates.trueOrigin: Mike Tyson, post-fight interview with Jim Gray, 2000, calling out Lennox Lewis.
candidates.whyNotable: The infamous 'I want to eat his children' rant — a genuinely delivered, endlessly re-shared anchor line sourced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: Real freedom is having nothing. I was freer when I didn't have a cent.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mike Tyson, Sports Illustrated, 1988.
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently quoted, reflective Tyson line with a clean Wikiquote citation to Sports Illustrated.

candidates.quote: Social media made y'all way too comfortable with disrespecting people and not getting punched in the face for it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Mike Tyson's own social media account; authenticity examined and broadly upheld by Snopes, though exact wording varies across reposts.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral modern Tyson line people specifically ask 'did he really post this?' about — Wikiquote lists it and Snopes examined it.

candidates.quote: These books ain't window dressing. I think Machiavelli's the most sophisticated writer outside of Shakespeare.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mike Tyson, quoted in The Telegraph.
candidates.whyNotable: Often-shared 'Tyson on literature' line that surprises people; sourced on Wikiquote to the Telegraph.

candidates.quote: The golden moments in the stream of life rush past us, and we see nothing but sand; the angels come to visit us, and we only know them when they are gone.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans)
candidates.whyNotable: The strongest line on appreciation-in-hindsight — the cost of not noticing what you have while you have it. Verified verbatim in the Gutenberg text; nearly every quote site reprints it with no source at all.
candidates.notes: Mary Ann Evans · Mary Ann Evans

candidates.quote: Always remember that you are absolutely unique. Just like everyone else.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI traces the earliest version to Jim Wright, assistant editorial director of The Dallas Morning News, March 1971 ("How can I be unique just like everybody else?"). The Mead credit appears to be a misreading of "Meade's Maxim" in John Peers' 1,001 Logical Laws (1979), p. 153 — 'Meade', not 'Mead'.
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook one-letter misattribution: a joke labelled 'Meade's Maxim' in a 1979 laws-of-life compilation drifted onto the anthropologist Margaret Mead around 2001 and has been shared as hers ever since.

candidates.quote: The first sign of civilization in an ancient culture was a femur that had been broken and then healed.
candidates.trueOrigin: First appears in print in Dr. Paul Brand and Philip Yancey, Fearfully and Wonderfully Made (1980), as Brand's decades-later recollection of a Mead lecture. No written or recorded Mead statement exists. Mead's documented answer on what marks civilization (Talks with Social Scientists, 1968) is the opposite kind of answer — cities, division of labor, record-keeping.
candidates.whyNotable: The viral 'compassion is the first sign of civilization' story: it survives only as one physician's memory published two decades after the fact, and contradicts what Mead is actually on record as saying.

candidates.quote: Art is a lie that makes us realize truth, at least the truth that is given us to understand.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine: from 'Picasso Speaks', The Arts, May 1923, p. 315; reprinted in MoMA's 1946 'Picasso: Fifty Years of His Art'.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, well-sourced Picasso statement from his 1923 The Arts interview, serving as a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Computers are useless. They can only give you answers.
candidates.trueOrigin: Traces to a 1964 Paris Review interview by William Fifield, where Picasso said of calculating machines 'But they are useless. They can only give you answers.' The modern 'computers' wording was refined over 1967-1986.
