candidates.whyNotable: One of Picasso's most-quoted lines that QI actually substantiates, sourcing it to a documented 1964 Paris Review interview even though the 'computers' wording was polished later.

candidates.quote: For our last number, I'd like to ask your help. Would the people in the cheaper seats clap your hands. And the rest of you, if you'll just rattle your jewellery.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine. Said from the stage at the Royal Variety Performance, London, 4 November 1963, in front of the Queen Mother — captured on the broadcast recording.
candidates.whyNotable: Lennon's best-documented ad-lib, preserved on tape and endlessly requoted as the moment the Beatles' cheek met the establishment — a real anchor against the fabrications.

candidates.quote: I think our society is run by insane people for insane objectives.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine. From a Lennon interview dated 6 June 1968, listed with that date in Wikiquote's sourced section.
candidates.whyNotable: Lennon's most-quoted political line and a staple of protest imagery; it is genuinely his, with a dated 1968 interview behind it rather than a meme trail.

candidates.quote: We're more popular than Jesus now; I don't know which will go first — rock and roll or Christianity.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine. Said to journalist Maureen Cleave for her profile published in London's Evening Standard, 4 March 1966.
candidates.whyNotable: The most consequential thing Lennon ever said in an interview — it triggered US radio bans and record burnings — and unlike the meme quotes it has a precise, contemporaneous published source.

candidates.quote: If you seek revenge, you should dig two graves, one for yourself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Japanese proverb tradition. Earliest match: William Elliot Griffis, 'The Mikado's Empire' (1876), rendered 'If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves'; 'revenge' replaces 'curse' by 1915. No connection to Confucius. Bezos cited it (attributing it to Confucius, while noting he was unsure) in a 2016 interview.
candidates.whyNotable: A classic fake-Confucius line that Bezos himself repeated in a 2016 interview while crediting Confucius — QI finds no Confucian basis and traces it to a Japanese proverb printed in an 1876 book about Japan.

candidates.quote: Custom is a violent and treacherous schoolmistress.
candidates.trueOrigin: Michel de Montaigne
candidates.whyNotable: The counterweight the theme usually lacks — habit as a force that installs itself unnoticed, which is exactly why it deserves deliberate design. The passage continues with custom slipping in "the foot of her authority" by degrees.

candidates.quote: If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer, because it was he, because it was I
candidates.trueOrigin: Michel de Montaigne
candidates.whyNotable: The most famous sentence ever written about a particular friendship (Montaigne on Étienne de La Boétie) — friendship beyond reasons.

candidates.quote: Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world; indeed, it's the only thing that ever has.
candidates.trueOrigin: No known Mead source. Earliest strong match is Donald Keys, Earth at Omega: Passage to Planetization (1982), p. 79, which credits Mead but gives no documentation. Related sentiments predate it (Norman Vincent Peale 1959, Patrick Haggerty 1963, R. H. Edwin Espy 1967). Mead's own Institute for Intercultural Studies conceded it could not locate when or where it was first cited.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the single most-quoted line in activism and nonprofit branding, printed on masthead and merchandise worldwide — and neither Wikiquote, QI, nor Mead's own institute can find it anywhere in her corpus.

candidates.quote: What people say, what people do, and what they say they do are entirely different things.
candidates.trueOrigin: No citation found. Harvard Library's reference service states plainly it cannot find one; the book Architecture and Field/Work (p. 80 n. 3) describes the line as 'a simplification of extensive writing by Mead on the fieldwork of anthropologists.' Wikiquote's earliest cite is Teaching Music Through Performance in Band, Vol. 3 (2000), p. 13 — 22 years posthumous.
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical epigraph of user research and UX — quoted in design decks constantly — yet Harvard Library says there is no citation, and the earliest print trace is a band-teaching manual from 2000.

candidates.quote: A person's a person, no matter how small.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely from Dr. Seuss, 'Horton Hears a Who!' (1954).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, book-sourced Seuss line that anchors the hub alongside the debunks; from Horton Hears a Who! (1954).

candidates.quote: The more that you read, the more things you will know. The more that you learn, the more places you'll go.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely from Dr. Seuss, 'I Can Read With My Eyes Shut!' (1978).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, book-sourced Seuss literacy line that serves as a verified anchor; from I Can Read With My Eyes Shut! (1978).

candidates.quote: Death is nature's way of saying, 'Your table is ready.'
candidates.trueOrigin: Credited to Robin Williams via Wikiquote (citing The Fourth...637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said, 1990); as a compact one-liner its ultimate origin is not fully pinned.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous gallows-humor line credited to Williams and sourced on Wikiquote, though the compact joke format means the exact origin is not ironclad — worth an anchor page with a light provenance caveat.

candidates.quote: I wonder what chairs think about all day: 'Oh, here comes another asshole.'
candidates.trueOrigin: Robin Williams, Reality...What a Concept (1979), per Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-circulated genuine Williams stand-up bit, sourced on Wikiquote to his 1979 special Reality...What a Concept — a verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: You're only given a little spark of madness. You mustn't lose it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Robin Williams, early stand-up / A Night at the Roxy era (late 1970s), as sourced on Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Williams' most-shared genuine lines about creativity, from his early stand-up and sourced on Wikiquote — a real anchor to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets
candidates.trueOrigin: Arthur Jones of Procter & Gamble, whose wording was "All organisations are perfectly designed to get the results they get." Paul Batalden carried it to the US Quality Council and into healthcare-improvement practice, where the reworded form spread and picked up Deming's name. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement documents the chain and states the Deming attribution is wrong.
candidates.whyNotable: The standard opening line of every process-improvement and change-management deck, credited to Deming almost universally; IHI traces it to a P&G colleague of Paul Batalden's and a different original wording.

candidates.quote: In God we trust. All others must bring data.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous. QI's earliest citation is pathologist Edwin R. Fisher testifying before a U.S. House subcommittee on September 7, 1978 ("In God we trust, others must provide data") — and Fisher himself called it a "well-recognized cliche," meaning it predated him. It appears in Mary Walton's The Deming Management Method (1986, p. 96) with no attribution to Deming or anyone else, which is likely how the Deming credit began.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared line pinned on Deming and the flagship data-culture slogan on every analytics slide deck; both Wikiquote and Quote Investigator reject the Deming credit outright, with QI stating there is no substantive support for assigning it to him.

candidates.quote: But suppose the child inherited my beauty and your brains?
candidates.trueOrigin: A floating joke that predates Monroe by decades, told earlier about George Bernard Shaw, Isadora Duncan, and others.
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'beauty and brains' comeback (often set as a Monroe-and-Einstein or Monroe-and-Bernard-Shaw exchange); QI shows the joke circulated long before Monroe and is a floating anecdote.

candidates.quote: Hollywood is a place where they'll pay you a thousand dollars for a kiss and fifty cents for your soul.
candidates.trueOrigin: First printed in Monroe's posthumous 1974 autobiography 'My Story' (published 12 years after her death); authenticity of the wording is contested.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted 'cynical Hollywood' Monroe lines; QI finds it only in her ghostwritten posthumous 1974 autobiography 'My Story,' so whether she actually said it is uncertain.

candidates.quote: Your margin is my opportunity.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source located; first appears secondhand in Adam Lashinsky, 'Amazon's Jeff Bezos: The Ultimate Disrupter,' Fortune, November 2012. QI explicitly notes it would help to know how Lashinsky learned of the expression.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-repeated Bezos business aphorism in tech/startup culture, yet Quote Investigator can find no primary Bezos utterance — the earliest match is a November 2012 Fortune cover story that merely calls it 'a favorite Bezos aphorism,' with no interview transcript or recording behind it.

candidates.quote: Buy land, they're not making it anymore.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous — circulating in Kansas newspapers by October 1905. Rogers wrote a longer, thematically related passage about ocean frontage in 1930, but the quip predates him; the Rogers credit starts in 1954.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-repeated real-estate quip in existence, split between Rogers and Mark Twain; QI shows it was already anonymous newspaper filler by 1905.

candidates.quote: Diplomacy is the art of saying "nice doggie" until you can find a rock.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Rogers. Appears unattributed in a 1953 issue of The Tennessee Conservationist; credited to Francis Rodman in Reader's Digest (1954), later to Wynn Catlin and to Winston Churchill (1955 speech reprint) — all post-date Rogers' 1935 death.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted lines about diplomacy, variously pinned on Rogers, Churchill and Wynn Catlin; Wikiquote shows every documented instance appears after Rogers died.

candidates.quote: Don't let yesterday use up too much of today.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed with no source for Rogers; it appears only in aggregator databases with no pre-1935 citation.
candidates.whyNotable: Among the most-shared "Will Rogers" lines on social media and greeting cards, yet Wikiquote flags it as misattributed and no primary citation exists.

candidates.quote: Even if you're on the right track, you'll get run over if you just sit there.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous. QI's earliest match is a March 1925 syndicated humor column, "Tom Sims Says" (The Sheboygan Press, The Indianapolis Times); the Rogers and Mark Twain credits both appear only long after their deaths.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the single most-shared fake Will Rogers line on motivational sites and LinkedIn; QI found no substantive evidence for Rogers and traces it to Tom Sims in 1925.

candidates.quote: Good judgment comes from experience, and a lot of that comes from bad judgment.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous — earliest instances (1932, 1943) carry no attribution; a 1945 Reader's Digest anecdote credits a Kentucky sage called "Uncle Zeke" via Gen. Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. Rita Mae Brown popularized it in 2001 as an old saying.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated for decades in "Will Rogers' Wisdom" chain emails; QI finds the Rogers attribution unsupported and the earliest versions anonymous.

candidates.quote: I am not so much concerned with the return on capital as I am with the return of capital.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eddie Cantor, after being burned in the stock market — reported in The National Underwriter, Vol. 45 (1941): "the life insurance policyholder is more interested in the return of his money than in the return on it."
candidates.whyNotable: A finance-industry favourite reprinted in investing books as Rogers' Depression wisdom; Wikiquote traces it to Eddie Cantor via a 1941 insurance trade journal.

candidates.quote: Thank goodness we don't get as much government as we pay for.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; circulating by 1946. A 1947 Nebraska newspaper quotes businessman Max Denney using it while disclaiming credit, and Charles F. Kettering used it by 1949, also denying authorship. The Rogers credit appears only in 1966.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial political-speech line credited to Rogers; QI dates the Rogers attribution to 1966, thirty-one years after his death, and calls the evidence very weak.

candidates.quote: Too many people spend money they haven't earned, to buy things they don't want, to impress people they don't like.
candidates.trueOrigin: Robert Quillen, syndicated humorist, June 1928: "Americanism: Using money you haven't earned to buy things you don't need to impress people you don't like." The Rogers credit surfaces in a 1975 New Mexico newspaper.
candidates.whyNotable: A personal-finance staple pinned on Rogers (and sometimes Will Smith); QI shows Robert Quillen wrote it in 1928 and Rogers only said a loosely related line about advertising in 1931.

candidates.quote: When the Okies left Oklahoma and moved to California, they raised the average intelligence level in both states.
candidates.trueOrigin: An anonymous, endlessly reworked joke. QI's earliest instance is a 1939 column by Herbert L. Carver (four years after Rogers died); the credit to Rogers first appears in 1970, and no matching line exists in his writings.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly repeated as Rogers' most famous zinger about his home state; QI shows it postdates his death and has no basis in his work.

candidates.quote: When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Muir
candidates.whyNotable: The clearest pre-ecology statement of interconnection — the go-to line for systems thinking, ecosystems, and 'everything is connected' arguments, and it predates the science it anticipates.

candidates.quote: Keep the faculty of effort alive in you by a little gratuitous exercise every day.
candidates.trueOrigin: William James
candidates.whyNotable: Italicised in the original as James's own practical maxim, and the closest any PD source gets to modern habit-stacking — willpower treated as a trainable muscle, exercised in small daily doses.

candidates.quote: We should not spoil what we have by desiring what we do not have, but remember that what we have too was the gift of fortune.
candidates.trueOrigin: Epicurus
candidates.whyNotable: The cleanest ancient statement of 'count what you have, not what you lack' — and the second clause (it was the gift of fortune) is exactly the reframe a gratitude talk needs. Bailey's 1926 translation is out of US copyright.

candidates.quote: It is not necessary to change. Survival is not mandatory.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source located in any Deming publication. The W. Edwards Deming Institute references it but cites no specific paper or book, and specialist reviewers find no evidence he made the exact statement. Deming did use survival as a theme — Out of the Crisis (1982) invokes Darwin — and the sourced line closest to it is "Learning is not compulsory; it's voluntary... But survival is not compulsory."
candidates.whyNotable: A change-management keynote staple credited to Deming everywhere from BrainyQuote to boardroom decks, with no publication behind it — the sourced Deming line it compresses says something meaningfully different.

candidates.quote: Uncontrolled variation is the enemy of quality.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unpinned to a primary Deming text. Wikiquote carries it only as attributed via a secondary source, Chang W. Kang and Paul H. Kvam, Basic Statistical Tools for Improving Quality (2012), which dates the supposed utterance to around 1980 without a primary citation.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple slogan in Six Sigma and quality-management training that Wikiquote can only support through a 2012 textbook's attribution, not through Deming's own writing.

candidates.quote: Without data, you're just another person with an opinion.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unpinned. Wikiquote lists it, but the only citation given is a Forbes article by Milo Jones and Philippe Silberzahn dated March 15, 2016 — twenty-three years after Deming's death, and a secondary repetition rather than a primary Deming source. No Deming book, lecture transcript, or seminar record is cited.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous in data-team culture decks and constantly paired with the "In God we trust" line, yet its best available citation is a 2016 magazine piece written long after Deming died.

candidates.quote: Learning is not compulsory... neither is survival.
candidates.trueOrigin: A garbled compression of a real Deming line. Wikiquote carries the sourced form "Learning is not compulsory; it's voluntary...But to survive, we must learn" from Deming: The Way We Knew Him (1995), with an explicit note that it is often cited in the punchier "neither is survival" form. The popular version inverts the meaning from an encouragement into a threat.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted management lines on the internet, and Wikiquote flags it directly as a misquotation of what Deming actually said — a clean documented-misquote page rather than a fabrication.

candidates.quote: There is no sense in being precise when you don't know what you're talking about.
candidates.trueOrigin: Quote Investigator traces the idea to von Neumann and Morgenstern's Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944) and finds the popular one-liner is a paraphrase reassigned to von Neumann without substantive citation. Notably, Deming's own 1945 review of that book contains the closely related "there is no point in using exact methods" phrasing — which is why the line circulates under his name too.
candidates.whyNotable: A heavily-shared statistics aphorism that floats between von Neumann and Deming; QI's investigation is the rare case where Deming's own 1945 writing is part of the documented chain rather than a spurious credit.
candidates.notes: also widely credited to W. Edwards Deming

candidates.quote: Why don't you come up and see me sometime?
candidates.whyNotable: Mae West in She Done Him Wrong (1933) actually says 'Why don't you come up sometime and see me?'

candidates.quote: If you can't measure it, you can't manage it
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in Drucker's writing — the Drucker Institute's own archivists say there is no evidence he ever wrote or said it. Also widely pinned on W. Edwards Deming, who argued the OPPOSITE: The New Economics (1993) reads "It is wrong to suppose that if you can't measure it, you can't manage it - a costly myth." The nearest real ancestor is Lord Kelvin's measurement dictum; the modern management form has no established author.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-used management-slide quote in business presentations, credited to Drucker almost universally — yet the Drucker Institute denies it and the Deming Institute publishes a dedicated page showing Deming said the reverse and called the idea a costly myth.

candidates.quote: What gets measured gets managed
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Drucker — the Drucker Institute states he never said it. The idea traces to V. F. Ridgway's 1956 paper "Dysfunctional Consequences of Performance Measurements", which argued AGAINST the maxim: Ridgway documented the harm caused by managing to measurable proxies. The popular version inverts a warning into a rule.
candidates.whyNotable: The shorter, even more quotable twin of the Drucker measurement line; the maxim now used to justify metrics programmes began life in 1956 as a documented critique of exactly that practice, and the man it is credited to never said it.

candidates.quote: I can accept failure. Everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare Jordan line with a hard print citation — his own book I Can't Accept Not Trying: Michael Jordan on the Pursuit of Excellence (HarperSanFrancisco, 1994) — which makes it a clean verified anchor against the fabrications.

candidates.quote: I've missed over 9,000 shots in my career. I've lost almost 300 games. 26 times I've been trusted to take the game-winning shot and missed. I've failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed.
candidates.whyNotable: Jordan's most-quoted lines anywhere, delivered in Nike's 'Failure' commercial and sourced by Wikiquote to Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh (1998) — and constantly mangled in circulation, with the counts inflated to 12,000 shots or the '26 times' dropped entirely.

candidates.quote: Never say never, because limits, like fears, are often just an illusion.
candidates.trueOrigin: Michael Jordan, Basketball Hall of Fame induction speech, September 11, 2009
candidates.whyNotable: Widely circulated as a standalone motivational line, it is genuinely Jordan's, delivered at the close of his 2009 Hall of Fame speech.

candidates.quote: The ceiling is the roof
candidates.whyNotable: Said on camera at halftime of the Duke–North Carolina game on 4 March 2017 while announcing Jordan Brand's UNC football deal; the malapropism became a UNC meme and an officially licensed T-shirt, so its provenance is unusually well documented for a viral line.

candidates.quote: As I began to love myself I found that anguish and emotional suffering are only warning signs
candidates.whyNotable: Viral 'On my birthday, Charlie Chaplin' poem; not by Chaplin — a modern text ('When I Began to Love Myself').

candidates.quote: There is only one thing that makes a dream impossible to achieve: the fear of failure.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist (1988), p. 141
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced and heavily shared Alchemist line (1988), useful as a verified anchor alongside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: Warriors of the light are not perfect. Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paulo Coelho, Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997)
candidates.whyNotable: A real, Wikiquote-sourced line from Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997), giving the hub a second genuine anchor beyond The Alchemist.

candidates.quote: When you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist (1988), p. 22
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line from The Alchemist and a real, sourced Coelho quote (p. 22 of the 1988 novel) that anchors the hub against the debunks.

candidates.quote: An intellectual is a man who says a simple thing in a difficult way; an artist is a man who says a difficult thing in a simple way.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Bukowski, Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, frequently-quoted Bukowski aphorism with a real source citation on Wikiquote (Notes of a Dirty Old Man, 1969), giving the hub a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: The free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it — basically because you feel good, very good, when you are near or with them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Bukowski, Tales of Ordinary Madness.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine and heavily-circulated Bukowski line sourced on Wikiquote to Tales of Ordinary Madness, useful as a verified real anchor among the misattributions.

candidates.quote: We are here to laugh at the odds and live our lives so well that Death will tremble to take us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Bukowski, Life Magazine (December 1988), 'The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture'.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely-shared Bukowski line with a solid citation — part of his answer in Life Magazine's December 1988 'The Meaning of Life' feature — making it a strong real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: They also serve who only stand and wait.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Milton
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical English line on waiting well: it reframes enforced delay as a form of service rather than idleness, which is exactly the note most patience slides are reaching for.

candidates.quote: Behind every great fortune there is a crime
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularised as the epigraph of Mario Puzo's 1969 novel The Godfather, where Puzo printed this concise form and credited it to Balzac. Quote Investigator finds Balzac's actual 1834 French sentence was narrower: "Le secret des grandes fortunes sans cause apparente est un crime oublié, parce qu'il a été proprement fait" — rendered in an 1896 English translation as "The secret of a great success for which you are at a loss to account is a crime that has never been found out, because it was properly executed." QI's verdict: the modern terse version is the product of decades of simplification and "no single person can be credited with the construction of the modern concise and forceful version." Balzac did not claim all great fortunes rest on crime.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line associated with The Godfather that is not a film line at all — it is the novel's epigraph, and the wording credited to Balzac is not Balzac's. QI traces the drift and names the intermediate claimants (Pierre Mille, C. Wright Mills, Jane Bryant Quinn among them).

candidates.quote: America is great because she is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, she will cease to be great.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Tocqueville — it appears nowhere in Democracy in America. Michael A. Ledeen (Tocqueville on American Character, 2001) documents the false attribution and names Colin Powell, Dwight Eisenhower, Bill Clinton, Ross Perot and Pat Buchanan as the public figures who spread it.
candidates.whyNotable: Wikiquote names Powell by name as one of five prominent Americans who propagated this fake Tocqueville line, making it the one documented Powell-adjacent misattribution at either authority — note the popular credit is to Tocqueville, not Powell.

candidates.quote: Organizations don't get things done. Plans and programs don't get things done. Only people get things done.
candidates.trueOrigin: Admiral Hyman G. Rickover. Powell reproduces the line in It Worked For Me (2012), pp. 278-279, explicitly recalling hearing Rickover say it at a promotion ceremony in the early 1970s; Wikiquote files it on the Rickover page.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates widely in leadership decks as a Colin Powell quote, but Wikiquote documents it as Rickover's line that Powell was quoting — Powell credited Rickover, the internet dropped the credit.

candidates.quote: That best portion of a good man's life, his little, nameless, unremembered acts of kindness and of love.
candidates.trueOrigin: William Wordsworth
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical Romantic tribute to small, quiet acts of kindness as the finest part of a good life.

candidates.quote: As the traveler who has once been from home is wiser than he who has never left his own doorstep, so a knowledge of one other culture should sharpen our ability to scrutinize more steadily, to appreciate more lovingly, our own.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Coming of Age in Samoa (William Morrow, 1928). The book is US public domain and is on Project Gutenberg (ebook 74750).
candidates.whyNotable: The rare Mead quote that is fully sourced to a primary text she wrote, and the source work is public domain — a clean verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: One of the oldest human needs is having someone to wonder where you are when you don't come home at night.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source located. Wikiquote's only citation is The Quotable Woman (Running Press, 1991), p. 53 — a compilation published 13 years after Mead's death.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial wedding-toast and loneliness-essay quote whose entire documentary trail is a single posthumous gift-book compilation.

candidates.quote: Every time we liberate a woman, we liberate a man.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote records it as attributed in La Abogada newsletter, Vol. 3 (1967), International Federation of Women Lawyers, p. 5 — attributed there, not quoted from a Mead publication.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of feminist and men's-allyship messaging; the trail stops at a 1967 lawyers' newsletter that itself only attributes it.

candidates.quote: I do not believe in using women in combat, because females are too fierce.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote cites Lloyd Cory, Quote Unquote (1977), p. 364 — a compilation published in Mead's lifetime but with no underlying speech or article identified.
candidates.whyNotable: Resurfaces in every women-in-combat policy debate; the only citation anyone has is a 1977 quotation anthology, not a Mead text.

candidates.quote: If we are to achieve a richer culture, rich in contrasting values, we must recognize the whole gamut of human potentialities, and so weave a less arbitrary social fabric, one in which each diverse human gift will find a fitting place.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine — Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), closing passage.
candidates.whyNotable: Her most-quoted line from an actual book, and the intellectual source of the 'small group can change the world' sentiment people wrongly quote instead.

candidates.quote: It is utterly false and cruelly arbitrary to put all the play and learning into childhood, all the work into middle age, and all the regrets into old age.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote's raw entry cites Male and Female (1949), Introduction; a rendering of the same page also lists Teacher's Treasury of Stories (1958). The 1949 book is the plausible primary — flag the conflict at build time.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared in life-design and retirement writing; two different sources circulate for it, so the page needs to pin down whether it is Male and Female (1949) or a 1958 anthology.

candidates.quote: Women want mediocre men, and men are working hard to be as mediocre as possible.
candidates.trueOrigin: Quote magazine, 15 June 1958 — contemporaneous with Mead, but a quotation digest rather than a Mead-authored text.
candidates.whyNotable: Her most-shared zinger, and one of the few widely circulated Mead lines with a contemporaneous printed citation rather than a posthumous one.

candidates.quote: Get over yourself! 'Cause it's not about you, man.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, interview with Patrick Bet-David, August 23, 2019 (YouTube).
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, dated interview line that Wikiquote sources precisely — a clean genuine anchor with an exact primary citation.

candidates.quote: I can't believe how fast 20 years went by... Mamba Out!
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, speech after his final game, April 13, 2016.
candidates.whyNotable: The iconic sign-off from Bryant's speech after his final NBA game, one of the most-quoted lines of his career and a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: No matter what, people are going to like you or not like you. So be authentic, and let them like you or not for who you actually are.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, The Mamba Mentality: How I Play (2018), 'Keep It Real.'
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, book-sourced Mamba Mentality line that is widely shared and gives the hub a real, citable anchor alongside the disputed material.

candidates.quote: The mamba mentality is a constant quest to try to be better today than you were yesterday.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, in his own words describing Mamba Mentality
candidates.whyNotable: Kobe's own verbatim definition of Mamba Mentality (as opposed to the many paraphrases), the anchor quote for the concept he created.

candidates.quote: I restore myself when I'm alone. A career is born in public — talent in privacy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marilyn Monroe, quoted in Ms. magazine, August 1972, p. 40.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine sourced Monroe line that Wikiquote cites to Ms. magazine (August 1972), useful as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: It's not quite true that I had nothing on. I had the radio on.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marilyn Monroe; earliest documented version in Sheilah Graham's June 1952 column.
candidates.whyNotable: Her celebrated quip about posing nude for a calendar; QI credits it to Monroe, with the earliest version appearing in a June 1952 gossip column.

candidates.quote: That's the trouble, a sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marilyn Monroe, LIFE magazine interview with Richard Meryman, August 1962.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare genuine, well-sourced Monroe line; QI documents it from her LIFE magazine interview with Richard Meryman published in August 1962, just before her death.

candidates.quote: I very frequently get the question: What's going to change in the next 10 years? I almost never get the question: What's not going to change in the next 10 years?
candidates.trueOrigin: Bezos, Harvard Business Review interview, October 2007 (earliest Bezos instance). Precursor framing: Wolfgang R. Schmitt, Rubbermaid, 1998 — 'Everybody's looking forward, thinking about what's going to change, and I thought I'd talk about what's not going to change.'
candidates.whyNotable: Bezos's signature strategic framing, confirmed by QI to an October 2007 Harvard Business Review interview and repeated by him in 2011 and 2012 — though QI also surfaces a near-identical 1998 framing from Rubbermaid CEO Wolfgang R. Schmitt, so Bezos gets credit for popularizing rather than originating it.

candidates.quote: If you absolutely can't tolerate critics, then don't do anything new or interesting.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jeff Bezos, 2016; Wikiquote sources it to BoingBoing, June 2016.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely reshared innovation line with a real sourced Wikiquote entry (June 2016), making it a solid verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: When the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jeff Bezos, April 2018; Wikiquote sources it to Business Insider, 21 April 2018.
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily quoted in product and UX circles, and usually circulated in this trimmed form rather than the fuller sourced wording ('The thing I have noticed is when the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right'), which makes it a useful exact-wording provenance page.

candidates.quote: Every organization should tolerate rebels who tell the emperor he has no clothes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Sourced by Wikiquote only to Oren Harari's The Powell Principles (2003); no Powell speech or book is cited, and the 'emperor has no clothes' framing is borrowed from Hans Christian Andersen.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of corporate culture decks credited to Powell, but like most of his management aphorisms its only documented source is Harari's book about him rather than Powell's own words.

candidates.quote: If you are going to achieve excellence in big things, you develop the habit in little matters. Excellence is not an exception, it is a prevailing attitude.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote appends an editorial note that the line 'evokes Will Durant's famous summation of Aristotle: Excellence then is not an act, but a habit' — and the wording itself comes via Oren Harari's The Powell Principles (2003), not from Powell directly.
candidates.whyNotable: A double provenance problem in one line: Wikiquote flags the idea as Will Durant's Aristotle summation (itself one of the most famous misattributions in circulation) while the wording is sourced only to a third-party book about Powell.

candidates.quote: Leadership is the art of accomplishing more than the science of management says is possible.
candidates.trueOrigin: Sourced by Wikiquote only to Oren Harari's The Powell Principles (2003), a business book about Powell; the section is explicitly headed as quotes taken from Harari's book rather than from Powell's own writing.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the most reproduced Powell leadership aphorism in management training, and its documented provenance runs through a ghost-adjacent business book rather than any Powell primary source.

candidates.quote: There are no secrets to success. It is the result of preparation, hard work and learning from failure.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wikiquote's sole source is Oren Harari's The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell (2003), p. 164 — a management book written about Powell, not by him. No Powell speech, memoir, or interview is cited.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared motivational 'Powell' lines on social media and in corporate decks, but its only documented source is a third-party leadership book about him rather than anything Powell wrote or said.

candidates.quote: You break it, you own it.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary utterance exists. Wikiquote's only source is Bob Woodward's Plan of Attack (2004), reporting a private warning Powell gave President Bush before the Iraq war. The popular 'Pottery Barn rule' label attached to it is itself a factual error — Pottery Barn has no such policy.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted Powell line and a fixture of foreign-policy commentary, yet it reaches us only through Woodward's secondhand paraphrase of a private 2002 dinner conversation, never from Powell in his own voice.

candidates.quote: A quotation is a handy thing to have about, saving one the trouble of thinking for oneself, always a laborious business.
candidates.trueOrigin: A. A. Milne, essay 'The Record Lie' in the 1920 collection If I May (QI notes Dorothy L. Sayers later voiced a similar, separate line via Lord Peter Wimsey in 1932).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, oft-quoted Milne aphorism that QI confirms and sources precisely, making a good real anchor amid the fakes.

candidates.quote: It is hard to be brave when you're only a Very Small Animal.
candidates.trueOrigin: A. A. Milne, Winnie-the-Pooh (1926), Chapter Seven (Piglet).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Piglet line from the original Winnie-the-Pooh, sourced on Wikiquote by chapter, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: when you are a Bear of Very Little Brain, and you Think of Things, you find sometimes that a Thing which seemed very Thingish inside you is quite different when it gets out into the open and has other people looking at it.
candidates.trueOrigin: A. A. Milne, The House at Pooh Corner (1928), Chapter Six (Pooh).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted Pooh passage sourced on Wikiquote to The House at Pooh Corner, serving as a real anchor beside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: A system must have an aim. Without an aim, there is no system.
candidates.whyNotable: The foundation of Deming's System of Profound Knowledge and a widely quoted systems-thinking line, sourced on Wikiquote to The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education (1993).

candidates.quote: Defects are not free. Somebody makes them, and gets paid for making them.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Deming's most-repeated and most characteristically blunt lines, sourced on Wikiquote to Out of the Crisis (1982), p. 11.

candidates.quote: Quality comes not from inspection, but from improvement of the production process.
candidates.whyNotable: The core thesis of Deming's quality philosophy, sourced on Wikiquote to Out of the Crisis (1982), p. 29 — a real anchor to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: I never met a man I didn't like.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Rogers — the fuller line, "I joked about every prominent man of my time, but I never met a man I didn't like," comes from his weekly column #219 (1927), first printed in the Boston Globe, 16 June 1930. It became his epitaph.
candidates.whyNotable: Rogers' signature line and the one carved on his memorial — a real, sourced anchor for the hub alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: The income tax has made more liars out of the American people than golf has.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rogers himself — his syndicated column, printed in The Chattanooga News, 7 April 1923; he reused it in November 1924 and in his 1924 book The Illiterate Digest.
candidates.whyNotable: His best-known tax joke, quoted every April, and QI confirms it with a 1923 column citation in his own syndicated writing.

candidates.quote: People are taking their comedians seriously and their politicians as a joke.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rogers himself — McNaught Syndicate column, printed in The Piqua Daily Call, 23 November 1932, originally "People are taking their comedians seriously, and their politicians as a joke, when it used to be vice versa."
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly re-shared as commentary on modern politics and confirmed by QI to a dated 1932 Rogers column, though the popular wording drops his closing clause.

candidates.quote: He who will not reason is a bigot; he who cannot is a fool; and he who dares not is a slave.
candidates.trueOrigin: William Drummond, preface to Academical Questions (1805). Carnegie found it carved in marble on a library mantelpiece at the home of Major Stokes, chief counsel of the Pennsylvania Railroad, and had it inscribed in his own New York and Skibo libraries — which is why quote sites now pin it on Carnegie. Lord Byron is the other common false credit; Byron quoted it in his 1819 notes to Childe Harold's Pilgrimage but explicitly credited Drummond.
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook case of the adopter eclipsing the author — Carnegie literally carved another man's line into his libraries and inherited the credit; QI traces it to William Drummond in 1805.

candidates.quote: War does not determine who is right — only who is left.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous. QI's earliest citation is an unattributed appearance in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, August 1931, popularized via Reader's Digest (February 1932). Carnegie voiced only precursors: 'War never settles who is right but who is wrong. Might, not right, conquers' (1907, National Arbitration and Peace Congress) and 'war never decides who is right, but merely who has the might' (1911). Bertrand Russell and Winston Churchill are the other common false credits.
candidates.whyNotable: A pacifist one-liner passed around under at least three famous names; QI finds no evidence for any of them and traces the modern wording to an anonymous 1931 newspaper filler.

candidates.quote: Be patient and tough; some day this pain will be useful to you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ovid
candidates.whyNotable: Two thousand years old and still the most usable line on enduring a bad stretch; the Latin "perfer et obdura" doubles as a memorable motto, and Perseus carries the original text.

candidates.quote: There is no wealth but life
candidates.trueOrigin: John Ruskin
candidates.whyNotable: Five words that redefine the whole subject; Ruskin's essay was Gandhi's stated turning point, which gives the line a documented afterlife most aphorisms lack.

candidates.quote: No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself, or get all the credit for doing it.
candidates.trueOrigin: A drifted wording of a real Carnegie remark. QI documents the authentic form in an interview published in the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 15 October 1899: 'No man will make a great business who wants to do it all himself, or to get all the credit of doing it.' The circulating 'leader' version swaps the noun and rewrites the tail; other variants substitute 'person' for 'man'.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared Carnegie leadership quote online is a mutated wording — QI pins the real 1899 sentence, which says 'business', not 'leader'.

candidates.quote: Three generations from shirtsleeves to shirtsleeves.
candidates.trueOrigin: Proverbial, not Carnegie's coinage. Wikiquote files it under 'Undated' with no primary Carnegie source — its only citation is a 2001 secondary work (George J. Borjas, Heaven's Door, p. 132). It is an American rendering of an older Lancashire proverb about clogs and three generations.
candidates.whyNotable: The wealth-decay proverb every estate planner attributes to Carnegie; Wikiquote can only source it to a 2001 book, never to Carnegie himself.

candidates.quote: To be popular is easy; to be right, when right is unpopular, is noble.
candidates.trueOrigin: Undated and unpinned. Wikiquote's 'Undated' section carries the fuller form — 'To be popular is easy; to be right when right is unpopular, is noble... I repudiate with scorn the immoral doctrine, "Our country, right or wrong"' — sourced only to a 2002 article in The Nation ('An Imperial Moment', 5 December 2002), with no contemporaneous Carnegie citation.
candidates.whyNotable: Carnegie's most-quoted anti-jingoism line survives only through a 2002 magazine retelling — no primary source has ever been produced.

candidates.quote: Watch the costs and the profits take care of themselves.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown. Wikiquote lists it in the 'Undated' section with no citation whatsoever — not a speech, not a book, not even a secondary source.
candidates.whyNotable: A cornerstone 'Carnegie management wisdom' line that Wikiquote carries with literally zero source attached.

candidates.quote: An aim in life is the only fortune worth finding.
candidates.trueOrigin: Robert Louis Stevenson. Wikiquote notes the line is cited to Stevenson inside Napoleon Hill's The Law of Success (1928): "An aim in life is the only fortune worth finding; and it is not to be found in foreign lands, but in the heart itself." The Jackie O credit traces to Helen Granat's Wisdom Through the Ages: Book Two (2003).
candidates.whyNotable: A Stevenson line that passed through Napoleon Hill's 1928 Law of Success and came out the other side attributed to Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis — Wikiquote documents the whole chain.

candidates.quote: Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, 'Managing for Business Effectiveness,' Harvard Business Review (1963).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted management aphorisms whose attribution is often doubted online; QI confirms Drucker articulated it in his 1963 HBR article.

candidates.quote: Strong people always have strong weaknesses too
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, The Effective Executive (1967).
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-shared leadership line; QI confirms Drucker wrote it in his 1967 book The Effective Executive.

candidates.quote: Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), p. 88.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely-sourced Drucker insight on success and change with a cited Wikiquote entry, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), p. 455.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared, genuinely-sourced Drucker line on organizations; strong verified anchor with a cited Wikiquote entry.

candidates.quote: There is only one valid definition of a business purpose: to create a customer
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, The Practice of Management (1954), p. 37.
candidates.whyNotable: A cornerstone Drucker management dictum with a sourced Wikiquote entry, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: There is surely nothing quite so useless as doing with great efficiency what should not be done at all
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, 'Managing for Business Effectiveness,' Harvard Business Review (1963).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely cited and sometimes questioned; QI confirms Drucker coined this exact wording in his 1963 HBR article, though earlier thematically similar remarks exist.

candidates.quote: Thirty years from now the big university campuses will be relics
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, interview published in Forbes (1997).
candidates.whyNotable: A famous and often-recirculated Drucker prediction; QI confirms he said it in a 1997 Forbes interview.

candidates.quote: Thirty years from now the big university campuses will be relics. Universities won't survive
candidates.trueOrigin: Drucker, in the Forbes interview 'Seeing things as they really are' by Robert Lenzner and Stephen S. Johnson, published March 10, 1997.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly recycled in every ed-tech disruption argument and often assumed apocryphal; QI verified the 1997 Forbes interview, and the thirty-year window closes in 2027.

candidates.quote: When a subject becomes totally obsolete we make it a required course
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, who used variant phrasings across 1969, 1976, and 1992 works.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular jab at academia; QI credits Drucker, who circulated the idea in multiple works from 1969 onward.

candidates.quote: Perhaps the most valuable result of all education is the ability to make yourself do the thing you have to do, when it ought to be done, whether you like it or not.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Henry Huxley
candidates.whyNotable: The single best definition of self-discipline in the PD canon, and it reframes discipline as the point of education rather than a precondition for it.

candidates.quote: A man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point where he does not discern any truth
candidates.trueOrigin: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground (1864), Part 1
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted passage from Notes from Underground, sourced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: It's life that matters, nothing but life — the process of discovering, the everlasting process
candidates.trueOrigin: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Idiot (1868-1869), Part 3
candidates.whyNotable: Genuine, often-shared line from The Idiot, sourced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: Love a man even in his sin, for that is the semblance of Divine Love
candidates.trueOrigin: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880), Book VI
candidates.whyNotable: Genuine line from The Brothers Karamazov (Father Zosima), sourced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what people fear most
candidates.trueOrigin: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment (1866), Part 1
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, frequently shared line from Crime and Punishment, sourced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: The mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive, but in finding something to live for
candidates.trueOrigin: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880)
candidates.whyNotable: One of his most-quoted lines; QI confirms it is genuinely from The Brothers Karamazov (Grand Inquisitor chapter), spoken by a character rather than Dostoevsky directly.

candidates.quote: The soul is healed by being with children
candidates.trueOrigin: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Idiot (1868-1869), spoken by Prince Myshkin
candidates.whyNotable: Often doubted as apocryphal, but QI confirms it is genuinely from The Idiot, spoken by Prince Myshkin (Russian: 'Через детей душа лечится').

candidates.quote: Effort only fully releases its reward after a person refuses to quit.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source located; Wikiquote holds it on the talk page as an unsourced quotation.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial motivational-poster line credited to Hill that Wikiquote removed from his page for lack of any citation.

candidates.quote: If you cannot do great things, do small things in a great way.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source located in any Hill work; Wikiquote holds it on the talk page as unsourced. The same line also circulates widely under Martin Luther King Jr.'s name.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-reproduced 'Napoleon Hill' lines on quote aggregators, yet Wikiquote could not source it to Hill and moved it off his page entirely.

candidates.quote: No man is ever whipped until he quits in his own mind.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source located; Wikiquote holds it on the talk page as an unsourced quotation.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as vintage Think and Grow Rich, but Wikiquote could not pin it to any page of any Hill book and moved it off his article.

candidates.quote: Patience, persistence and perspiration make an unbeatable combination for success.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source located; listed first among the unsourced quotations on Wikiquote's Napoleon Hill talk page.
candidates.whyNotable: The alliterative 'three Ps' line is one of the most-circulated Hill quotes and heads Wikiquote's list of Hill quotations removed for being unsourced.

candidates.quote: Strength and growth come only through continuous effort and struggle.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source located. Held on Wikiquote's talk page as an unsourced quotation. Note that Think and Grow Rich (p. 112) contains a thematically similar passage about the strongest oak of the forest, which may be the paraphrase's seed.
candidates.whyNotable: Extremely widely shared as a Hill line, but Wikiquote lists it among the unsourced quotations removed from his page — it reads like a compression of his oak-tree passage rather than his actual text.

candidates.quote: The ladder of success is never crowded at the top.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source located. Wikiquote removed it from the Napoleon Hill page to the talk page as an unsourced quotation; the sentiment also circulates under other motivational-speaker names.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of Hill quote-card roundups that Wikiquote has stripped from his page for having no locatable source in any Hill work.

candidates.quote: Whatever the mind of man can conceive and believe, it can achieve.
candidates.trueOrigin: Hill popularized the idea but did not write this sentence. QI shows a 1906 anonymous motto ("What man can conceive, man can achieve") in Orlando K. Fitzsimmons' Metamorphose; Hill's actual 1937 Think and Grow Rich wording was "anything the mind could conceive and believe" — no "achieve". The three-word popular formula was crystallized by Hill's own self-help organization circa 1952-1954.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared line on the internet credited to Napoleon Hill, yet the exact popular wording is a 1950s organizational rewrite of Hill's own looser 1937 sentence — and Wikiquote's own page cites it only as a bare 'p.32'.

candidates.quote: Don't look for big things, just do small things with great love. The smaller the thing, the greater must be our love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mother Teresa, in 'Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light' (2007).
candidates.whyNotable: The verified source of the ubiquitous 'do small things with great love' meme; Wikiquote cites it to 'Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light' (2007), letting the page correct the many mangled paraphrases.

candidates.quote: The biggest disease today is not leprosy or tuberculosis, but rather the feeling of being unwanted.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mother Teresa, quoted in Malcolm Muggeridge, 'Something Beautiful for God' (1971).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Mother Teresa line that anchors the hub; Wikiquote cites it to Malcolm Muggeridge's 'Something Beautiful for God' (1971).

candidates.quote: Patience, and shuffle the cards.
candidates.trueOrigin: Miguel de Cervantes
candidates.whyNotable: The wittiest entry — patience paired with the practical business of dealing again rather than waiting passively. Proverbial in both Spanish and English since the 17th century.

candidates.quote: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.
candidates.trueOrigin: Booker T. Washington
candidates.whyNotable: Releasing resentment framed as self-defence of the soul, written by a man born into slavery — enormous moral weight, and fully public domain unlike the 20th-century civil-rights lines it anticipates.

candidates.quote: I was born with an enormous need for affection, and a terrible need to give it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Hepburn, from a New York Times interview (April 22, 1991).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely quoted, genuinely sourced Hepburn line that serves as a real anchor amid the fakes.

candidates.quote: Living is like tearing through a museum. Not until later do you really start absorbing what you saw, thinking about it, looking it up in a book, and remembering — because you can't take it all in at once.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Hepburn, cited in "Audrey Hepburn: A Bio-bibliography" (1994) by David Hofstede.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Hepburn reflection documented in a Wikiquote-cited biography, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charlotte Brontë
candidates.whyNotable: The best short line in fiction on the cost of holding a grudge — 'registering wrongs' names the behaviour precisely, and it comes from a woman with every reason to keep score.

candidates.quote: An army marches on its stomach
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified source; earliest attributions post-date Napoleon by decades, also credited to Frederick the Great.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-pinned Napoleon lines; QI finds no contemporaneous source and shows the credit appeared decades after his death, also attributed to Frederick the Great.

candidates.quote: Imagination rules the world
candidates.trueOrigin: Ascribed to Napoleon by Las Cases from an 1816 conversation; possibly derived from Blaise Pascal.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently cited as Napoleon's; QI notes it rests on a secondhand 1816 conversation recorded by Las Cases and may echo Pascal.

candidates.quote: Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake
candidates.trueOrigin: No reliable primary source; QI finds only a loosely related paraphrase in an 1836 history.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared strategy quip; QI could find no solid Napoleon source and only a loosely similar remark in an 1836 history book.

candidates.quote: Our strategy in going after this army is very simple. First we are going to cut it off, and then we are going to kill it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Powell — spoken as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff at a Pentagon press briefing, 23 January 1991, announcing the Gulf War plan against Saddam Hussein's army.
candidates.whyNotable: The defining soundbite of the Gulf War and of Powell's military career, with an unusually clean primary source — a dated, on-the-record Pentagon briefing rather than a memoir recollection.

candidates.quote: The only land we ever asked for was enough land to bury our dead.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Powell, but the date is routinely wrong online: Wikiquote sources it to the State Department's MTV Global Discussion of 14 February 2002, while it is popularly retold as an ad-lib at Davos 2003 in reply to the Archbishop of Canterbury.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared patriotic line whose attribution is solid but whose venue and date are near-universally misreported — a clean 'right speaker, wrong occasion' page rather than a fake-quote page.

candidates.quote: There can be no doubt that Saddam Hussein has biological weapons and the capability to rapidly produce more, many more.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Powell — Remarks to the United Nations Security Council, 5 February 2003. Wikiquote pairs it with his September 2005 Barbara Walters interview in which he called the speech a 'blot' on his record that 'will always be a part of my record'.
candidates.whyNotable: The most consequential sentence Powell ever spoke and one he publicly repudiated on camera, which makes it a rare anchor where the verified attribution and the speaker's own retraction are both documented in the same Wikiquote entry.

candidates.quote: Success ultimately rests on small things, lots of small things.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Powell — his own memoir It Worked For Me: In Life and Leadership (2012), p. 18.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the few widely circulated Powell maxims that Wikiquote pins to Powell's own book with a page number, making it a reliable verified anchor against the Harari-sourced lines that dominate his quote pages.

candidates.quote: The healthiest competition occurs when average people win by putting in above-average effort.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Powell — his memoir My American Journey (1996).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared meritocracy line that Wikiquote pins to Powell's own autobiography, giving the hub a second primary-sourced anchor from Powell's own pen rather than a third-party leadership book.

candidates.quote: A man always has two reasons for doing anything: a good reason and the real reason.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown/anonymous. QI traces a French-flavored precursor to James Parton (1872) and a close match in a 1905 speech by Mrs. Walter B. Helm, who credited only 'some wise person.' The Morgan attribution first appears in Owen Wister's 1930 memoir, well after Morgan's 1913 death. Wikiquote's 'Reason' page carries the same Wister-sourced attribution.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared 'J. P. Morgan' line in business and negotiation writing; QI finds the Morgan credit only appears in 1930, seventeen years after his death, while a strong match circulated anonymously by 1905.

candidates.quote: Will you have sugar and cream in your nose?
candidates.creditedTo: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, as a child, to J. P. Morgan
candidates.trueOrigin: QI's earliest version is a 1928 telling by Mary Roberts Rinehart with no Morgan/Morrow names attached; the cast was assigned later. Dwight Morrow did not join the bank until after Morgan's 1913 death, and Anne Morrow Lindbergh denied the story in 1999, saying there was not a grain of truth in it. True origin unknown.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-retold J. P. Morgan anecdote — the child warned not to mention his famous nose — which QI shows probably never happened, and which Anne Morrow Lindbergh herself flatly denied.

candidates.quote: Grief is the price we pay for love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Elizabeth II
candidates.whyNotable: The modern canonical line on bereavement — eight words, endlessly quoted since, and inscribed at the Queen Elizabeth II September 11th Garden. No public-domain equal exists for this exact thought stated this plainly.

candidates.quote: Always look for the helpers. There's always someone who is trying to help.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fred Rogers, 'Mister Rogers Talks with Parents' (Berkley Books, 1983), p. 177
candidates.whyNotable: Rogers' single most-quoted line, recirculated after every disaster; genuinely his, sourced to 'Mister Rogers Talks with Parents' (1983) and 'You Are Special' (1995) on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: As human beings, our job in life is to help people realize how rare and valuable each one of us really is.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fred Rogers, 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood: Thoughts For All Ages'
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-shared, genuinely-Rogers line documented on Wikiquote (Mister Rogers' Neighborhood: Thoughts For All Ages) — a real anchor to sit alongside the debunks on a Rogers hub.

candidates.quote: You've made this day a special day, by just your being you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fred Rogers, U.S. Senate subcommittee testimony, May 1, 1969
candidates.whyNotable: Rogers' signature spoken sign-off, delivered in his famous May 1, 1969 U.S. Senate testimony; genuine and sourced on Wikiquote (song-lyric tail deliberately trimmed).

candidates.quote: It will fluctuate.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI's earliest documented telling is an October 1922 Wall Street Journal item crediting Henry Poor (d. 1905) with an anecdote about John D. Rockefeller; the story was later reassigned to J. P. Morgan, William Rockefeller, Jay Gould and Jesse Livermore. QI calls the supporting evidence 'problematic.' Wikiquote does list 'It will fluctuate' in its sourced Quotes section via Jean Strouse's Morgan: American Financier (1999), so the two authorities do not fully agree.
candidates.whyNotable: The classic Wall Street anecdote — Morgan asked what the stock market will do — but QI's earliest instance (1922 Wall Street Journal) tells it about John D. Rockefeller, with the tale only later reassigned to Morgan.

candidates.quote: Well, I don't know as I want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do. I hire him to tell how to do what I want to do.
candidates.trueOrigin: Reported secondhand by Ida Tarbell in The Life of Elbert H. Gary (1925); no contemporaneous record of Morgan saying it.
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted line in legal-profession commentary about Morgan; Wikiquote files it under 'Attributed' because it survives only secondhand in Ida Tarbell's biography of Elbert H. Gary.

candidates.quote: If you have to ask the price, you can't afford it.
candidates.trueOrigin: No contemporary source. Wikiquote's earliest citation for this exact wording is Business Education World (Gregg Publishing, 1961). Morgan biographer Jean Strouse considers the maxim implausible for him. Earlier and differently-worded yacht replies attributed to Morgan appear in the 1920s press.
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive rich-man's brush-off, universally pinned on Morgan and a yacht, yet Wikiquote can only file it under 'Attributed' with a 1961 print source — nearly fifty years after his death.

candidates.quote: Half of what I say is meaningless, but I say it so that the other half may reach you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kahlil Gibran, Sand and Foam (1926)
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, Wikiquote-sourced Gibran aphorism from Sand and Foam — a real anchor line to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kahlil Gibran
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive statement that grief enlarges rather than diminishes capacity — the line people reach for when comforting someone who fears the loss has hollowed them out.

candidates.quote: Work is love made visible.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kahlil Gibran, The Prophet (1923), 'On Work'
candidates.whyNotable: One of Gibran's most-quoted genuine lines, from 'On Work' in The Prophet — a strong verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: Your pain is the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kahlil Gibran, The Prophet (1923), 'On Pain'
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely-quoted line from The Prophet that Wikiquote sources directly — a verified anchor in the public domain.

candidates.quote: Elegance is refusal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; popularized by Diana Vreeland in her 1980 book 'Allure,' though Vreeland explicitly said she did not know who originated it.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous fashion-caption line pinned on Chanel; QI found no evidence she ever said it and traces its popularity to Diana Vreeland, who herself disclaimed authorship, leaving the true origin anonymous.

candidates.quote: Nature gives you the face you have at twenty; it is up to you to merit the face you have at fifty.
candidates.trueOrigin: An older proverb about deserving one's face; earliest anchor an 1891 anecdote crediting Edwin M. Stanton ('A man of fifty is responsible for his face'). A three-part version was credited to Chanel in September 1938 Paris Vogue.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared 'wisdom' quote; QI shows the responsible-for-your-face idea circulated since at least the 1880s (traced to Edwin M. Stanton) and was credited to George Orwell, Mae West, and others, making Chanel a late adopter rather than the originator.

candidates.quote: Our homes are our prisons; let us find freedom in their decoration.
candidates.trueOrigin: From the 1938 Chanel-credited Vogue maxims; possibly derived from or co-written by Pierre Reverdy.
candidates.whyNotable: A design-blog favorite attributed to Chanel; QI ties it to the same 1938 Vogue maxims collection that poet Pierre Reverdy may have authored, so Chanel's sole authorship is unconfirmed.

candidates.quote: The only beautiful eyes are those that look at us tenderly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Published under Chanel's name in Paris Vogue, September 1938, but the maxims may have been ghost-composed by poet Pierre Reverdy.
candidates.whyNotable: A romantic line shared as pure Chanel; QI confirms it appeared in Chanel's September 1938 Vogue maxims but notes a biography suggests poet Pierre Reverdy may have actually composed the maxims, clouding authorship.

candidates.quote: Some people believe football is a matter of life and death. I can assure you it is much, much more important than that.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Shankly, on a Granada TV chat show hosted by Shelley Rohde, 20 May 1981
candidates.whyNotable: Shankly's most-quoted line, delivered tongue-in-cheek; his biographer stresses it was never meant literally.

candidates.quote: A football team is like a piano. You need eight men to carry it and three who can play the damn thing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Shankly, quoted by John Toshack via Kevin McCarra, 'How Benitez built Liverpool,' The Guardian (21 Jan 2006).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-quoted Shankly aphorism on team roles, sourced at Wikiquote to a Guardian recollection by John Toshack.

candidates.quote: We don't see things as they are; we see them as we are.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI labels it anonymous. Close matches appear in an 1801 Sydney Smith sermon and an 1831 newspaper article. Also credited to Anais Nin, the Babylonian Talmud, Immanuel Kant, G. T. W. Patrick and H. M. Tomlinson; the Talmud ascription 'does not have strong support.' Covey's own 7 Habits wording is 'We see the world, not as it is, but as we are.'
candidates.whyNotable: A four-way attribution scramble (Nin, the Talmud, Kant, Covey) that QI resolves to anonymous with an 1801 antecedent — ideal fact-check material.

candidates.quote: We judge ourselves by our intentions and others by their behavior.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI traces the family of sayings to Reverend William Nevins, in an 1836 posthumous compilation: 'We should judge ourselves by our motives, but others by their actions.' Popularized in the 1930 form by U.S. diplomat Dwight Morrow. Covey used an unattributed variant in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective Families (1997): 'We then judge ourselves by our motives — and others by their behavior.'
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as a Covey original in management and therapy writing; QI shows the thought is 160 years older, from an 1836 Nevins compilation.

candidates.quote: Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not in Frankl's writings. QI credits the underlying idea to psychologist Rollo May, 'Freedom and Responsibility Re-Examined' (1963), which discussed 'the capacity to pause between stimulus and response.' Covey said he read the passage in an unnamed book on a 1969 Hawaii sabbatical and disclaimed authorship; his 7 Habits (1989) discussion of Frankl caused the Frankl misattribution.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the single most-circulated fake Frankl quote, and Covey is the documented vector — he popularized it, disclaimed writing it, and could never name the book he read it in.
candidates.notes: most often pinned on Viktor Frankl

candidates.quote: You may climb the ladder of success only to find it is leaning against the wrong wall.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI tentatively credits Allen Raine (pseudonym of Welsh novelist Anne Adaliza Evans) via an 1915 Brooklyn Daily Eagle citation. Also wrongly credited to Thomas Merton and H. Jackson Brown; QI found no evidence for Merton. Covey used it in 1986 lectures and in 7 Habits (1989).
candidates.whyNotable: A management-cliche staple credited to Covey (and to Merton) that QI traces back to a 1915 newspaper citation of Allen Raine, decades before Covey was born.

candidates.quote: Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things.
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker (efficiency/effectiveness form, 1963 Harvard Business Review and 1974 Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices) and Warren Bennis (the management/leadership variant). Covey quoted it in 7 Habits (1989) crediting 'both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis'; the credit then collapsed onto Covey. An 1869 Harrisburg Telegraph item has the underlying idea.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of leadership slide decks credited to Covey; Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed and QI traces the two halves to Drucker and Bennis.

candidates.quote: Genius is really only the power of making continuous efforts.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous essay published in Mining and Scientific Press, June 1895, partly derived from Robert Burns Wilson's 1887 essay "And So—I Gave Up Trying!". The Elbert Hubbard credit began in 1911 when Alice Hubbard reprinted the anonymous essay in a chapter devoted to her husband.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple motivational line credited variously to Elbert Hubbard, Kin Hubbard and Dale Carnegie; QI traces it to an anonymous 1895 essay and pinpoints the exact 1911 reprint that created the false Hubbard credit.

candidates.quote: I can't write a book commensurate with Shakespeare, but I can write a book by me.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walter Alexander Raleigh (1861–1922), Oxford professor of English, in a 1907 letter to Thomas Herbert Warren, published posthumously by Lady Raleigh in 1926 — not Sir Walter Raleigh the Elizabethan explorer, who died in 1618. Carnegie quoted it in How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) and was careful to note it was not the coat-in-the-mud Raleigh; later compilations dropped that distinction.
candidates.whyNotable: A textbook two-people-one-name mixup: the writing-advice line is constantly credited to the Elizabethan explorer, and QI shows Carnegie got it right in 1948 while the compilations that copied him got it wrong.

candidates.quote: Just for today, I will try to live through this day only, and not tackle all my problems at once.
candidates.trueOrigin: Dr. Frank Crane, whose column "DR CRANE SAYS" in the Boston Globe of 29 May 1921 carried the ten "Just for Today" resolutions with a copyright notice claiming authorship. Carnegie reprinted the program in How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948), saying he had given away hundreds of copies, but credited Sybil F. Partridge — apparently confusing it with an unrelated 1880 devotional piece of the same name.
candidates.whyNotable: The opening line of the "Just for Today" program that spread through self-help and recovery culture; QI shows Carnegie's 1948 book attached the wrong author's name to Frank Crane's 1921 column.

candidates.quote: When life gives you lemons, make lemonade.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous, circulating by May 1907 ("And if you get a lemon, why / Just make the lemonade"). Elbert Hubbard wrote his own variant in The Philistine in July 1908. Carnegie printed it in How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) as "When you have a lemon, make a lemonade" but explicitly credited businessman Julius Rosenwald, disclaiming authorship.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-repeated proverbs in English, routinely credited to Carnegie or Elbert Hubbard; QI shows it was anonymous by 1907 and that Carnegie openly disclaimed it.

candidates.quote: Fear defeats more people than any other one thing in the world.
candidates.trueOrigin: Originator unknown. Earliest documented instance is a 1936 Los Angeles Times advertisement crediting Elbert Hubbard, who died in 1915 with no supporting citation in his lifetime.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where Carnegie himself credited three different people for the same line — Napoleon in 1937, Elbert Hubbard in 1941, Emerson in his 1962 revision — never once with a source, and his books drove its spread.

candidates.quote: Once you replace negative thoughts with positive ones, you'll start having positive results.
candidates.trueOrigin: Willie Nelson, who used it as an epigraph in his 2006 book The Tao of Willie: A Guide to the Happiness in Your Heart. The theme runs through earlier self-help writing — Carnegie's How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948), Norman Vincent Peale, James K. Van Fleet, John C. Maxwell — but none of them wrote this formulation.
candidates.whyNotable: A social-media staple shuffled between Willie Nelson, Dale Carnegie and Norman Vincent Peale; QI credits the specific wording to Nelson's 2006 book.

candidates.quote: Be so good they can't ignore you
candidates.whyNotable: Real Steve Martin advice, but the compressed meme wording is a paraphrase.

candidates.quote: If you let money pile up, it starts to stink. But if you spread it around then it can do a lot of good.
candidates.trueOrigin: Quote Investigator traces the money/muck simile to Francis Bacon's 1625 essays ("Money is like Muck, not good except it be spread") and to an extended version Bacon credited to "Mr. Bettenham" in his 1625 Apophthegmes; Thornton Wilder's 1956 play The Matchmaker and Clint Murchison Jr. (1961) carried the modern manure phrasing. Branson himself credited Wilder.
candidates.whyNotable: The single best-documented Branson attribution problem — he is widely quoted as the author of the money-is-manure line, but QI dates the core simile to 1625, three and a half centuries before him.

candidates.quote: Software is eating the world
candidates.whyNotable: Genuine (2011 WSJ) — an 'actually real, here's the source' tech entry.

candidates.quote: I think there is a world market for maybe five computers
candidates.whyNotable: Attributed to IBM's Watson (1943); no evidence he ever said it.

candidates.quote: Half the money I spend on advertising is wasted; the trouble is I don't know which half.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Wanamaker is QI's leading candidate — first credited to him in a 1919 speech by Rev. Roy L. Smith — but QI found no direct written or spoken instance from Wanamaker, so the ascription stays uncertain. Ogilvy quoted it in Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963) and explicitly disclaimed credit, crediting Wanamaker and the first Lord Leverhulme.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line in advertising, routinely pinned on Ogilvy in marketing decks and LinkedIn posts even though he named someone else as the source.

candidates.quote: No one ever went broke underestimating the intelligence of the American public.
candidates.trueOrigin: H. L. Mencken, in a syndicated column dated September 18, 1926: 'No one in this world, so far as I know, has ever lost money by underestimating the intelligence of the great masses of the plain people.' The short modern wording is a decades-long compression. Ogilvy reproduced the line in Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963), credited it to Mencken, and argued strongly against it — yet the credit still migrates to him, and also to P. T. Barnum and Louis B. Mayer.
candidates.whyNotable: Ogilvy is one of three names QI lists as receiving this credit without evidence; he actually quoted Mencken in order to disagree with him, an inversion that makes for a strong fact-check page.

candidates.quote: When I let go of what I am, I become what I might be.
candidates.trueOrigin: Modern interpretive paraphrase of the Tao Te Ching; not a faithful translation of Laozi
