candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular 'letting go' line quoted as pure Lao Tzu; it derives from modern interpretive translations of the Tao Te Ching rather than a literal rendering of the original text.

candidates.quote: If you think you are too small to make a difference, try sleeping with a mosquito.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest documented use attributed to Anita Roddick (Time, Jan 1993); no genuine Dalai Lama source, often relabeled an African proverb.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitously captioned as a Dalai Lama or 'African proverb' line, but Wikiquote's earliest trace is a 1993 Time magazine attribution to Anita Roddick, with Dalai Lama credits only appearing from 2004.

candidates.quote: Everything that can be invented has been invented
candidates.whyNotable: Attributed to the 1899 US Patent Commissioner; a documented fabrication — he never said it.

candidates.quote: Sometimes I sit and think, and sometimes I just sit.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous Maine fisherman, in newspapers by February 1905 (via the Boston Record); popularized by William Gunning King's 1906 Punch cartoon. Predates Pooh entirely.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently pinned on Pooh (and on Satchel Paige); QI traces it to an anonymous Maine fisherman quip circulating by 1905, popularized by a 1906 Punch cartoon.

candidates.quote: A man who is his own lawyer has a fool for a client.
candidates.trueOrigin: A legal proverb predating Lincoln by centuries; QI finds versions in print long before his birth, with no evidence he coined it.
candidates.whyNotable: Routinely pinned on lawyer-Lincoln; QI shows the maxim is an old proverb he did not originate.

candidates.quote: Better to remain silent and be thought a fool than to speak and remove all doubt.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence from Lincoln or Twain; QI's earliest match is Maurice Switzer's 1907 book, echoing Proverbs 17:28. First tied to Lincoln in Golden Book magazine (Nov 1931).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the internet's most misattributed maxims, credited to both Lincoln and Twain; QI traces it to a 1907 humor book and the Book of Proverbs.

candidates.quote: Whatever you are, be a good one.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to novelist William Makepeace Thackeray, who reportedly said 'Whatever you are, try to be a good one' (recorded in Laurence Hutton's 1897 memoir); the Lincoln attribution surfaced only decades after his death.
candidates.whyNotable: An enormously popular motivational line on posters and mugs; documented as Thackeray's, not Lincoln's.

candidates.quote: You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich. You cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Rev. William J. H. Boetcker, from his 1916 pamphlet later known as 'The Ten Cannots'; a 1942 leaflet ('Lincoln on Limitations') printed genuine Lincoln lines alongside Boetcker's with the attributions swapped.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Lincoln quotes; the pro-capitalism 'Ten Cannots' were repeated as Lincoln's by Reagan (1992 RNC) and George H.W. Bush before fact-checkers traced them to Boetcker.

candidates.quote: There is only one way to avoid criticism: do nothing, say nothing, and be nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Elbert Hubbard, Little Journeys to the Homes of American Statesmen (1898), p. 370
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared motivational line credited to Aristotle; both Wikiquote and Quote Investigator trace the earliest strong match to Elbert Hubbard (1898), not Aristotle.

candidates.quote: Those who can, do; those who cannot, teach.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Bernard Shaw, Man and Superman (1903)
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently mis-pinned on Aristotle; Wikiquote credits George Bernard Shaw's Man and Superman (1903): 'He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches.'

candidates.quote: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.
candidates.trueOrigin: Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), Ch. II, paraphrasing Nicomachean Ethics Book II.4 / Book I.7
candidates.whyNotable: One of the single most-shared 'Aristotle' quotes on the internet; Wikiquote traces the exact wording to Will Durant's 1926 The Story of Philosophy, where Durant was summarizing Aristotle rather than quoting him.

candidates.quote: He who knows not, and knows not he knows not, is a fool; shun him. He who knows not, and knows he knows not, is simple; teach him. He who knows, and knows not he knows, is asleep; awaken him. He who knows, and knows he knows, is wise; follow him.
candidates.trueOrigin: 19th-century proverb (documented 1866-1889); a precursor appears in Margaret of Valois, 1654
candidates.whyNotable: A four-part 'levels of knowledge' maxim widely reattributed to Bruce Lee by around 2017; QI found no connection to Lee and traces it to a 19th-century proverb (a three-part 'Oriental maxim' by 1866, the full four-part 'Arabic proverb' in Toronto's The Globe by 1885, and Spurgeon's 1889 Salt-Cellars).

candidates.quote: Called or uncalled, God will be present.
candidates.trueOrigin: Latin 'Vocatus atque non vocatus, Deus aderit' — Jung took it from Erasmus, who traced it to an ancient Spartan/Greek proverb. Jung only popularized it (carved over his door and on his tomb); he did not author it.
candidates.whyNotable: Jung's famous motto is routinely credited to Jung himself, but Wikiquote documents that he borrowed it from Erasmus, who attributed it to an ancient proverb.

candidates.quote: The great tragedy of Science — the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Henry Huxley, in an 1870 address to the British Association in Liverpool, published in Nature.
candidates.whyNotable: Popular scientific aphorism sometimes credited to Darwin (an 1901 newspaper gave him a variant); QI confirms it belongs to his ally Thomas Henry Huxley.

candidates.quote: Better a diamond with a flaw than a pebble without
candidates.trueOrigin: Ming Dynasty scholar Jiao Hong (1540-1620)
candidates.whyNotable: Popular 'wisdom' line credited to Confucius that Wikiquote reassigns to Ming scholar Jiao Hong.

candidates.quote: I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest partial match traced to Xunzi; no evidence Confucius (or Benjamin Franklin) said it
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous 'active learning' maxim pinned on Confucius; QI and Wikiquote trace the earliest partial match to Xunzi.

candidates.quote: Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall
candidates.trueOrigin: Oliver Goldsmith (18th-century), whose fictional 'Chinese' letters led readers to think it was Confucian
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular resilience quote credited to Confucius; QI concludes Oliver Goldsmith crafted it.

candidates.quote: The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step
candidates.trueOrigin: Laozi, Tao Te Ching, Chapter 64
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'Confucius' lines online, but Wikiquote reassigns it to Laozi's Tao Te Ching.

candidates.quote: Sometimes you will never know the value of a moment until it becomes a memory.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed by Wikiquote to Georges Duhamel, 'The Heart's Domain' (1919); no basis in Seuss's work.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely reposted sentimental 'Seuss' line that Wikiquote reassigns to Georges Duhamel's 1919 book.

candidates.quote: Applause is the spur of noble minds, the end and aim of weak ones.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Caleb Colton, Lacon (1820), vol. 1, no. 324. Wikiquote: not found in Burke's writings.
candidates.whyNotable: A much-quoted aphorism on fame and vanity that Wikiquote says is almost certainly Colton's, not Burke's.

candidates.quote: Beauty is the promise of happiness.
candidates.trueOrigin: Stendhal, De L'Amour (1822), ch. 17: "La beauté n'est que la promesse du bonheur" ("Beauty is no more than the promise of happiness").
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Burke because he wrote the era's famous treatise on beauty (A Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful, 1757) — Wikiquote reassigns it to Stendhal.

candidates.quote: If it is not necessary to change, it is necessary not to change.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lucius Cary, 2nd Viscount Falkland, speech in the House of Commons, 22 November 1641. Wikiquote notes the line has also been pinned on Disraeli, William Gerard Hamilton, George Bernard Shaw and John F. Kennedy (who quoted it).
candidates.whyNotable: A conservatism-defining maxim credited to Burke on countless slides and op-eds; Wikiquote traces it to Falkland in 1641, over a century before Burke was born.

candidates.quote: If you can be well without health, you may be happy without virtue.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Fuller, Gnomologia: Adages and Proverbs (1732) — an existing proverb collection published when Burke was three years old; Wikiquote finds it nowhere in Burke's writings.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates as Burke on virtue-and-wellbeing lists; Wikiquote pins its first known appearance to Fuller's 1732 proverb collection.

candidates.quote: Sin has many tools, but a lie is the handle which fits them all.
candidates.trueOrigin: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858).
candidates.whyNotable: A heavily shared line about lying that Wikiquote flags as not Burke at all but Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., writing 61 years after Burke's death.

candidates.quote: Society can overlook murder, adultery or swindling — it never forgives the preaching of a new gospel.
candidates.trueOrigin: Frederic Harrison, essay "Ruskin as Prophet", in Tennyson, Ruskin, Mill, and Other Literary Estimates (1899).
candidates.whyNotable: A favourite epigraph for essays on heresy and dissent, credited to Burke but written by Frederic Harrison a century after Burke died.

candidates.quote: The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: No known Burke source. Wikiquote's nearest real Burke line is "When bad men combine, the good must associate..." (Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents, 1770). QI's earliest close match is Rev. Charles F. Aked, San Jose Mercury Herald, 31 Oct 1916 ("for evil men to accomplish their purpose it is only necessary that good men should do nothing"); the earliest credit to Burke is Sir R. Murray Hyslop, Fourth International Congregational Council, 5 July 1920. Wikiquote also flags John Stuart Mill's St Andrews address (1 Feb 1867): "Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing."
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line attributed to Burke and one of the most-shared fake quotes on the internet — Wikiquote catalogues 70+ circulating variants precisely because there is no original.

candidates.quote: Those who don't know history are doomed to repeat it.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Santayana, The Life of Reason (1905): "Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it." QI found no closely matching statement anywhere in Burke; the nearest genuine Burke line is "People will not look forward to posterity, who never look backward to their ancestors" (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790).
candidates.whyNotable: The best-known history aphorism in English, routinely split between Santayana, Churchill and Burke — QI documents newspaper columnists crediting Burke by name in 2010 and 2011 and calls the attribution unsubstantiated.

candidates.quote: Those who dance appear insane to those who cannot hear the music.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Nietzsche source located; a similar image appears in Germaine de Stael's 'On Germany' (1813) and it circulated as an 'old proverb' by the 1920s.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Nietzsche lines; QI and Wikiquote find no Nietzsche source — the sentiment predates him as a 19th-century proverb.

candidates.quote: The darker the night, the brighter the stars, the deeper the grief, the closer is God!
candidates.trueOrigin: Apollon Maykov, untitled poem (1878)
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as a line from Crime and Punishment, but Wikiquote traces it to Apollon Maykov's 1878 untitled poem, not Dostoevsky at all.

candidates.quote: Trust no one in whom the desire to punish is strong
candidates.trueOrigin: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-1885)
candidates.whyNotable: Passed around as Dostoevsky (and sometimes Goethe), but Wikiquote confirms the source is Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra: 'Distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful.'

candidates.quote: The more I practice, the luckier I get.
candidates.trueOrigin: The luck-and-hard-work family traces to Coleman Cox, 'Listen to This' (1922); golfer Gary Player popularized the golf phrasing
candidates.whyNotable: Golf's most-circulated 'luck' line predates every golfer it's credited to, going back to Coleman Cox in 1922.

candidates.quote: I do not believe in a fate that falls on men however they act; but I do believe in a fate that falls on them unless they act.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actually written by G. K. Chesterton in 'On Holland,' Illustrated London News (29 April 1922).
candidates.whyNotable: A 'fate' quote pinned on Buddha; Wikiquote reassigns it to G. K. Chesterton (1922).

candidates.quote: To understand everything is to forgive everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: Generally reported as a French proverb ('tout comprendre c'est tout pardonner'); attached to Buddha without sources as early as Farm Journal Vol. 34 (1910).
candidates.whyNotable: Common 'Buddha' aphorism on forgiveness; Wikiquote shows it is really a French proverb attached to Buddha with no source.

candidates.quote: Success does not consist in never making blunders, but in never making the same one a second time.
candidates.trueOrigin: Josh Billings (Henry Wheeler Shaw), c. 1874
candidates.whyNotable: A common motivational-poster 'Shaw' line that Wikiquote reassigns to humorist Josh Billings (H. W. Shaw), a name-collision misattribution.

candidates.quote: A free people ought not only to be armed and disciplined, but they should have sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence from any who might attempt to abuse them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Corruption of Washington's authentic First Annual Address (8 January 1790); the 'sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence' continuation is a modern fabrication.
candidates.whyNotable: A doctored gun-rights favorite: Washington's genuine 1790 line ('A free people ought not only to be armed, but disciplined...') was corrupted with a fabricated tail about arms and ammunition, which Quote Investigator debunked.

candidates.quote: Associate yourself with men of good quality if you esteem your own reputation, for it is better to be alone than in bad company.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rule 56 of 'Rules of Civility & Decent Behaviour in Company and Conversation,' maxims composed by French Jesuits in the 1590s and copied by young Washington c. 1744 as a penmanship exercise.
candidates.whyNotable: Passed around as original Washington counsel, but it is Rule 56 of the 'Rules of Civility' he copied as a schoolboy from a 16th-century French Jesuit courtesy manual.

candidates.quote: Firearms stand next in importance to the Constitution itself. They are the American people's liberty teeth and keystone under independence.
candidates.trueOrigin: C. S. Wheatley, 'Older Ideas of Firearms,' Hunter-Trader-Trapper magazine, September 1926; misattributed to Washington and spread through 1970s-80s newspapers.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-circulated fake gun-rights quotes; Quote Investigator and Wikiquote both trace it to a 1926 opinion piece by C. S. Wheatley, not to any Washington address.

candidates.quote: Government is like fire, a dangerous servant and a fearful master.
candidates.trueOrigin: Metaphor traced by Quote Investigator to John Tillotson's 1682 sermon 'The Danger of Zeal Without Knowledge'; the Washington ascription (from 1902) is unsupported.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as Washington wisdom, but Quote Investigator found no 18th/19th-century link to him and traced the 'servant/master' fire metaphor to a 1682 sermon by Archbishop John Tillotson.

candidates.quote: The government of the United States is not, in any sense, founded on the Christian religion.
candidates.trueOrigin: Article 11 of the Treaty of Tripoli (1796-97), written by U.S. Consul Joel Barlow; signed into force under John Adams, not authored by Washington.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently cited in church-and-state debates as Washington's words, but it is Article 11 of the Treaty of Tripoli, drafted by Joel Barlow and ratified under President John Adams in 1797.

candidates.quote: The marvel of all history is the patience with which men and women submit to burdens unnecessarily laid upon them by their governments.
candidates.trueOrigin: U.S. Senator William Edgar Borah, quoted in The Reader's Digest, Vol. 8, Issue 2, 1929, p. 776 — not Washington.
candidates.whyNotable: Shared as founding-father wisdom about tyranny, but Wikiquote documents it was written by U.S. Senator William E. Borah and published in Reader's Digest in 1929.

candidates.quote: None are so old as those who have outlived enthusiasm.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; first tied to Thoreau in Kate Sanborn's A Year of Sunshine (1886) with no citation to his writings
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently quoted as Thoreau but never found in his works; Wikiquote's earliest Thoreau attributions are late-19th-century quotation anthologies (1886, 1894).

candidates.quote: Truths and roses have thorns about them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pre-existing proverb; printed in Joseph Dennie's The Port Folio (1809) and a 1811 Spanish textbook before Thoreau recorded it
candidates.whyNotable: Though Thoreau copied it into his 1838 journal, Wikiquote shows it was a proverb already in print before his birth (The Port Folio, 1809), so he did not originate it.

candidates.quote: My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me.
candidates.trueOrigin: Harris Weinstock (May 1914), per Wikiquote; misattributed to Ford by 1948.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared friendship quote pinned on Ford; Wikiquote documents it actually originated with Harris Weinstock in 1914 and was misattributed to Ford by 1948.

candidates.quote: If a man does not know to what port he is sailing, no wind is favorable.
candidates.trueOrigin: Seneca the Younger (Epistulae Morales), not Socrates. JFK quoted it in a 1960 Raleigh, NC speech crediting Socrates; Wikiquote and QI note the true source is Seneca.
candidates.whyNotable: JFK cited this to Socrates, but it derives from Seneca the Younger — a documented misattribution noted on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: And God said, Love your enemy, and I obeyed Him and loved myself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Garbled paraphrase of Gibran's actual Sand and Foam (1926) line: 'My enemy said to me, "Love your enemy." And I obeyed him and loved myself.'
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-circulated reworded version that swaps Gibran's own words and misattributes the paraphrase; Wikiquote flags it as a corruption of the genuine Sand and Foam aphorism.

candidates.quote: Out of suffering have emerged the strongest souls; the most massive characters are seared with scars.
candidates.trueOrigin: Edwin Hubbell Chapin, as quoted in Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895)
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely-shared 'resilience' line pinned on Gibran across BrainyQuote/PassItOn; Wikiquote traces it to 19th-century American preacher Edwin Hubbell Chapin, not Gibran.

candidates.quote: Many people think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices
candidates.trueOrigin: Bishop William Fitzjames Oldham; earliest documented 1906 in Zion's Herald (also later credited to Edward R. Murrow and William James)
candidates.whyNotable: A widely circulated aphorism pinned on Rockne (who quoted it in a 1926 newspaper column, in quotation marks, without claiming it); QI reassigns the origin to Methodist bishop William Fitzjames Oldham, documented in 1906.

candidates.quote: Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie (1880s); the underlying idea is proverbial, but the famous fishing formulation is hers, not Lao Tzu's
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'ancient wisdom' proverbs pinned on Lao Tzu (also Confucius, Maimonides, Mao); QI traces the striking modern formulation to Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie in the 1880s, not any Chinese sage.

candidates.quote: What I hear, I forget. What I say, I remember. What I do, I understand.
candidates.trueOrigin: Xun Zi (荀子), 3rd century BCE; not Lao Tzu
candidates.whyNotable: A staple education/learning-pyramid quote pinned on Lao Tzu (and Confucius); Wikiquote traces the actual saying to the Chinese philosopher Xun Zi.

candidates.quote: I have from an early age abjured the use of meat, and the time will come when men such as I will look upon the murder of animals as they now look upon the murder of men.
candidates.trueOrigin: Novelist Dmitri Merezhkovsky, 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci' (1901) — a fictional line, not Leonardo's words.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple vegetarian/animal-rights quote; Wikiquote shows it was fabricated from Dmitri Merezhkovsky's 1901 novel 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci' and appears nowhere in Leonardo's own writings, though he was genuinely vegetarian.

candidates.quote: First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win.
candidates.trueOrigin: Nicholas Klein, 1918 Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America convention address ('First they ignore you. Then they ridicule you. And then they attack you and want to burn you. And then they build monuments to you.')
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Gandhi lines; there is no record of Gandhi saying it and QI/Wikiquote trace the closest variant to a 1918 US trade-union address by Nicholas Klein.

candidates.quote: God has no religion.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pre-dates Gandhi; appears in Henry Whitney Bellows, Re-statements of Christian Doctrine (1867). Gandhi attribution dates from the 1980s.
candidates.whyNotable: A tidy interfaith aphorism credited to Gandhi, but Wikiquote documents it predating him — e.g. in Henry Whitney Bellows's sermons (1867) — with the Gandhi attribution only appearing in the 1980s.

candidates.quote: If you're going to be a bear, be a grizzly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest instance is George Hyde Preston's short story 'An Inside Tip,' Cosmopolitan Magazine, June 1908 (used in a stock-market context); no Gandhi connection.
candidates.whyNotable: An implausibly aggressive line to pin on a pacifist; QI found no evidence Gandhi said it and traces the phrase to a 1908 Cosmopolitan short story.

candidates.quote: When you arise in the morning, think of what a precious privilege it is to be alive - to breathe, to think, to enjoy, to love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Elbert Hubbard, published in his magazine The Fra (vol. 12, issue 6), not by Marcus Aurelius.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial 'morning motivation' quote credited to Marcus Aurelius that Wikiquote reassigns to New Thought writer Elbert Hubbard, who published it in his magazine The Fra.

candidates.quote: I would have written a shorter letter, but I did not have the time.
candidates.trueOrigin: Blaise Pascal, Lettres provinciales (1657): 'I have made this longer than usual because I have not had time to make it shorter.'
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Twain, but the line predates him — it's from Blaise Pascal's Lettres provinciales (1657).

candidates.quote: Everything that is done in the world is done by hope.
candidates.trueOrigin: Martin Luther, leader of the Protestant Reformation (16th century).
candidates.whyNotable: A classic namesake mix-up: Wikiquote attributes it to Martin Luther, the 16th-century Protestant Reformer, not Martin Luther King Jr.

candidates.quote: Hate destroys the hater.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous proverb documented from at least 1897 (Henry Norman, A. P. Buchman); King used a fuller variant in 1957.
candidates.whyNotable: Popularly attributed to King, but QI shows the proverb circulated by the 1890s; King's actual line was 'hate destroys the hater as well as the hated' in his 1957 'Loving Your Enemies' sermon.

candidates.quote: Justice runs down like water, and righteousness like a mighty stream.
candidates.trueOrigin: Book of Amos 5:24 (Hebrew Bible); King quoted it in speeches.
candidates.whyNotable: Made famous by King's 'I Have a Dream' delivery, but the words are scripture — Amos 5:24 — which Wikiquote lists as the true source.

candidates.quote: The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.
candidates.trueOrigin: Theodore Parker, 'Ten Sermons of Religion' (1853); King popularized a condensed form starting 1958.
candidates.whyNotable: Iconic line universally pinned on King, but QI shows it was coined by abolitionist minister Theodore Parker in 1853; King quoted it (in quotation marks) rather than authoring it.

candidates.quote: It isn't the mountains ahead to climb that wear you out; it's the pebble in your shoe.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; earliest instance is a 1916 trade publication with no attribution. Ali and Jerry Falwell attributions are recent and historically unsupported.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as Ali wisdom; QI documents the saying appearing anonymously as far back as 1916, long before any Ali attribution.

candidates.quote: An army of sheep led by a lion is better than an army of lions led by a sheep
candidates.trueOrigin: Ancient proverb, traced by QI to Plutarch and figures such as Chabrias and Alexander the Great.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral leadership meme credited to Napoleon; QI traces the adage to Plutarch and ancient Greek figures (Chabrias, Alexander), not Napoleon.

candidates.quote: England is a nation of shopkeepers
candidates.trueOrigin: Phrase appears in Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776), predating Napoleon.
candidates.whyNotable: Popularly cast as Napoleon's dig at Britain; the phrase predates him in Adam Smith's 1776 Wealth of Nations.

candidates.quote: Give them a whiff of grapeshot
candidates.trueOrigin: Phrase coined by Thomas Carlyle in The French Revolution (1837).
candidates.whyNotable: Tied to Napoleon's crushing of the 1795 Paris uprising; Wikiquote shows the phrasing originates with Thomas Carlyle's 1837 The French Revolution.

candidates.quote: The more sand has escaped from the hourglass of our life, the clearer we should see through it
candidates.trueOrigin: Johann Paul Friedrich Richter (pen name Jean Paul), in his 1795 novel Hesperus oder 45 Hundsposttage; in English by 1837 in The New-York Mirror. QI hypothesizes the pen name "Jean Paul" also drove a parallel misattribution to Jean-Paul Sartre.
candidates.whyNotable: QI traced this widely shared aphorism to a German Romantic novelist; the Machiavelli credit is a bare graft with no textual basis.

candidates.quote: I like work: it fascinates me. I can sit and look at it for hours.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jerome K. Jerome, Three Men in a Boat (1889).
candidates.whyNotable: Popular 'lazy' aphorism routinely pinned on Wilde; Wikiquote reassigns it to Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men in a Boat.

candidates.quote: I'm not young enough to know everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: J. M. Barrie, The Admirable Crichton (1903).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to Wilde, but both Wikiquote and Quote Investigator assign it to J. M. Barrie's play The Admirable Crichton.

candidates.quote: I am always doing that which I can not do, in order that I may learn how to do it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Vincent van Gogh, in a letter to Anthon van Rappard dated August 18, 1885.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Picasso but Wikiquote reassigns it to Vincent van Gogh's 1885 letter, making it a clean documented misattribution.

candidates.quote: The urge to destroy is also a creative urge.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mikhail Bakunin, in 'Reaction in Germany' (1842); the Picasso credit spread after a 2018 Banksy Instagram post.
candidates.whyNotable: Recently viral as a Picasso line via Banksy, but Wikiquote documents it as Mikhail Bakunin's 1842 phrase, not Picasso's.

candidates.quote: Even a stopped clock is right twice a day.
candidates.trueOrigin: An old English-language proverb; Coelho merely used a version in Brida (1990)
candidates.whyNotable: Sometimes cited as a Coelho line because a character says it in his 1990 novel Brida, but QI documents it as a long-standing proverb far predating Coelho.

candidates.quote: There is always a well-known solution to every human problem—neat, plausible, and wrong
candidates.trueOrigin: H. L. Mencken, essay 'The Divine Afflatus' (1917).
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates under several management names including Drucker, but QI traces it to H. L. Mencken's 1917 essay.

candidates.quote: Atheism is a disease of the soul, before it becomes an error of the understanding.
candidates.trueOrigin: William Fleming, as quoted in Samuel Austin Allibone's 'Prose Quotations from Socrates to Macaulay'; not Plato's words.
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-cited 'Plato' line in religious debate; Wikiquote identifies the real author as 19th-century writer William Fleming.

candidates.quote: Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.
candidates.trueOrigin: Scottish author Ian Maclaren (pen name of Rev. John Watson), c. 1897-1898; original phrasing used 'Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared feel-good lines pinned on Plato; both Wikiquote and QI trace it to a late-1890s Scottish preacher, ~2,400 years after Plato.

candidates.quote: Music is a moral law. It gives soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and charm and gaiety to life and to everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: Does not appear in Plato; first attributed to him in John Lubbock's 'The Pleasures of Life, Part II' (1889).
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved 'Plato' music quote plastered across posters and album notes; Wikiquote traces the attribution to an 1889 Lubbock book.

candidates.quote: Necessity is the mother of invention.
candidates.trueOrigin: An English proverb read into Benjamin Jowett's flowery Victorian translation of Republic II 369c; Plato's literal text is only 'our need will be the real creator.'
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous proverb credited to Plato only via Jowett's loose translation; Wikiquote documents the literal Greek says no such thing.

candidates.quote: Only the dead have seen the end of war.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Santayana, 'Soliloquies in England' (1922); no source in Plato exists. Popularized as 'Plato' by a 1990s film and a Ridley Scott quote.
candidates.whyNotable: Famously misattributed to Plato (even carved as such at Imperial War Museum); Wikiquote flags the real author as Santayana.

candidates.quote: You can discover more about a person in an hour of play than in a year of conversation.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase of Richard Lingard's 1670 'A Letter of Advice to a Young Gentleman,' which read 'you will then learn more of him in one hour, than in seven years conversation.'
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely-shared 'Plato' line QI debunks, tracing it to a 1670 English advice pamphlet with no connection to Plato.

candidates.quote: The man who grasps principles can successfully select his own methods. The man who tries methods, ignoring principles, is sure to have trouble.
candidates.trueOrigin: Harrington Emerson, The Twelve Principles of Efficiency (1912)
candidates.whyNotable: A classic name-collision misattribution: QI shows it was written by efficiency engineer Harrington Emerson, whom the fame of Ralph Waldo Emerson eclipsed.

candidates.quote: To laugh often and much; to win the respect of intelligent people and the affection of children... to know even one life has breathed easier because you have lived. This is to have succeeded.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bessie Anderson Stanley, 'What is Success?' in Heart Throbs Volume Two (1911)
candidates.whyNotable: The ubiquitous 'What is Success?' poem pinned on Emerson across the internet; Wikiquote credits Bessie Anderson Stanley's 1911 essay in Heart Throbs, Volume Two.

candidates.quote: An acre of performance is worth a whole world of promise
candidates.trueOrigin: James Howell, British historian, 1655 (in his published collection of familiar letters); later also misattributed to William Dean Howells via name confusion.
candidates.whyNotable: Several 2006 Auerbach remembrance pieces credited this line to him, but QI shows he only borrowed it; the phrase originated with British historian James Howell in 1655 ('An acre of performance is worth the whole Land of promise').

candidates.quote: Sometimes I sits and thinks, and sometimes I just sits.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI traces it to an anonymous Maine fisherman quoted in February 1905 (via the Boston Record); the Paige credit is a retroactive 2009 newspaper misattribution. Also misattributed to A. A. Milne and Lucy Maud Montgomery.
candidates.whyNotable: A folksy line frequently credited to Paige, but QI documents it circulating from a 1905 Maine fisherman decades before Paige was famous.

candidates.quote: If you wish to be loved, love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Seneca does quote 'Si vis amari, ama' in Epistulae Morales, Epistle IX, but he explicitly attributes it to Hecato of Rhodes. It is Hecato's line, relayed by Seneca.
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved one-liner pinned on Seneca as its author; Wikiquote's Misattributed section notes Seneca himself credited Hecato of Rhodes.

candidates.quote: Religion is regarded by the common people as true, by the wise as false, and by rulers as useful.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source exists in Seneca; the wording derives from Edward Gibbon, 'The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire' Vol. I, Ch. II ('...all considered by the people as equally true; by the philosopher as equally false; and by the magistrate as equally useful'). Elbert Hubbard's 1904 claim that Gibbon was 'freely translating Seneca' seeded the misattribution.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared cynical-about-religion line pinned on Seneca; Wikiquote's Disputed section traces it to Gibbon, not Seneca.

candidates.quote: There is nothing noble in being superior to some other man. The true nobility is in being superior to your previous self.
candidates.trueOrigin: Quote Investigator tentatively credits W. L. Sheldon, a lecturer for the Ethical Society of St. Louis, whose essay 'What to Believe: An Ethical Creed' (April 1897) contains this precise formulation. Also widely misattributed to Ernest Hemingway (from an inauthentic 1963 Playboy piece). Neither Seneca nor Hemingway wrote it.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral self-improvement line split between Seneca and Hemingway; QI reassigns it to ethicist W. L. Sheldon in 1897.

candidates.quote: The mind is like an iceberg, it floats with one-seventh of its bulk above water.
candidates.trueOrigin: Figurative iceberg-of-mind simile traced to Hon. B. G. Northrop, 1884; in wide circulation before Freud received credit.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of psychology classes pinned on Freud, but QI and Wikiquote trace the iceberg simile to B. G. Northrop (1884), predating Freud's credit (1929).

candidates.quote: Know thyself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Delphic maxim (Temple of Apollo at Delphi); Seven Sages of Greece
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly attributed to Socrates but it is the Delphic maxim inscribed at the Temple of Apollo, traditionally ascribed to the Seven Sages (often Solon or Chilon) and predating Socrates.

candidates.quote: Do what you can, with what you've got, where you are.
candidates.trueOrigin: Roosevelt attributed the saying to Bill Widener of Widener's Valley, Virginia, in his 1913 autobiography, calling it 'homely philosophy'; QI notes related earlier phrasings by others. Roosevelt popularized but did not originate it.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous resourcefulness maxim universally credited to TR, but Roosevelt himself disclaimed it in his 1913 autobiography and credited a Virginia neighbor; a textbook case of a real quoter being turned into the author.

candidates.quote: I am much less interested in what is called God's word than in God's deeds.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Burroughs, The Atlantic Monthly (1921).
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated as an Edison quote on religion, but Wikiquote traces it to naturalist John Burroughs writing in The Atlantic Monthly (1921).

candidates.quote: There is no expedient to which a man will not go to avoid the labor of thinking.
candidates.trueOrigin: Sir Joshua Reynolds (18th-century Discourses); Edison merely displayed the line.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Edison because he posted it on placards around his factory, but Wikiquote flags it as originally the words of painter Sir Joshua Reynolds.

candidates.quote: I sincerely believe that banking institutions are more dangerous to our liberties than standing armies.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase compiled from three separate Jefferson letters (1813-1817); the fused wording first appears in 1895
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as a clean Jefferson quote, but Wikiquote shows the popular one-liner is a stitched paraphrase of three separate Jefferson letters (1813-1817), first appearing in this form in 1895.

candidates.quote: The best government is that which governs least.
candidates.trueOrigin: Motto of the United States Magazine and Democratic Review (1837); later quoted by Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: A small-government slogan routinely credited to Jefferson; Wikiquote shows it as the 1837 motto of the United States Magazine and Democratic Review, later used by Thoreau, with no Jefferson source.

candidates.quote: The price of freedom is eternal vigilance.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Philpot Curran, 1790 speech ("The Right of Election of the Lord Mayor of Dublin")
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly attributed to Jefferson but never found in his writings; Wikiquote traces the phrasing to John Philpot Curran's 1790 speech on the right of election.

candidates.quote: When governments fear the people, there is liberty. When the people fear the government, there is tyranny.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Basil Barnhill, in a 1914 published debate (Barnhill vs. Tichenor)
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Jefferson lines on freedom; Wikiquote traces it to John Basil Barnhill's 1914 socialist debate writings, first pinned on Jefferson only in 1945.

candidates.quote: I dream my painting, and then I paint my dream.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot — French original "Je rêve mon tableau, et plus tard je peindrai mon rêve" documented by at least 1908
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'poetic' lines pinned on Van Gogh since the 1990s; Wikiquote traces it to painter Camille Corot, not Van Gogh.

candidates.quote: I would rather die of passion than of boredom.
candidates.trueOrigin: Émile Zola — the character Octave Mouret in Zola's 1883 novel Au Bonheur des Dames ("je préfère crever de passion que de crever d'ennui!"); Van Gogh merely quoted Zola in an Oct. 1884 letter
candidates.whyNotable: Widely captioned to Van Gogh, but QI shows it originated with Émile Zola in 1883 and Van Gogh only quoted it a year later.

candidates.quote: Anything that is too stupid to be spoken is sung
candidates.trueOrigin: Pierre de Beaumarchais, Le Barbier de Seville (1775)
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Voltaire but Wikiquote traces it to Beaumarchais's Le Barbier de Seville (1775): 'what isn't worth saying is sung.'

candidates.quote: I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it
candidates.trueOrigin: Evelyn Beatrice Hall (pen name S. G. Tallentyre), The Friends of Voltaire (1906)
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-cited fake Voltaire line; both Wikiquote and QI trace it to biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall, who coined it in 1906 as a summary of Voltaire's attitude, not a real quote.

candidates.quote: Judge a man by his questions rather than by his answers
candidates.trueOrigin: Pierre-Marc-Gaston, duc de Levis, Maximes et reflexions (1808)
candidates.whyNotable: A popular inspirational line credited to Voltaire that Wikiquote reassigns to the duc de Levis's 1808 Maximes et reflexions.

candidates.quote: Nothing can be more contrary to religion and the clergy than reason and common sense
candidates.trueOrigin: Paul-Henri Thiry, Baron d'Holbach, Theologie portative (1768)
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently shared anti-clerical zinger that Wikiquote attributes instead to Baron d'Holbach's Theologie portative (1768).

candidates.quote: He who has injured thee was either stronger or weaker than thee. If weaker, spare him; if stronger, spare thyself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Seneca the Younger, De Ira (On Anger), Book III, Chapter V.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated as Shakespearean wisdom, but it is actually Stoic philosophy from Seneca the Younger.

candidates.quote: Nothing is more common than the wish to be remarkable.
candidates.trueOrigin: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858).
candidates.whyNotable: Popularized as Shakespeare (notably via the show Criminal Minds) but is actually a line from Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.

candidates.quote: There is plenty of time to sleep in the grave.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase of Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1741-1758) ('There will be sleeping enough in the grave').
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently pinned on Shakespeare, but Wikiquote traces the sentiment to Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack, not any Shakespeare work.

candidates.quote: Time is very slow for those who wait, very fast for those who are scared, very long for those who lament, very short for those who celebrate, but for those who love, time is eternal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rephrasing of Henry van Dyke's sundial verses (Yaddo estate), documented in Alice Morse Earle's Old-Time Gardens (1901).
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular 'Shakespeare' meditation on time and love; QI finds no Shakespeare support and traces it to a sundial verse by Henry van Dyke.

candidates.quote: When I saw you I fell in love, and you smiled because you knew.
candidates.trueOrigin: Arrigo Boito, libretto for Verdi's opera Falstaff (1893), sung by Fenton ('Come ti vidi / M'innamorai...').
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared romantic 'Shakespeare' (often 'Romeo and Juliet') lines online; QI traces it to Arrigo Boito's libretto for Verdi's 1893 opera Falstaff.

candidates.quote: You have enemies? Good. That means you've stood up for something, sometime in your life
candidates.trueOrigin: Victor Hugo, 'Villemain' (1845), from his journal Choses Vues.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared empowerment quote that is actually Victor Hugo's, from his 1845 essay 'Villemain' in Choses Vues.

candidates.quote: Always go to other people's funerals; otherwise they won't go to yours.
candidates.trueOrigin: Appeared in Punch magazine, January 1911 or earlier
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as a Berra witticism, but Wikiquote traces the joke to Punch magazine (1911 or earlier), long before it was ever pinned on Berra.

candidates.quote: Never answer an anonymous letter.
candidates.trueOrigin: A 19th-century joke predating Berra
candidates.whyNotable: A commonly repeated Yogi-ism, but Wikiquote dates the joke to the 19th century; Berra initially denied it before later embracing the attribution.

candidates.quote: Nobody goes there anymore. It's too crowded.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous joke in early-20th-century newspapers; assigned to Berra in 1962
candidates.whyNotable: A classic paradox routinely credited to Berra, but QI documents the gag in early-20th-century newspapers, with the attribution to Berra only appearing in 1962.

candidates.quote: Duty makes us do things well, but love makes us do them beautifully.
candidates.trueOrigin: Phillips Brooks (d. 1893), as documented in 'Primary Education' (1916).
candidates.whyNotable: Listed in Wikiquote's Misattributed section for Ziglar; the line actually originates with 19th-century clergyman Phillips Brooks.

candidates.quote: If you live to be a hundred, I want to live to be a hundred minus one day, so I never have to live without you.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Milne source; the 'live forever less a day' sentiment predates and is separate from Pooh, variously credited to Tom Phillips, Walter Kerr and Jack Valenti.
candidates.whyNotable: A wildly popular sentimental 'Pooh' line printed on cards and mugs; QI finds no evidence Milne wrote it and traces the sentiment to unrelated later sources.

candidates.quote: People say nothing is impossible, but I do nothing every day.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; an anonymous modern gag retrofitted onto Winnie-the-Pooh with no source in Milne.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous 'lazy Pooh' joke image-macro; QI found no substantive evidence Milne or the Pooh books ever used it and marks it apocryphal.

candidates.quote: Folks are usually about as happy as they make up their minds to be.
candidates.trueOrigin: No substantive evidence Lincoln used the expression; QI's earliest matches are 20th-century and unconnected to Lincoln.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous feel-good line pinned on Lincoln across social media; QI found no support for the attribution.

candidates.quote: Give me six hours to chop down a tree and I will spend the first four sharpening the axe.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Lincoln said it; QI finds the 'sharpen the axe' preparation proverb only much later and unlinked to Lincoln.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of productivity and leadership decks; QI shows the vivid Lincoln version has no 19th-century basis.

candidates.quote: I destroy my enemies when I make them my friends.
candidates.trueOrigin: No substantive evidence Lincoln said it; QI traces the sentiment to much earlier sources with no Lincoln connection.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as Lincoln wisdom (and quoted in speeches); QI found no contemporaneous evidence tying it to him.

candidates.quote: Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn't, pays it
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous advertising copy (1920s bank ads); Einstein attribution first appears 1988.
candidates.whyNotable: The finance world's favorite fake Einstein line; QI finds no evidence Einstein, Rothschild, or Rockefeller ever said it and traces the 'eighth wonder' label for compound interest to anonymous 1920s bank advertising, first pinned on Einstein by a financial analyst in 1988.

candidates.quote: Everybody is a genius. But if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, it will live its whole life believing that it is stupid
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; earliest attribution ~2004 self-help writing, allegory predates Einstein by decades.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral education/self-esteem meme; QI finds no Einstein source and traces the earliest close match to ~2004 (Matthew Kelly's self-help book 'The Rhythm of Life'), with the fish-and-tree allegory circulating among educators for over a century.

candidates.quote: If the bee disappeared off the surface of the globe, man would have only four years left to live
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; earliest appearance a 1994 beekeepers' protest pamphlet in Brussels.
candidates.whyNotable: An environmentalist rallying cry falsely credited to Einstein; Snopes finds no such statement in any Einstein compilation and traces it to a 1994 Brussels beekeepers' protest pamphlet, listed under 'Probably not by Einstein' in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

candidates.quote: If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; no Einstein source, commonly reassigned to Richard Feynman or Ernest Rutherford without evidence.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of teaching and startup slide decks; listed among Einstein's misattributed quotes with no evidence he said it, and often traced instead to later figures like Feynman or Rutherford.

candidates.quote: Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities because it is the quality which guarantees all others.
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularized by Winston Churchill (1931); not from Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: Often attributed to Aristotle in leadership circles; Quote Investigator finds the ascription unsupported, with the phrasing tied to Winston Churchill (1931) and later writers.

candidates.quote: Tell 'em what you're going to tell 'em; next, tell 'em; next, tell 'em what you told 'em.
candidates.trueOrigin: 20th-century public-speaking lore; not traceable to Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: A public-speaking maxim routinely credited to Aristotle's Rhetoric; Quote Investigator finds the ascription unsupported and points to 20th-century speech instructors.

candidates.quote: The place where your talent meets the world's needs is the job God has in mind for you.
candidates.trueOrigin: 20th-century origin (linked to Marcus Bach / Albert Schweitzer paraphrases); not Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'find your calling' quote credited to Aristotle; Quote Investigator finds no support for the Aristotle ascription and points to 20th-century sources like Marcus Bach.

candidates.quote: The worst form of inequality is to try to make unequal things equal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Condensed by Laurence J. Peter (Peter's People, 1979); loose gloss on Politics III.V.8
candidates.whyNotable: A political-meme staple; Wikiquote traces the condensed 'Aristotle's Axiom' wording to Laurence J. Peter's 1979 Peter's People via a 1916 Treitschke translation, only loosely based on Politics III.V.8.

candidates.quote: Tolerance and apathy are the last virtues of a dying society.
candidates.trueOrigin: No known source; not in any extant Aristotle work
candidates.whyNotable: A viral culture-war line pinned on Aristotle; Wikiquote states it is not found in any extant work of Aristotle.

candidates.quote: Elementary, my dear Watson
candidates.trueOrigin: Not written by Conan Doyle. Wikiquote's Misattributed section states the complete phrase "does not appear in any of the 60 Holmes stories written by Doyle"; the closest is The Crooked Man (1893), where "Elementary" and "my dear Watson" sit a paragraph apart and in the wrong order. The exact phrase was already a press cliche before any film: Quote Investigator traces a Holmes parody in The Northampton Mercury (1901, "Elementary, my dear Potson"), the exact wording in The Globe (1908), and frequent newspaper use 1909-1913. It appears in ch. 19 of P. G. Wodehouse's novel Psmith, Journalist (1915). First screen use is the 1929 Paramount film The Return of Sherlock Holmes (the first Holmes sound film), written by Basil Dean and Garrett Fort, spoken by Clive Brook as "Elementary, my dear Watson, elementary"; it recurs in the 1935 film The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes. Wikiquote's page for THIS 1939 film (20th Century Fox; dir. Alfred L. Werker; written by Edwin Blum and William A. Drake, partially based on William Gillette's 1899 stage play) lists the line among Basil Rathbone's Holmes lines, but the 1939 film did NOT originate it — it inherited a phrase already ~30 years old in print and 10 years old on screen.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most famous line the public believes it read in the Sherlock Holmes stories, and it is in none of them. Two error classes stack: (1) the wrong-source error — it is pinned on Conan Doyle, who never wrote it; (2) the origination error this site exists to correct — popular film writing routinely credits the 1939 film / Basil Rathbone with coining it (one mainstream source states it was "first uttered by Basil Rathbone" here), which both authorities contradict. Even the 1929 film did not coin it: the New York Times review noted audiences already knew the phrase. Corroborated by Snopes (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/elementary-my-dear-watson/). QI: https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/07/14/watson/

candidates.quote: Anyone who doesn't believe in miracles is not a realist.
candidates.trueOrigin: David Ben-Gurion, first Prime Minister of Israel, as cited in "Psychosocial Care of the Dying Patient" (1978); Wikiquote reassigns it to him.
candidates.whyNotable: Commonly circulated as a Hepburn line; Wikiquote reassigns it to David Ben-Gurion.

candidates.quote: Happy girls are the prettiest.
candidates.trueOrigin: A fragment of the post-2007 "I believe in pink" internet passage that Wikiquote lists as misattributed; no lifetime Hepburn source exists.
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily shared as a standalone Hepburn line, but it is lifted from the same fabricated "I believe in pink" passage Wikiquote debunks.

candidates.quote: I believe in pink. I believe that laughing is the best calorie burner. I believe in kissing, kissing a lot. I believe in being strong when everything seems to be going wrong. I believe that happy girls are the prettiest girls. I believe that tomorrow is another day and I believe in miracles.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Hepburn ever said or wrote it; Wikiquote traces the earliest documented appearance to an unidentified MySpace member circa 2007-08, well after her 1993 death, before it was pinned on her in outlets like Glamour (2012).
candidates.whyNotable: A wildly viral feel-good "I believe in pink" passage; Wikiquote flags it as a post-2007 internet fabrication with no lifetime source.

candidates.quote: Say anything you want. Just spell my name right.
candidates.trueOrigin: Long-running showbiz trope; QI's earliest strong evidence is P. T. Barnum (1888 newspapers), predating the Ruth attribution by decades.
candidates.whyNotable: A publicity catchphrase pinned on Ruth (a 1932 Florida column) that QI reassigns: the earliest strong evidence is P. T. Barnum in 1888, and the line is a widespread trope also credited to Cohan, Mae West and others.

candidates.quote: It's not the will to win but the will to prepare to win that makes the difference.
candidates.trueOrigin: Predates Bryant; QI traces versions to Fielding Yost (1930) and Vernon Law (1965)
candidates.whyNotable: Bryant is the popular attribution, but the formulation circulated in sports decades before him.

candidates.quote: Beer is proof that God loves us and wants us to be happy
candidates.trueOrigin: A misquotation of Franklin's real 1779 letter to Andre Morellet, which praised wine (not beer) as 'a constant proof that God loves us, and loves to see us happy.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Franklin lines on beer coasters and merch; Wikiquote and QI show Franklin actually wrote it about WINE, not beer, in a 1779 letter to the Abbe Morellet.

candidates.quote: By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Franklin said or wrote it in any form.
candidates.whyNotable: An extremely common productivity/motivational quote credited to Franklin; Wikiquote finds no evidence he coined any form of it.

candidates.quote: Democracy is two wolves and a lamb voting on what to have for lunch
candidates.trueOrigin: Not found in Franklin's works; earliest documented uses date to circa 1990 (Gary Strand) and 1992 (Marvin Simkin).
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of libertarian social-media posts falsely branded as Franklin; Wikiquote finds nothing in his writings, with earliest known instances from Usenet-era authors Gary Strand (1990) and Marvin Simkin (1992).

candidates.quote: Tell me and I forget. Teach me and I may remember. Involve me and I learn.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Franklin wrote it; the idea traces to far older proverbs (often linked to the Chinese Xunzi), with the modern three-part wording emerging in the 20th century.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous classroom-poster quote credited to Franklin; QI finds no substantive evidence he crafted it, with the sentiment echoing much older proverbs including the Chinese Xunzi.

candidates.quote: The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Franklin said it; earliest documented forms appear in a 1981 Narcotics Anonymous pamphlet, with an earlier variant from Osho (1975).
candidates.whyNotable: A viral motivational meme pinned interchangeably on Franklin, Einstein, and Twain; Wikiquote finds no evidence for any of them, tracing it to a 1981 Narcotics Anonymous text and an earlier 1975 Osho variant.

candidates.quote: We do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing
candidates.trueOrigin: An anonymous modern rewording of a statement by psychologist G. Stanley Hall in Adolescence (1904); not Franklin's.
candidates.whyNotable: A feel-good aging quote widely attributed to Franklin (and George Bernard Shaw); Wikiquote identifies it as an anonymous modern variant of a line from G. Stanley Hall's 1904 'Adolescence.'

candidates.quote: When the people find that they can vote themselves money, that will herald the end of the republic
candidates.trueOrigin: Unsourced; the same sentiment is separately misattributed to Alexis de Tocqueville and Alexander Fraser Tytler, with no evidence for Franklin.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular political-warning quote pinned on Franklin (and also on Tocqueville and Tytler); Wikiquote finds no evidence any of them wrote it.

candidates.quote: Some people feel the rain. Others just get wet.
candidates.trueOrigin: Most likely Roger Miller (documented on a 1972 ABC TV special)
candidates.whyNotable: Commonly pinned on 'the two famous Bobs' (Marley and Dylan), but Quote Investigator traces the earliest evidence to country singer Roger Miller on a 1972 TV special, with Marley attributions only appearing around 2007.

candidates.quote: The greatness of a man is not in how much wealth he acquires, but in his integrity and his ability to affect those around him positively.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unsourced; no verified origin, surfaced on social media long after Marley's death
candidates.whyNotable: A viral Facebook-era inspirational line credited to Marley that Wikiquote contributors flag as unsourced and unlike his voice, circulating widely only in recent years.

candidates.quote: Truth is, everybody is going to hurt you; you just gotta find the ones worth suffering for.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown internet-era origin; no source before roughly 2001
candidates.whyNotable: One of the single most-shared fake Marley quotes online, yet Wikiquote's talk page notes he never said it and no use can be traced before ~2001, two decades after his death.

candidates.quote: You will never find justice in a world where criminals make the rules.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; no verified source predating the internet attribution
candidates.whyNotable: A protest-sign and social-media staple (also seen as '...where criminals make the laws') that Wikiquote lists as misattributed to Marley with no genuine source.

candidates.quote: Help is the sunny side of control.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous. Earliest documented use 1984 (Robin Norwood, attributing it to an unnamed friend); most influentially popularized by Anne Lamott (2012 Redbook article, 2017 TED talk). Brené Brown attributed it to Lamott in Atlas of the Heart (2021).
candidates.whyNotable: A tidy therapy-speak line pinned on Brené Brown (she used it in Atlas of the Heart crediting Anne Lamott); QI names Brown among its attributees but traces the real origin to no one — first documented 1984 via therapist Robin Norwood crediting an unnamed friend, later popularized by Anne Lamott.

candidates.quote: The perfect way is only difficult for those who pick and choose. Do not like, do not dislike; all will then be clear. Make a hairbreadth difference and heaven and earth are set apart; if you want the truth to stand clear before you, never be for or against. The struggle between 'for' and 'against' is the mind's worst disease.
candidates.trueOrigin: Sengcan (Third Zen Patriarch), Xinxin Ming; the ancient text is public domain but this specific English translation may not be
candidates.whyNotable: Printed in Bruce Lee's own Tao of Jeet Kune Do (1975) and Striking Thoughts (2000) and endlessly quoted as his, but it is a passage from the Xinxin Ming by Sengcan, the Third Chinese Chan (Zen) Patriarch — it entered Lee's books via his personal notes.

candidates.quote: You will continue to suffer if you have an emotional reaction to everything that is said to you. True power is sitting back and observing everything with logic. True power is restraint.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous social-media saying; earliest full documented instance a 2016 tweet, origin unknown
candidates.whyNotable: A massively shared 'stoic wisdom' meme pinned on Bruce Lee (and sometimes Warren Buffett); QI found no evidence either man said it and traces the earliest full instance to a 2016 tweet by Cindy Flores, with fragments circulating anonymously since ~2009.

candidates.quote: Comparison is the thief of joy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Origin unknown; QI located no support for Lewis, Roosevelt, or Twain. Modern phrasing with no verified author.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely viral aphorism variously pinned on Lewis, Theodore Roosevelt, and Mark Twain; Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence for any of them.

candidates.quote: Integrity is doing the right thing, even when no one is watching.
candidates.trueOrigin: Traced to Elsie Robinson's 1943 newspaper column and an unattributed 1965 Journal of Clinical Psychology reference; not in Lewis.
candidates.whyNotable: A wildly popular motivational-poster line pinned on Lewis; Wikiquote finds it nowhere in his works and traces it to Elsie Robinson's 1943 newspaper column.

candidates.quote: Most of the evil in this world is done by people with good intentions.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI documents versions linked to T.S. Eliot and others; no substantive evidence Lewis wrote this exact line.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely circulated as Lewis; Quote Investigator traces the sentiment across T.S. Eliot and others and finds no solid basis for the Lewis ascription.

candidates.quote: You are never too old to set another goal, or to dream a new dream.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary source in Lewis; QI found no substantive supporting evidence. Also credited to motivational speaker Les Brown.
candidates.whyNotable: A graduation-card staple attributed to Lewis with no primary source; both Wikiquote and Quote Investigator find no evidence he wrote it (also credited to Les Brown).

candidates.quote: You can't go back and change the beginning, but you can start where you are and change the ending.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI traces the 'we can make a new ending' family of quotes to sources such as Maria Robinson; no support for a Lewis origin.
candidates.whyNotable: A social-media favorite credited to Lewis; Quote Investigator traces the 'make a new ending' idea to Maria Robinson and others, with no evidence for Lewis.

candidates.quote: You don't have a soul. You are a soul. You have a body.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase of George MacDonald; earliest reference an unsourced 1892 attribution in The British Friend. Not found anywhere in Lewis's writing.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the single most-shared fake C.S. Lewis lines; Wikiquote notes it is falsely pinned on Mere Christianity and actually traces to an 1892 paraphrase of George MacDonald.

candidates.quote: The deep critical thinker has become the misfit of the world. This is not a coincidence. To maintain order and control you must isolate the intellectual, the sage, the philosopher, the savant before their ideas awaken people.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in any of Jung's works; a modern social-media fabrication in Jung's name. Wikiquote lists it as 'Attributed' with no citation.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral anti-establishment 'wake up sheeple' quote-card pinned on Jung with zero basis in his writings; Wikiquote flags it as unsourced.

candidates.quote: There are three types of people: those who make things happen, those who watch things happen, and those who wonder what happened
candidates.trueOrigin: Nicholas Murray Butler, President of Columbia University, in a March 1931 speech at the University of California ('There are the few who make things happen, the many more who watch things happen, and the overwhelming majority who have no notion of what happens')
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared motivational maxim pinned on many names; QI traces it to Butler in 1931 and lists Casey Stengel among the people incorrectly credited.

candidates.quote: A mathematician is a blind man in a dark room looking for a black cat which isn't there.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earlier variants (using a 'black hat') attributed to Lord Bowen and William James; no evidence Darwin ever said it.
candidates.whyNotable: A stock joke about mathematicians (and metaphysicians) falsely pinned on Darwin; QI and Wikiquote trace earlier 'black hat' variants to Lord Bowen and William James.

candidates.quote: I was a young man with uninformed ideas. I threw out queries, suggestions, wondering all the time over everything; and to my astonishment the ideas took like wildfire. People made a religion of them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Invented by the evangelist 'Lady Hope' in a 1915 account; refuted by Darwin's family, who confirmed she was never present during his final illness.
candidates.whyNotable: The centerpiece of the fabricated 'Lady Hope' deathbed-recantation story in which Darwin supposedly disavowed evolution; his daughter Henrietta stated the whole tale 'has no foundation whatever.'

candidates.quote: In the struggle for survival, the fittest win out at the expense of their rivals because they succeed in adapting themselves best to their environment.
candidates.trueOrigin: A summary sentence written by textbook authors Wallbank, Taylor and Bailkey in the 1940s history text 'Civilization Past and Present,' not Darwin's own words.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated for decades as a line from On the Origin of Species; the Darwin Correspondence Project lists it among 'six things Darwin never said.'

candidates.quote: It is not the strongest of the species that survives, nor the most intelligent that survives. It is the one that is most adaptable to change.
candidates.trueOrigin: A 1963 paraphrase of Darwin's ideas by Louisiana State University business professor Leon C. Megginson, later hardened into a fake direct quotation; also misattributed to Clarence Darrow.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Darwin quotes, plastered on corporate slides and motivational posters; QI and the Darwin Correspondence Project confirm Darwin never wrote it.

candidates.quote: The Creator has an inordinate fondness for beetles.
candidates.trueOrigin: Most likely J.B.S. Haldane (exact wording apocryphal; earliest documented version 1959 calls it 'possibly apocryphal'), not Darwin.
candidates.whyNotable: A witty line about the abundance of beetle species frequently pinned on Darwin the famous beetle collector; QI traces it instead to geneticist J.B.S. Haldane.

candidates.quote: Before you leave the house, look in the mirror and remove one piece of jewelry.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous fashion adage predating Chanel's attribution; in print by 1949 and attributed to numerous figures.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-repeated Chanel styling maxims; QI found it already circulating as 'an old policy' by 1949 and credited over the years to Gracie Allen, Joan Rivers's mother, and others, with no solid tie to Chanel.

candidates.quote: The secret to creativity is knowing how to hide your sources.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified for Chanel; the saying evolved among multiple 20th-century writers (also widely misattributed to Einstein and C.E.M. Joad).
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'creativity' line pinned interchangeably on Chanel and Albert Einstein; QI found no support for either and traced early variants to other writers, making both attributions spurious.

candidates.quote: A picture is worth a thousand words
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Chinese; popularized by advertising man Fred R. Barnard in the 1920s, later dressed up as a Chinese proverb
candidates.whyNotable: Often billed as an ancient Chinese/Confucius proverb; QI shows the 'Chinese origin' claim is late, weak, and a 1920s ad-man invention.

candidates.quote: The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is now
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous American saying; QI finds no evidence it is a Chinese proverb, earliest use 1967
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly labeled a Confucius/Chinese proverb, but QI finds the creator anonymous and the Chinese attribution weak and late.

candidates.quote: Be who you are and say what you feel, because those who mind don't matter and those who matter don't mind.
candidates.trueOrigin: The 'those who mind don't matter' half traces to Bernard Baruch (popularized 1948) and appears in print as anonymous wisdom as early as 1938; the combined feel-good version pinned on Seuss has no citation in his work.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous 'be yourself' Seuss meme; QI shows the core saying predates Seuss and belongs to Bernard Baruch, with no evidence Seuss ever wrote the combined line.

candidates.quote: You know you're in love when you can't fall asleep because reality is finally better than your dreams.
candidates.trueOrigin: Circulates on social media credited to Seuss with no citation; not found in any Seuss work. Origin unknown.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial romantic-caption fake Seuss line flagged by Wikiquote as attributed to him with no source.

candidates.quote: Great minds discuss ideas; average minds discuss events; small minds discuss people.
candidates.trueOrigin: Precursors predate Roosevelt; the tiered form is linked in QI's analysis to a lineage associated with historian Henry Thomas Buckle (1821-1862), not Eleanor Roosevelt.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular tiered aphorism pinned on Roosevelt, but QI and Wikiquote trace its lineage to earlier sources (associated with historian Henry Thomas Buckle), not to her.

candidates.quote: You wouldn't worry so much about what other people think of you if you realized how seldom they do.
candidates.trueOrigin: Olin Miller, a professional humorist, identified by QI as the most likely originator.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely attributed to Roosevelt, but QI traces the remark to jokesmith Olin Miller, whom it names as the most likely originator.

candidates.quote: For sale: baby shoes, never worn.
candidates.trueOrigin: A six-word story with no connection to Hemingway; near-identical newspaper classified ads ('baby carriage, never used') circulated from 1906, and the 'Hemingway bet at Luchow's' legend was invented decades later (literary agent Peter Miller, 1974; John de Groot's 1989 play 'Papa').
candidates.whyNotable: Hemingway's single most-shared fake quote; QI shows versions predate him to when he was 7 and it was first pinned on him only in 1989, nearly 30 years after his death.

candidates.quote: There is nothing to writing. All you do is sit down at a typewriter and bleed.
candidates.trueOrigin: Traces to sportswriters, not Hemingway: Walter Winchell quoted Red Smith in 1949 ('sit down at the typewriter, open your veins, and bleed'), and Paul Gallico used similar language in 1946.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous 'writer's inspiration' quote the Hemingway Society explicitly disowns as undocumented in anything he wrote or said.

candidates.quote: Most people are not seeking truth; they are searching for comfort in illusions.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in Nietzsche located; origin unknown, likely a modern paraphrase.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular quote-card line flagged by Wikiquote as misattributed with no located source in Nietzsche's works.

candidates.quote: Nobody is more inferior than those who insist on being equal.
candidates.trueOrigin: No genuine Nietzsche source; earliest verifiable appearance is a fictional 'mock interview' by Richard Marshall.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared on social media as Nietzsche; Wikiquote finds the only traceable source is a mock/satirical interview, not Nietzsche.

candidates.quote: They muddy the waters to make them look deep.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Nietzsche in Robert C. Solomon's 'Spirituality for the Skeptic' (2002) with no specific source given.
candidates.whyNotable: A punchy line often credited to Nietzsche; Wikiquote traces the attribution to Robert C. Solomon's 2002 book with no primary Nietzsche source.

candidates.quote: The degree of civilization in a society can be judged by entering its prisons
candidates.trueOrigin: Not present in The House of the Dead; apocryphal, no located source
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly cited as from The House of the Dead, but Wikiquote notes the line does not actually appear in that work.

candidates.quote: Tolerance will reach such a level that intelligent people will be banned from thinking so as not to offend the imbeciles
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified source; unsupported modern fabrication circulated online
candidates.whyNotable: A viral social-media 'prophecy' pinned on Dostoevsky with no verified source in any of his works, per Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: Believe nothing, no matter where you read it or who has said it, not even if I have said it, unless it agrees with your own reason and your own common sense.
candidates.trueOrigin: A distorted paraphrase that actually contradicts the Kalama Sutta it is drawn from; Wikiquote flags it as a bad/spurious translation with no canonical basis.
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'believe nothing... unless it agrees with your reason' quote; Wikiquote shows it is a corrupted rendering that inverts the actual Kalama Sutta.

candidates.quote: England and America are two countries separated by a common language.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not verified in Shaw; QI traces the 'common language' quip through several attributions without a confirmed origin
candidates.whyNotable: A staple 'Shaw wit' line, but QI could not locate it in Shaw's writings or interviews and documents the idea circulating without a solid Shaw source.

candidates.quote: I learned long ago never to wrestle with a pig. You get dirty, and besides, the pig likes it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest documented use credited to Cyrus S. Ching, Time magazine, 1950
candidates.whyNotable: A popular aphorism pinned on Shaw (also on Twain and Lincoln); Wikiquote's earliest solid citation is Cyrus S. Ching in Time (1950), not Shaw.

candidates.quote: If you have an apple and I have an apple and we exchange these apples then you and I will still each have one apple. But if you have an idea and I have an idea and we exchange these ideas, then each of us will have two ideas.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not found in Shaw; Wikiquote notes an early version credited to Charles F. Brannan
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'wisdom' lines pinned on Shaw; Wikiquote reassigns it, with the exchange-of-ideas framing traced to others including Charles F. Brannan, and it does not appear in Shaw's works.

candidates.quote: It is the mark of a truly intelligent person to be moved by statistics.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Shaw; QI documents it drifting onto him, possibly confused with Bertrand Russell
candidates.whyNotable: QI shows the line was reassigned to Shaw by 1981, plausibly via confusion between Bernard Shaw and Bertrand Russell.

candidates.quote: Youth is wasted on the young.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; QI documents anonymous/variant forms from 1931 onward, ascription to Shaw uncertain
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitously credited to Shaw, but QI finds no instance in his writings; the earliest 1931 matches only loosely tie to him and the pithy modern form is unverified.

candidates.quote: Fighting for peace is like screwing for virginity.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous Vietnam-era protest slogan; earliest documented print citation is a protest sign reported in the Omaha Sunday World-Herald, 19 May 1968
candidates.whyNotable: Perhaps the most-quoted 'Carlin' antiwar line; lexicographer Barry Popik documents it as an anonymous 1968 picket-sign slogan with no evidence of any Carlin routine.

candidates.quote: Never argue with an idiot. They drag you down to their level and beat you with experience.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous, evolved from 1878 newspaper phrasings; strongest single claim is Jean Cocteau (credited by Yul Brynner, 1956). Twain attribution also refuted by scholar Matt Seybold.
candidates.whyNotable: A double-magnet quote pinned on both Twain and Carlin; QI calls the Carlin credit spurious and traces the idea back through Proverbs 26:4 and 19th-century newspapers.

candidates.quote: Never underestimate the power of stupid people in large groups.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; complete form printed in the Minneapolis Morning Tribune, 28 April 1959, author unknown
candidates.whyNotable: A staple Carlin meme, but QI finds no substantive evidence he ever said it — the line was circulating in US newspapers forty years before the 2000 attribution to him.

candidates.quote: People sleep peaceably in their beds at night only because rough men stand ready to do violence on their behalf.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Orwell. The earliest known formulation is a 1993 Washington Times column by film critic Richard Grenier, who was paraphrasing (not quoting) Orwell's ideas on pacifism from 'Notes on Nationalism' and his Kipling essay; later writers wrapped the paraphrase in quotation marks and pinned it on Orwell.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Orwell lines; QI traces it to a 1993 Grenier paraphrase that was mistaken for a direct quotation.

candidates.quote: The further a society drifts from truth, the more it will hate those who speak it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Orwell. It appeared unattributed in a May 2009 opinion piece by Selwyn Duke and was first pinned on Orwell online around February 2011; there is no Orwell source.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral social-media 'Orwell' line that Wikiquote traces to a 2009 Selwyn Duke op-ed, not Orwell.

candidates.quote: There are some ideas so absurd that only an intellectual could believe them.
candidates.trueOrigin: A garbled paraphrase. Orwell's genuine line (from 'Notes on Nationalism', 1945) is 'One has to belong to the intelligentsia to believe things like that: no ordinary man could be such a fool.' The popular 'only an intellectual could believe them' wording is often also attributed to Bertrand Russell.
candidates.whyNotable: A punchier rewrite of a real Orwell sentence; QI documents the authentic phrasing and the drift into this snappier misquote.

candidates.quote: To enforce the lies of the present, it is necessary to erase the truths of the past.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not a direct Orwell quote. Attributed to Orwell by Keith Olbermann on MSNBC in 2006; it paraphrases themes from Nineteen Eighty-Four rather than quoting Orwell.
candidates.whyNotable: A cable-news paraphrase of 1984's memory-hole theme that hardened into a fake direct quote.

candidates.quote: Government is not reason, it is not eloquence, it is force; like fire, a troublesome servant and a fearful master.
